## Getting to Know Lean — 1.7. Characters, Strings, and Slices {#fpil-getting-to-know-lean-17-characters-strings-and-slices}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Getting-to-Know-Lean/Characters___-Strings___-and-Slices/

In Lean, strings contain Unicode text.
Specifically, they are sequences of characters, and characters are Unicode code points.
Strings are written in double quotes, and individual characters are written in single quotes.
The type of strings is `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` and the type of characters is `[Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)`.

Strings can be appended with the `++` operator:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "Hello, " ++ "world"
```

```lean
"Hello, world"
```

A character can be added to the end of a string using `[String.push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___push)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [String.push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___push) "Hello" '!'
```

```lean
"Hello!"
```

This function can also be called using the [dot notation]](#fpil-behind-the-scenes) that is used with structure accessors:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "Hello".[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___push) '!'
```

```lean
"Hello!"
```

### 1.7.1. Slices {#fpil-string-slices}

Strings are represented by their UTF-8 encoding as an array of bytes paired with a cached character count.
This means that removing even a single character from a string can result in copying the remaining characters to a new string.

To allow string-processing code to be written from small, composable pieces, many string operations return *string slices*, which are regions of some other string.
String slices have the type `[String.Slice](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___mk)`.
A slice contains a reference to a string along with the start and end positions of the slice, and multiple slices can share the same string.
Operations such as dropping prefixes of strings return slices rather than allocating new strings, and large parts of the string API are also implemented for slices.

Operations that return slices include `String.trimAscii`, which returns a slice that drops leading and trailing space, tab, newline, and carriage return characters from a string; `[String.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___drop)` and `String.dropEnd`, which drop the specified number of characters from the start or end of a string; and `[String.dropWhile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___dropWhile)` and `String.dropEndWhile`, which respectively remove all the characters that match a pattern from the beginning or end of a string.
The patterns used to search in strings are distinct from those used for [pattern matching]](#fpil-pattern-matching); in the string API, they are function arguments that specify characters or specific substrings to match.
The string slice API includes all the slice-producing string functions as well, which makes it possible to write string manipulations as a series of incremental steps without risking intermediate string copying.

This code removes characters from the beginning and end of a string without allocating an intermediate string:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (("small tortoiseshell".[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___drop) 6).[dropEnd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___dropEnd) 5).[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
```

```lean
"tortoise"
```

The function `[String.Slice.copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)` returns a copy of the region of the underlying string that the slice indicates.
The initial call to `[String.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___drop)` returns a slice, and the call to `[String.Slice.dropEnd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___dropEnd)` returns an adjusted slice.
The final call to `[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)` creates a string once more.

Unlike strings, slices do not cache a character count.
Because the UTF-8 encoding of characters may occupy multiple bytes, there's no efficient way to check the length of a string slice.
However, checking whether it is empty can be accomplished with `[String.Slice.isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___isEmpty)`.

### 1.7.2. Matching {#fpil-string-matching}

Functions that match parts of strings, such as `[String.dropWhile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___dropWhile)` and `String.dropEndWhile`, are overloaded.
They can be called with a variety of different *patterns*, each of which matches substrings in its own way.

The pattern can be a character, in which case runs of the character are removed:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "red admiral".dropEndWhile 'l'
```

```lean
red admira
```

The output is not in quotes because it is a string slice, and string slices are displayed without surrounding quotes.
The pattern may also be a string, in which case runs of the complete string are removed:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "the the butterfly".[dropWhile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___dropWhile) "the "
```

```lean
butterfly
```

Incomplete matches are not removed:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("a gray grayling".[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___drop) 2).[dropWhile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___dropWhile) "gray "
```

```lean
grayling
```

The pattern may also be a function that returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` or `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Characters are removed until the function returns `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
The slice is converted to a string in order to illustrate that the trailing space remains:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("red admiral".dropEndWhile [Char.isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha)).[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
```

```lean
"red "
```

### 1.7.3. Messages You May Meet {#fpil-string-messages-you-may-meet}

The overloaded string-matching functions are implemented using features that are explained later in the book, namely [type classes](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/#type-classes) and [dependent types](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/#dependent-types).
There are two error messages in particular that are useful to learn to read before learning about those features of Lean.

Calling the functions without a pattern results in an error:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "red admiral".dropEndWhile
```

```lean
don't know how to synthesize implicit argument `ρ`
  @String.dropEndWhile ?m.2 "red admiral"
context:
⊢ Type
```

This error is stating that Lean can't determine which pattern type to use, because no pattern was provided.
It can be fixed by providing a pattern.

When the functions are called with an argument that isn't a valid pattern, there is a compile-time error:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) "12345abcde".dropEndWhile [12]
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [String.Slice.Pattern.BackwardPattern](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___Pattern___BackwardPattern___mk) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)12[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

This error message means that `String.dropEndWhile` is not overloaded for the pattern `[12]`.
It can be fixed by providing a meaningful pattern, such as a function, character, or string.

---



## Getting to Know Lean — 1.8. Additional Conveniences {#fpil-getting-to-know-lean-18-additional-conveniences}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Getting-to-Know-Lean/Additional-Conveniences/

Lean contains a number of convenience features that make programs much more concise.

### 1.8.1. Automatic Implicit Parameters {#fpil-automatic-implicit-parameters}

When writing polymorphic functions in Lean, it is typically not necessary to list all the implicit parameters.
Instead, they can simply be mentioned.
If Lean can determine their type, then they are automatically inserted as implicit parameters.
In other words, the previous definition of `length`:

```lean
def length {α : Type} (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => 0
| y :: ys => [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (length ys)
```

can be written without `{α : Type}`:

```lean
def length (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => 0
| y :: ys => [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (length ys)
```

This can greatly simplify highly polymorphic definitions that take many implicit parameters.

### 1.8.2. Pattern-Matching Definitions {#fpil-pattern-matching-definitions}

When defining functions with `def`, it is quite common to name an argument and then immediately use it with pattern matching.
For instance, in `length`, the argument `xs` is used only in `match`.
In these situations, the cases of the `match` expression can be written directly, without naming the argument at all.

The first step is to move the arguments' types to the right of the colon, so the return type is a function type.
For instance, the type of `length` is `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Then, replace the `:=` with each case of the pattern match:

```lean
def length : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => 0
| y :: ys => [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (length ys)
```

This syntax can also be used to define functions that take more than one argument.
In this case, their patterns are separated by commas.
For instance, `drop` takes a number `n` and a list, and returns the list after removing the first `n` entries.

```lean
def drop : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
| [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), xs => xs
| _, [] => []
| [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n, x :: xs => drop n xs
```

Named arguments and patterns can also be used in the same definition.
For instance, a function that takes a default value and an optional value, and returns the default when the optional value is `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, can be written:

```lean
def fromOption (default : α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α → α
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => default
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => x
```

This function is called `[Option.getD](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___getD)` in the standard library, and can be called with dot notation:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "salmonberry").[getD](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___getD) ""
```

```lean
"salmonberry"
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none).[getD](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___getD) ""
```

```lean
""
```

### 1.8.3. Local Definitions {#fpil-local-definitions}

It is often useful to name intermediate steps in a computation.
In many cases, intermediate values represent useful concepts all on their own, and naming them explicitly can make the program easier to read.
In other cases, the intermediate value is used more than once.
As in most other languages, writing down the same code twice in Lean causes it to be computed twice, while saving the result in a variable leads to the result of the computation being saved and re-used.

For instance, `unzip` is a function that transforms a list of pairs into a pair of lists.
When the list of pairs is empty, then the result of `unzip` is a pair of empty lists.
When the list of pairs has a pair at its head, then the two fields of the pair are added to the result of unzipping the rest of the list.
This definition of `unzip` follows that description exactly:

```lean
def unzip : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
(x :: (unzip xys).[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), y :: (unzip xys).[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

Unfortunately, there is a problem: this code is slower than it needs to be.
Each entry in the list of pairs leads to two recursive calls, which makes this function take exponential time.
However, both recursive calls will have the same result, so there is no reason to make the recursive call twice.

In Lean, the result of the recursive call can be named, and thus saved, using `let`.
Local definitions with `let` resemble top-level definitions with `def`: it takes a name to be locally defined, arguments if desired, a type signature, and then a body following `:=`.
After the local definition, the expression in which the local definition is available (called the *body* of the `let`-expression) must be on a new line, starting at a column in the file that is less than or equal to that of the `let` keyword.
A local definition with `let` in `unzip` looks like this:

```lean
def unzip : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
let unzipped : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β := unzip xys
(x :: unzipped.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), y :: unzipped.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

To use `let` on a single line, separate the local definition from the body with a semicolon.

Local definitions with `let` may also use pattern matching when one pattern is enough to match all cases of a datatype.
In the case of `unzip`, the result of the recursive call is a pair.
Because pairs have only a single constructor, the name `unzipped` can be replaced with a pair pattern:

```lean
def unzip : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
let (xs, ys) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β := [unzip]](#fpil-WithPattern___unzip) xys
(x :: xs, y :: ys)
```

Judicious use of patterns with `let` can make code easier to read, compared to writing the accessor calls by hand.

The biggest difference between `let` and `def` is that recursive `let` definitions must be explicitly indicated by writing `let rec`.
For instance, one way to reverse a list involves a recursive helper function, as in this definition:

```lean
def reverse (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
let rec helper : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
| [], soFar => soFar
| y :: ys, soFar => [helper]](#fpil-reverse___helper) ys (y :: soFar)
[helper]](#fpil-reverse___helper) xs []
```

The helper function walks down the input list, moving one entry at a time over to `soFar`.
When it reaches the end of the input list, `soFar` contains a reversed version of the input.

### 1.8.4. Type Inference {#fpil-type-inference}

In many situations, Lean can automatically determine an expression's type.
In these cases, explicit types may be omitted from both top-level definitions (with `def`) and local definitions (with `let`).
For example, the recursive call to `unzip` does not need an annotation:

```lean
def unzip : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
let unzipped := unzip xys
(x :: unzipped.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), y :: unzipped.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

As a rule of thumb, omitting the types of literal values (like strings and numbers) usually works, although Lean may pick a type for literal numbers that is more specific than the intended type.
Lean can usually determine a type for a function application, because it already knows the argument types and the return type.
Omitting return types for function definitions will often work, but function parameters typically require annotations.
Definitions that are not functions, like `unzipped` in the example, do not need type annotations if their bodies do not need type annotations, and the body of this definition is a function application.

Omitting the return type for `unzip` is possible when using an explicit `match` expression:

```lean
def unzip (pairs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β)) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) pairs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
let unzipped := unzip xys
(x :: unzipped.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), y :: unzipped.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

Generally speaking, it is a good idea to err on the side of too many, rather than too few, type annotations.
First off, explicit types communicate assumptions about the code to readers.
Even if Lean can determine the type on its own, it can still be easier to read code without having to repeatedly query Lean for type information.
Secondly, explicit types help localize errors.
The more explicit a program is about its types, the more informative the error messages can be.
This is especially important in a language like Lean that has a very expressive type system.
Thirdly, explicit types make it easier to write the program in the first place.
The type is a specification, and the compiler's feedback can be a helpful tool in writing a program that meets the specification.
Finally, Lean's type inference is a best-effort system.
Because Lean's type system is so expressive, there is no “best” or most general type to find for all expressions.
This means that even if you get a type, there's no guarantee that it's the *right* type for a given application.
For instance, `14` can be a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` or an `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) 14
```

```lean
14 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (14 : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat))
```

```lean
14 : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

Missing type annotations can give confusing error messages.
Omitting all types from the definition of `unzip`:

```lean
def unzip pairs :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) pairs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => ([], [])
| (x, y) :: xys =>
let unzipped := unzip xys
(x :: unzipped.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk), y :: unzipped.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

leads to a message about the `match` expression:

```lean
Invalid match expression: This pattern contains metavariables:
  [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

This is because `match` needs to know the type of the value being inspected, but that type was not available.
A “metavariable” is an unknown part of a program, written `?m.XYZ` in error messages—they are described in the [section on Polymorphism]](#fpil-polymorphism).
In this program, the type annotation on the argument is required.

Even some very simple programs require type annotations.
For instance, the identity function just returns whatever argument it is passed.
With argument and type annotations, it looks like this:

```lean
def id (x : α) : α := x
```

Lean is capable of determining the return type on its own:

```lean
def id (x : α) := x
```

Omitting the argument type, however, causes an error:

```lean
def id x := x
```

```lean
Failed to infer type of binder `x`
```

In general, messages that say something like “failed to infer” or that mention metavariables are often a sign that more type annotations are necessary.
Especially while still learning Lean, it is useful to provide most types explicitly.

### 1.8.5. Simultaneous Matching {#fpil-simultaneous-matching}

Pattern-matching expressions, just like pattern-matching definitions, can match on multiple values at once.
Both the expressions to be inspected and the patterns that they match against are written with commas between them, similarly to the syntax used for definitions.
Here is a version of `drop` that uses simultaneous matching:

```lean
def drop (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n, xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), ys => ys
| _, [] => []
| [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n , y :: ys => drop n ys
```

Simultaneous matching resembles matching on a pair, but there is an important difference.
Lean tracks the connection between the expression being matched and the patterns, and this information is used for purposes that include checking for termination and propagating static type information.
As a result, the version of `sameLength` that matches a pair is rejected by the termination checker, because the connection between `xs` and `x :: xs'` is obscured by the intervening pair:

```lean
def sameLength (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) (xs, ys) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ([], []) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| (x :: xs', y :: ys') => sameLength xs' ys'
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
fail to show termination for
  sameLength
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Not considering parameter α of sameLength:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
Not considering parameter β of sameLength:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
Cannot use parameter xs:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    sameLength xs' ys'
Cannot use parameter ys:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    sameLength xs' ys'


Could not find a decreasing measure.
The basic measures relate at each recursive call as follows:
(<, ≤, =: relation proved, ? all proofs failed, _: no proof attempted)
              xs ys
1) 1816:28-46  ?  ?
Please use `termination_by` to specify a decreasing measure.
```

Simultaneously matching both lists is accepted:

```lean
def sameLength (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs, ys [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [], [] => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| x :: xs', y :: ys' => [sameLength]](#fpil-Both___sameLength) xs' ys'
| _, _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

### 1.8.6. Natural Number Patterns {#fpil-natural-number-patterns}

In the section on [datatypes and patterns]](#fpil-datatypes-and-patterns), `even` was defined like this:

```lean
def even (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) k => [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) (even k)
```

Just as there is special syntax to make list patterns more readable than using `[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` and `[List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` directly, natural numbers can be matched using literal numbers and `+`.
For example, `even` can also be defined like this:

```lean
def even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| n + 1 => [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) (even n)
```

In this notation, the arguments to the `+` pattern serve different roles.
Behind the scenes, the left argument (`n` above) becomes an argument to some number of `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` patterns, and the right argument (`1` above) determines how many `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s to wrap around the pattern.
The explicit patterns in `halve`, which divides a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` by two and drops the remainder:

```lean
def halve : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => 0
| [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => 0
| [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n) => halve n + 1
```

can be replaced by numeric literals and `+`:

```lean
def halve : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => 0
| 1 => 0
| n + 2 => [halve]](#fpil-Match___halve) n + 1
```

Behind the scenes, both definitions are completely equivalent.
Remember: `[halve]](#fpil-Match___halve) n + 1` is equivalent to `([halve]](#fpil-Match___halve) n) + 1`, not `[halve]](#fpil-Match___halve) (n + 1)`.

When using this syntax, the second argument to `+` should always be a literal `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Even though addition is commutative, flipping the arguments in a pattern can result in errors like the following:

```lean
def halve : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => 0
| 1 => 0
| 2 + n => halve n + 1
```

```lean
Invalid pattern(s): `n` is an explicit pattern variable, but it only occurs in positions that are inaccessible to pattern matching:
  .([Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 2 n)
```

This restriction enables Lean to transform all uses of the `+` notation in a pattern into uses of the underlying `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, keeping the language simpler behind the scenes.

### 1.8.7. Anonymous Functions {#fpil-anonymous-functions}

Functions in Lean need not be defined at the top level.
As expressions, functions are produced with the `fun` syntax.
Function expressions begin with the keyword `fun`, followed by one or more parameters, which are separated from the return expression using `=>`.
For instance, a function that adds one to a number can be written:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x => x + 1
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Type annotations are written the same way as on `def`, using parentheses and colons:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun (x : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) => x + 1
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

Similarly, implicit parameters may be written with curly braces:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun {α : Type} (x : α) => x
```

```lean
fun {α} x => x : {α : Type} → α → α
```

This style of anonymous function expression is often referred to as a *lambda expression*, because the typical notation used in mathematical descriptions of programming languages uses the Greek letter λ (lambda) where Lean has the keyword `fun`.
Even though Lean does permit `λ` to be used instead of `fun`, it is most common to write `fun`.

Anonymous functions also support the multiple-pattern style used in `def`.
For instance, a function that returns the predecessor of a natural number if it exists can be written:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun
| 0 => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| n + 1 => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n
```

```lean
fun x =>
  match x with
  | 0 => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
  | n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Note that Lean's own description of the function has a named argument and a `match` expression.
Many of Lean's convenient syntactic shorthands are expanded to simpler syntax behind the scenes, and the abstraction sometimes leaks.

Definitions using `def` that take arguments may be rewritten as function expressions.
For instance, a function that doubles its argument can be written as follows:

```lean
def double : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := fun
| 0 => 0
| k + 1 => [double]](#fpil-Double___double) k + 2
```

When an anonymous function is very simple, like `fun x => x + 1`, the syntax for creating the function can be fairly verbose.
In that particular example, six non-whitespace characters are used to introduce the function, and its body consists of only three non-whitespace characters.
For these simple cases, Lean provides a shorthand.
In an expression surrounded by parentheses, a centered dot character `·` can stand for a parameter, and the expression inside the parentheses becomes the function's body.
That particular function can also be written `(· + 1)`.

The centered dot always creates a function out of the *closest* surrounding set of parentheses.
For instance, `(· + 5, 3)` is a function that returns a pair of numbers, while `((· + 5), 3)` is a pair of a function and a number.
If multiple dots are used, then they become parameters from left to right:

```lean
(· , ·) 1 2
```

```lean
(1, ·) 2
```

```lean
(1, 2)
```

Anonymous functions can be applied in precisely the same way as functions defined using `def` or `let`.
The command `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (fun x => x + x) 5` results in:

```lean
10
```

while `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (· * 2) 5` results in:

```lean
10
```

### 1.8.8. Namespaces {#fpil-namespaces}

Each name in Lean occurs in a *namespace*, which is a collection of names.
Names are placed in namespaces using `.`, so `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` is the name `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` in the `List` namespace.
Names in different namespaces do not conflict with each other, even if they are otherwise identical.
This means that `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` and `[Array.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___map)` are different names.
Namespaces may be nested, so `Project.Frontend.User.loginTime` is the name `loginTime` in the nested namespace `Project.Frontend.User`.

Names can be directly defined within a namespace.
For instance, the name `[double]](#fpil-Nat___double)` can be defined in the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` namespace:

```lean
def Nat.double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := x + x
```

Because `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is also the name of a type, dot notation is available to call `[Nat.double]](#fpil-Nat___double)` on expressions with type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (4 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)).[double]](#fpil-Nat___double)
```

```lean
8
```

In addition to defining names directly in a namespace, a sequence of declarations can be placed in a namespace using the `namespace` and `end` commands.
For instance, this defines `triple` and `quadruple` in the namespace `NewNamespace`:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) NewNamespace
def triple (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 3 * x
def quadruple (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 2 * x + 2 * x
end NewNamespace
```

To refer to them, prefix their names with `NewNamespace.`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) NewNamespace.triple
```

```lean
NewNamespace.triple (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) NewNamespace.quadruple
```

```lean
NewNamespace.quadruple (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Namespaces may be *opened*, which allows the names in them to be used without explicit qualification.
Writing `open` `MyNamespace ``in` before an expression causes the contents of `MyNamespace` to be available in the expression.
For example, `timesTwelve` uses both `quadruple` and `triple` after opening `NewNamespace`:

```lean
def timesTwelve (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
open NewNamespace in
quadruple (triple x)
```

Namespaces can also be opened prior to a command.
This allows all parts of the command to refer to the contents of the namespace, rather than just a single expression.
To do this, place the `open`﻿` ... ``in` prior to the command.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) NewNamespace [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) quadruple
```

```lean
NewNamespace.quadruple (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Function signatures show the name's full namespace.
Namespaces may additionally be opened for *all* following commands for the rest of the file.
To do this, simply omit the `in` from a top-level usage of `open`.

### 1.8.9. `if let` {#fpil-if-let}

When consuming values that have a sum type, it is often the case that only a single constructor is of interest.
For example, given this type that represents a subset of Markdown inline elements:

```lean
inductive Inline : Type where
| lineBreak
| string : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Inline]](#fpil-Inline)
| emph : [Inline]](#fpil-Inline) → [Inline]](#fpil-Inline)
| strong : [Inline]](#fpil-Inline) → [Inline]](#fpil-Inline)
```

a function that recognizes string elements and extracts their contents can be written:

```lean
def Inline.string? (inline : [Inline]](#fpil-Inline)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) inline [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Inline.string]](#fpil-Inline___string) s => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) s
| _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

An alternative way of writing this function's body uses `if` together with `let`:

```lean
def Inline.string? (inline : [Inline]](#fpil-Inline)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfLet) [let](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfLet) [Inline.string]](#fpil-Inline___string) s := inline [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfLet)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) s
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfLet) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

This is very much like the pattern-matching `let` syntax.
The difference is that it can be used with sum types, because a fallback is provided in the `else` case.
In some contexts, using `if let` instead of `match` can make code easier to read.

### 1.8.10. Positional Structure Arguments {#fpil-positional-structure-arguments}

The [section on structures]](#fpil-structures) presents two ways of constructing structures:

1. The constructor can be called directly, as in `Point.mk 1 2`.
2. Brace notation can be used, as in `{ x := 1, y := 2 }`.

In some contexts, it can be convenient to pass arguments positionally, rather than by name, but without naming the constructor directly.
For instance, defining a variety of similar structure types can help keep domain concepts separate, but the natural way to read the code may treat each of them as being essentially a tuple.
In these contexts, the arguments can be enclosed in angle brackets `⟨` and `⟩`.
A `Point` can be written `⟨1, 2⟩`.
Be careful!
Even though they look like the less-than sign `<` and greater-than sign `>`, these brackets are different.
They can be input using `\<` and `\>`, respectively.

Just as with the brace notation for named constructor arguments, this positional syntax can only be used in a context where Lean can determine the structure's type, either from a type annotation or from other type information in the program.
For instance, `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ⟨1, 2⟩` yields the following error:

```lean
Invalid `⟨...⟩` notation: The expected type of this term could not be determined
```

This error occurs because there is no type information available.
Adding an annotation, such as in `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (⟨1, 2⟩ : Point)`, solves the problem:

```lean
{ x := 1.000000, y := 2.000000 }
```

### 1.8.11. String Interpolation {#fpil-string-interpolation}

In Lean, prefixing a string with `s!` triggers *interpolation*, where expressions contained in curly braces inside the string are replaced with their values.
This is similar to `f`-strings in Python and `$`-prefixed strings in C#.
For instance,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) s!"three fives is {NewNamespace.triple 5}"
```

yields the output

```lean
"three fives is 15"
```

Not all expressions can be interpolated into a string.
For instance, attempting to interpolate a function results in an error.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) s!"three fives is {NewNamespace.triple}"
```

yields the error

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  ToString ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

This is because there is no standard way to convert functions into strings.
Just as the compiler maintains a table that describes how to display the result of evaluating expressions of various types, it maintains a table that describes how to convert values of various types into strings.
The message `failed to synthesize instance` means that the Lean compiler didn't find an entry in this table for the given type.
The chapter on [type classes](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/#type-classes) describes this mechanism in more detail, including the means of adding new entries to the table.

## Getting to Know Lean — 1.9. Summary {#fpil-getting-to-know-lean-19-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Getting-to-Know-Lean/Summary/

### 1.9.1. Evaluating Expressions {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Evaluating-Expressions}

In Lean, computation occurs when expressions are evaluated.
This follows the usual rules of mathematical expressions: sub-expressions are replaced by their values following the usual order of operations, until the entire expression has become a value.
When evaluating an `if` or a `match`, the expressions in the branches are not evaluated until the value of the condition or the match subject has been found.

Once they have been given a value, variables never change.
Similarly to mathematics but unlike most programming languages, Lean variables are simply placeholders for values, rather than addresses to which new values can be written.
Variables' values may come from global definitions with `def`, local definitions with `let`, as named arguments to functions, or from pattern matching.

### 1.9.2. Functions {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Functions}

Functions in Lean are first-class values, meaning that they can be passed as arguments to other functions, saved in variables, and used like any other value.
Every Lean function takes exactly one argument.
To encode a function that takes more than one argument, Lean uses a technique called currying, where providing the first argument returns a function that expects the remaining arguments.
To encode a function that takes no arguments, Lean uses the `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` type, which is the least informative possible argument.

There are three primary ways of creating functions:

1. Anonymous functions are written using `fun`.
   For instance, a function that swaps the fields of a `Point` can be written `fun (point : Point) => { x := point.y, y := point.x : Point }`
2. Very simple anonymous functions are written by placing one or more centered dots `·` inside of parentheses.
   Each centered dot becomes an argument to the function, and the parentheses delimit its body.
   For instance, a function that subtracts one from its argument can be written as `(· - 1)` instead of as `fun x => x - 1`.
3. Functions can be defined using `def` or `let` by adding an argument list or by using pattern-matching notation.

### 1.9.3. Types {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Types}

Lean checks that every expression has a type.
Types, such as `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, `Point`, `{α : Type} → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, and `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) ⊕ ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)))`, describe the values that may eventually be found for an expression.
Like other languages, types in Lean can express lightweight specifications for programs that are checked by the Lean compiler, obviating the need for certain classes of unit test.
Unlike most languages, Lean's types can also express arbitrary mathematics, unifying the worlds of programming and theorem proving.
While using Lean for proving theorems is mostly out of scope for this book, *[Theorem Proving in Lean 4](https://leanprover.github.io/theorem_proving_in_lean4/)* contains more information on this topic.

Some expressions can be given multiple types.
For instance, `3` can be an `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` or a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
In Lean, this should be understood as two separate expressions, one with type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and one with type `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, that happen to be written in the same way, rather than as two different types for the same thing.

Lean is sometimes able to determine types automatically, but types must often be provided by the user.
This is because Lean's type system is so expressive.
Even when Lean can find a type, it may not find the desired type—`3` could be intended to be used as an `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`, but Lean will give it the type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` if there are no further constraints.
In general, it is a good idea to write most types explicitly, only letting Lean fill out the very obvious types.
This improves Lean's error messages and helps make programmer intent more clear.

Some functions or datatypes take types as arguments.
They are called *polymorphic*.
Polymorphism allows programs such as one that calculates the length of a list without caring what type the entries in the list have.
Because types are first class in Lean, polymorphism does not require any special syntax, so types are passed just like other arguments.
Naming an argument in a function type allows later types to mention that name, and when the function is applied to an argument, the type of the resulting term is found by replacing the argument's name with the actual value it was applied to.

### 1.9.4. Structures and Inductive Types {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Structures-and-Inductive-Types}

Brand new datatypes can be introduced to Lean using the `structure` or `inductive` features.
These new types are not considered to be equivalent to any other type, even if their definitions are otherwise identical.
Datatypes have *constructors* that explain the ways in which their values can be constructed, and each constructor takes some number of arguments.
Constructors in Lean are not the same as constructors in object-oriented languages: Lean's constructors are inert holders of data, rather than active code that initializes an allocated object.

Typically, `structure` is used to introduce a product type (that is, a type with just one constructor that takes any number of arguments), while `inductive` is used to introduce a sum type (that is, a type with many distinct constructors).
Datatypes defined with `structure` are provided with one accessor function for each field.
Both structures and inductive datatypes may be consumed with pattern matching, which exposes the values stored inside of constructors using a subset of the syntax used to call said constructors.
Pattern matching means that knowing how to create a value implies knowing how to consume it.

### 1.9.5. Strings and Slices {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Strings-and-Slices}

Strings are sequences of characters, which are themselves Unicode code points.
Their run-time representation consists of an array of bytes in the UTF-8 encoding and a cached character count field.
Because Lean is a pure functional language, operations such as trimming whitespace from strings would normally need to copy them.
This is avoided by having many functions on strings return [string slices]](#fpil---tech-term-string-slices), which pair a reference to a string with starting and ending positions.
Slices can be manipulated by updating these starting and ending positions, avoiding copying.

### 1.9.6. Recursion {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Getting-to-Know-Lean--Summary--Recursion}

A definition is recursive when the name being defined is used in the definition itself.
Because Lean is an interactive theorem prover in addition to being a programming language, there are certain restrictions placed on recursive definitions.
In Lean's logical side, circular definitions could lead to logical inconsistency.

In order to ensure that recursive definitions do not undermine the logical side of Lean, Lean must be able to prove that all recursive functions terminate, no matter what arguments they are called with.
In practice, this means either that recursive calls are all performed on a structurally-smaller piece of the input, which ensures that there is always progress towards a base case, or that users must provide some other evidence that the function always terminates.
Similarly, recursive inductive types are not allowed to have a constructor that takes a function *from* the type as an argument, because this would make it possible to encode non-terminating functions.

## Hello, World! {#fpil-hello-world}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Hello___-World___/

While Lean has been designed to have a rich interactive environment in which programmers can get quite a lot of feedback from the language without leaving the confines of their favorite text editor, it is also a language in which real programs can be written.
This means that it also has a batch-mode compiler, a build system, a package manager, and all the other tools that are necessary for writing programs.

While the [previous chapter]](#fpil-getting-to-know) presented the basics of functional programming in Lean, this chapter explains how to start a programming project, compile it, and run the result.
Programs that run and interact with their environment (e.g. by reading input from standard input or creating files) are difficult to reconcile with the understanding of computation as the evaluation of mathematical expressions.
In addition to a description of the Lean build tools, this chapter also provides a way to think about functional programs that interact with the world.
