## Hello, World! — 2.5. Additional Conveniences {#fpil-hello-world-25-additional-conveniences}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Hello___-World___/Additional-Conveniences/

### 2.5.1. Nested Actions {#fpil-nested-actions}

Many of the functions in `feline` exhibit a repetitive pattern in which an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action's result is given a name, and then used immediately and only once.
For instance, in `dump`:

```lean
partial def dump (stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) [bufsize]](#fpil-bufsize)
if buf.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___isEmpty) then
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
dump stream
```

the pattern occurs for `stdout`:

```lean
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
```

Similarly, `fileStream` contains the following snippet:

```lean
let fileExists ← filename.[pathExists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___pathExists)
if [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) fileExists then
```

When Lean is compiling a `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` block, expressions that consist of a left arrow immediately under parentheses are lifted to the nearest enclosing `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)`, and their results are bound to a unique name.
This unique name replaces the origin of the expression.
This means that `dump` can also be written as follows:

```lean
partial def dump (stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) bufsize
if buf.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___isEmpty) then
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else
(← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)).[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
dump stream
```

This version of `dump` avoids introducing names that are used only once, which can greatly simplify a program.
`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that Lean lifts from a nested expression context are called *nested actions*.

`fileStream` can be simplified using the same technique:

```lean
def fileStream (filename : [System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) (← filename.[pathExists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___pathExists)) then
(← [IO.getStderr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStderr)).[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"File not found: {filename}"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
else
let handle ← [IO.FS.Handle.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Handle___mk) filename [IO.FS.Mode.read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Mode___read)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([IO.FS.Stream.ofHandle](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___ofHandle) handle))
```

In this case, the local name of `handle` could also have been eliminated using nested actions, but the resulting expression would have been long and complicated.
Even though it's often good style to use nested actions, it can still sometimes be helpful to name intermediate results.

It is important to remember, however, that nested actions are only a shorter notation for `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that occur in a surrounding `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` block.
The side effects that are involved in executing them still occur in the same order, and execution of side effects is not interspersed with the evaluation of expressions.
Therefore, nested actions cannot be lifted from the branches of an `if`.

For an example of where this might be confusing, consider the following helper definitions that return data after announcing to the world that they have been executed:

```lean
def getNumA : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
(← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)).[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "A"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 5
```

```lean
def getNumB : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
(← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)).[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "B"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 7
```

These definitions are intended to stand in for more complicated `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` code that might validate user input, read a database, or open a file.

A program that prints `0` when number A is five, or number B otherwise, might be written as follows:

```lean
def test : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (← getNumA) == 5 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (← getNumB)
(← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)).[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"The answer is {a}"
```

This program would be equivalent to:

```lean
def test : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let x ← getNumA
let y ← getNumB
let a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x == 5 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) y
(← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)).[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"The answer is {a}"
```

which runs `getNumB` regardless of whether the result of `getNumA` is equal to `5`.
To prevent this confusion, nested actions are not allowed in an `if` that is not itself a line in the `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)`, and the following error message results:

```lean
Nested action `← getNumB` must be nested inside a `do` expression.
```

### 2.5.2. Flexible Layouts for `do` {#fpil-do-layout-syntax}

In Lean, `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` expressions are whitespace-sensitive.
Each `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action or local binding in the `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` is expected to start on its own line, and they should all have the same indentation.
Almost all uses of `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` should be written this way.
In some rare contexts, however, manual control over whitespace and indentation may be necessary, or it may be convenient to have multiple small actions on a single line.
In these cases, newlines can be replaced with a semicolon and indentation can be replaced with curly braces.

For instance, all of the following programs are equivalent:

```lean
-- This version uses only whitespace-sensitive layout
def main : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "How would you like to be addressed?"
let name := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Hello, {name}!"
```

```lean
-- This version is as explicit as possible
def main : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) {
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin);
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout);
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "How would you like to be addressed?";
let name := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii;
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Hello, {name}!"
}
```

```lean
-- This version uses a semicolon to put two actions on the same line
def main : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin); let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "How would you like to be addressed?"
let name := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Hello, {name}!"
```

Idiomatic Lean code uses curly braces with `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)` very rarely.

### 2.5.3. Running `IO` Actions With `#eval` {#fpil-eval-io}

Lean's `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` command can be used to execute `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions, rather than just evaluating them.
Normally, adding a `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` command to a Lean file causes Lean to evaluate the provided expression, convert the resulting value to a string, and provide that string as a tooltip and in the info window.
Rather than failing because `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions can't be converted to strings, `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` executes them, carrying out their side effects.
If the result of execution is the `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` value `()`, then no result string is shown, but if it is a type that can be converted to a string, then Lean displays the resulting value.

This means that, given the prior definitions of `countdown` and `runActions`,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) runActions (countdown 3)
```

displays

```lean
3
2
1
Blast off!
```

This is the output produced by running the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action, rather than some opaque representation of the action itself.
In other words, for `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions, `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` both *evaluates* the provided expression and *executes* the resulting action value.

Quickly testing `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions with `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` can be much more convenient that compiling and running whole programs.
However, there are some limitations.
For instance, reading from standard input simply returns empty input.
Additionally, the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action is re-executed whenever Lean needs to update the diagnostic information that it provides to users, and this can happen at unpredictable times.
An action that reads and writes files, for instance, may do so unexpectedly.

---



## Hello, World! — 2.6. Summary {#fpil-hello-world-26-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Hello___-World___/Summary/

### 2.6.1. Evaluation vs Execution {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Hello___-World___--Summary--Evaluation-vs-Execution}

Side effects are aspects of program execution that go beyond the evaluation of mathematical expressions, such as reading files, throwing exceptions, or triggering industrial machinery.
While most languages allow side effects to occur during evaluation, Lean does not.
Instead, Lean has a type called `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` that represents *descriptions* of programs that use side effects.
These descriptions are then executed by the language's run-time system, which invokes the Lean expression evaluator to carry out specific computations.
Values of type `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α` are called *`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions*.
The simplest is `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`, which returns its argument and has no actual side effects.

`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions can also be understood as functions that take the whole world as an argument and return a new world in which the side effect has occurred.
Behind the scenes, the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` library ensures that the world is never duplicated, created, or destroyed.
While this model of side effects cannot actually be implemented, as the whole universe is too big to fit in memory, the real world can be represented by a token that is passed around through the program.

An `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action `main` is executed when the program starts.
`main` can have one of three types:

- `main : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` is used for simple programs that cannot read their command-line arguments and always return exit code `0`,
- `main : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)` is used for programs without arguments that may signal success or failure, and
- `main : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)` is used for programs that take command-line arguments and signal success or failure.

### 2.6.2. `do` Notation {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Hello___-World___--Summary--do--Notation}

The Lean standard library provides a number of basic `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that represent effects such as reading from and writing to files and interacting with standard input and standard output.
These base `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions are composed into larger `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions using `do` notation, which is a built-in domain-specific language for writing descriptions of programs with side effects.
A `do` expression contains a sequence of *statements*, which may be:

- expressions that represent `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions,
- ordinary local definitions with `let` and `:=`, where the defined name refers to the value of the provided expression, or
- local definitions with `let` and `←`, where the defined name refers to the result of executing the value of the provided expression.

`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that are written with `do` are executed one statement at a time.

Furthermore, `if` and `match` expressions that occur immediately under a `do` are implicitly considered to have their own `do` in each branch.
Inside of a `do` expression, *nested actions* are expressions with a left arrow immediately under parentheses.
The Lean compiler implicitly lifts them to the nearest enclosing `do`, which may be implicitly part of a branch of a `match` or `if` expression, and gives them a unique name.
This unique name then replaces the origin site of the nested action.

### 2.6.3. Compiling and Running Programs {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Hello___-World___--Summary--Compiling-and-Running-Programs}

A Lean program that consists of a single file with a `main` definition can be run using `lean --run FILE`.
While this can be a nice way to get started with a simple program, most programs will eventually graduate to a multiple-file project that should be compiled before running.

Lean projects are organized into *packages*, which are collections of libraries and executables together with information about dependencies and a build configuration.
Packages are described using Lake, a Lean build tool.
Use `lake new` to create a Lake package in a new directory, or `lake init` to create one in the current directory.
Lake package configuration is another domain-specific language.
Use `lake build` to build a project.

### 2.6.4. Partiality {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Hello___-World___--Summary--Partiality}

One consequence of following the mathematical model of expression evaluation is that every expression must have a value.
This rules out both incomplete pattern matches that fail to cover all constructors of a datatype and programs that can fall into an infinite loop.
Lean ensures that all `match` expressions cover all cases, and that all recursive functions are either structurally recursive or have an explicit proof of termination.

However, some real programs require the possibility of looping infinitely, because they handle potentially-infinite data, such as POSIX streams.
Lean provides an escape hatch: functions whose definition is marked `partial` are not required to terminate.
This comes at a cost.
Because types are a first-class part of the Lean language, functions can return types.
Partial functions, however, are not evaluated during type checking, because an infinite loop in a function could cause the type checker to enter an infinite loop.
Furthermore, mathematical proofs are unable to inspect the definitions of partial functions, which means that programs that use them are much less amenable to formal proof.

---



## Interlude: Propositions, Proofs, and Indexing {#fpil-interlude-propositions-proofs-and-indexing}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Interlude___-Propositions___-Proofs___-and-Indexing/

Like many languages, Lean uses square brackets for indexing into arrays and lists.
For instance, if `woodlandCritters` is defined as follows:

```lean
def woodlandCritters : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
["hedgehog", "deer", "snail"]
```

then the individual components can be extracted:

```lean
def hedgehog := woodlandCritters[0]
def deer := woodlandCritters[1]
def snail := woodlandCritters[2]
```

However, attempting to extract the fourth element results in a compile-time error, rather than a run-time error:

```lean
def oops := woodlandCritters[3]
```

```lean
failed to prove index is valid, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the index is valid
  - Use `a[i]!` notation instead, runtime check is performed, and 'Panic' error message is produced if index is not valid
  - Use `a[i]?` notation instead, result is an `Option` type
  - Use `a[i]'h` notation instead, where `h` is a proof that index is valid
⊢ 3 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) woodlandCritters.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

This error message is saying Lean tried to automatically mathematically prove that `3 < woodlandCritters.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)` (i.e. `3 < [List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) woodlandCritters`), which would mean that the lookup was safe, but that it could not do so.
Out-of-bounds errors are a common class of bugs, and Lean uses its dual nature as a programming language and a theorem prover to rule out as many as possible.

Understanding how this works requires an understanding of three key ideas: propositions, proofs, and tactics.

### Propositions and Proofs {#fpil-propositions-and-proofs}

A *proposition* is a statement that can be true or false.
All of the following English sentences are propositions:

- `1 + 1 = 2`
- Addition is commutative.
- There are infinitely many prime numbers.
- `1 + 1 = 15`
- Paris is the capital of France.
- Buenos Aires is the capital of South Korea.
- All birds can fly.

On the other hand, nonsense statements are not propositions.
Despite being grammatical, none of the following are propositions:

- 1 + green = ice cream
- All capital cities are prime numbers.
- At least one gorg is a fleep.

Propositions come in two varieties: those that are purely mathematical, relying only on our definitions of concepts, and those that are facts about the world.
Theorem provers like Lean are concerned with the former category, and have nothing to say about the flight capabilities of penguins or the legal status of cities.

A *proof* is a convincing argument that a proposition is true.
For mathematical propositions, these arguments make use of the definitions of the concepts that are involved as well as the rules of logical argumentation.
Most proofs are written for people to understand, and leave out many tedious details.
Computer-aided theorem provers like Lean are designed to allow mathematicians to write proofs while omitting many details, and it is the software's responsibility to fill in the missing explicit steps.
These steps can be mechanically checked.
This decreases the likelihood of oversights or mistakes.

In Lean, a program's type describes the ways it can be interacted with.
For instance, a program of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` is a function that takes a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` argument and produces a list of strings.
In other words, each type specifies what counts as a program with that type.

In Lean, propositions are in fact types.
They specify what counts as evidence that the statement is true.
The proposition is proved by providing this evidence, which is checked by Lean.
On the other hand, if the proposition is false, then it will be impossible to construct this evidence.

For example, the proposition `1 + 1 = 2` can be written directly in Lean.
The evidence for this proposition is the constructor `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, which is short for *reflexivity*.
In mathematics, a relation is *reflexive* if every element is related to itself; this is a basic requirement in order to have a sensible notion of equality.
Because `1 + 1` computes to `2`, they are really the same thing:

```lean
def onePlusOneIsTwo : 1 + 1 = 2 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

On the other hand, `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` does not prove the false proposition `1 + 1 = 15`:

```lean
def onePlusOneIsFifteen : 1 + 1 = 15 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
has type
  ?m.16 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.16
but is expected to have type
  1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 15
```

This error message indicates that `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` can prove that two expressions are equal when both sides of the equality statement are already the same number.
Because `1 + 1` evaluates directly to `2`, they are considered to be the same, which allows `onePlusOneIsTwo` to be accepted.
Just as `Type` describes types such as `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, and `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) × ([Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)))` that represent data structures and functions, `Prop` describes propositions.

When a proposition has been proven, it is called a *theorem*.
In Lean, it is conventional to declare theorems with the `theorem` keyword instead of `def`.
This helps readers see which declarations are intended to be read as mathematical proofs, and which are definitions.
Generally speaking, with a proof, what matters is that there is evidence that a proposition is true, but it's not particularly important *which* evidence was provided.
With definitions, on the other hand, it matters very much which particular value is selected—after all, a definition of addition that always returns `0` is clearly wrong.
Because the details of a proof don't matter for later proofs, using the `theorem` keyword enables greater parallelism in the Lean compiler.

The prior example could be rewritten as follows:

```lean
def OnePlusOneIsTwo : Prop := 1 + 1 = 2
theorem onePlusOneIsTwo : [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo) := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

### Tactics {#fpil-tactics}

Proofs are normally written using *tactics*, rather than by providing evidence directly.
Tactics are small programs that construct evidence for a proposition.
These programs run in a *proof state* that tracks the statement that is to be proved (called the *goal*) along with the assumptions that are available to prove it.
Running a tactic on a goal results in a new proof state that contains new goals.
The proof is complete when all goals have been proven.

To write a proof with tactics, begin the definition with `by`.
Writing `by` puts Lean into tactic mode until the end of the next indented block.
While in tactic mode, Lean provides ongoing feedback about the current proof state.
Written with tactics, `onePlusOneIsTwo` is still quite short:

```lean
theorem onePlusOneIsTwo : 1 + 1 = 2 := by⊢ 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactic invokes a *decision procedure*, which is a program that can check whether a statement is true or false, returning a suitable proof in either case.
It is primarily used when working with concrete values like `1` and `2`.
The other important tactics in this book are `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, short for “simplify,” and `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)`, which can automatically prove many theorems.

Tactics are useful for a number of reasons:

1. Many proofs are complicated and tedious when written out down to the smallest detail, and tactics can automate these uninteresting parts.
2. Proofs written with tactics are easier to maintain over time, because flexible automation can paper over small changes to definitions.
3. Because a single tactic can prove many different theorems, Lean can use tactics behind the scenes to free users from writing proofs by hand. For instance, an array lookup requires a proof that the index is in bounds, and a tactic can typically construct that proof without the user needing to worry about it.

Behind the scenes, indexing notation uses a tactic to prove that the user's lookup operation is safe.
This tactic takes many facts about arithmetic into account, combining them with any locally-known facts to attempt to prove that the index is in bounds.

The `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` tactic is a workhorse of Lean proofs.
It rewrites the goal to as simple a form as possible.
In many cases, this rewriting simplifies the statement so much that it can be automatically proved.
Behind the scenes, a detailed formal proof is constructed, but using `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` hides this complexity.

Like `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)`, the `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` tactic is used to finish proofs.
It uses a collection of techniques from SMT solvers that can prove a wide variety of theorems.
Unlike `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` can never make progress towards a proof without completing it entirely; it either succeeds fully or fails.
The `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` tactic is very powerful, customizable, and extensible; due to this power and flexibility, its output when it fails to prove a theorem contains a lot of information that can help trained Lean users diagnose the reason for the failure.
This can be overwhelming in the beginning, so this chapter uses only `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` and `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`.

### Connectives {#fpil-connectives}

The basic building blocks of logic, such as “and”, “or”, “true”, “false”, and “not”, are called *logical connectives*.
Each connective defines what counts as evidence of its truth.
For example, to prove a statement “*A* and *B*”, one must prove both *A* and *B*.
This means that evidence for “*A* and *B*” is a pair that contains both evidence for *A* and evidence for *B*.
Similarly, evidence for “*A* or *B*” consists of either evidence for *A* or evidence for *B*.

In particular, most of these connectives are defined like datatypes, and they have constructors.
If `A` and `B` are propositions, then “`A` and `B`” (written `A ∧ B`) is a proposition.
Evidence for `A ∧ B` consists of the constructor `[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)`, which has the type `A → B → A ∧ B`.
Replacing `A` and `B` with concrete propositions, it is possible to prove `1 + 1 = 2 ∧ "Str".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "ing" = "String"` with `[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`.
Of course, `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` is also powerful enough to find this proof:

```lean
theorem addAndAppend : 1 + 1 = 2 ∧ "Str".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "ing" = "String" := by⊢ 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) "Str".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "ing" [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) "String"
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Similarly, “`A` or `B`” (written `A ∨ B`) has two constructors, because a proof of “`A` or `B`” requires only that one of the two underlying propositions be true.
There are two constructors: `[Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)`, with type `A → A ∨ B`, and `[Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)`, with type `B → A ∨ B`.

Implication (if `A` then `B`) is represented using functions.
In particular, a function that transforms evidence for `A` into evidence for `B` is itself evidence that `A` implies `B`.
This is different from the usual description of implication, in which `A → B` is shorthand for `¬A ∨ B`, but the two formulations are equivalent.

Because evidence for an “and” is a constructor, it can be used with pattern matching.
For instance, a proof that `A` and `B` implies `A` or `B` is a function that pulls the evidence of `A` (or of `B`) out of the evidence for `A` and `B`, and then uses this evidence to produce evidence of `A` or `B`:

```lean
theorem andImpliesOr : A ∧ B → A ∨ B :=
fun andEvidence =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) andEvidence [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) a b => [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) a
```

| Connective | Lean Syntax | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| True | `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` | `[True.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` |
| False | `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` | No evidence |
| `A` and `B` | `A ∧ B` | `[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) : A → B → A ∧ B` |
| `A` or `B` | `A ∨ B` | Either `[Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) : A → A ∨ B` or `[Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) : B → A ∨ B` |
| `A` implies `B` | `A → B` | A function that transforms evidence of `A` into evidence of `B` |
| not `A` | `¬A` | A function that would transform evidence of `A` into evidence of `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` |

The `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactic can prove theorems that use these connectives.
For example:

```lean
theorem onePlusOneOrLessThan : 1 + 1 = 2 ∨ 3 < 5 := by⊢ 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) 3 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 5 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
theorem notTwoEqualFive : ¬(1 + 1 = 5) := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
theorem trueIsTrue : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) := by⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
theorem trueOrFalse : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∨ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := by⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
theorem falseImpliesTrue : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) → [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) := by⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) → [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### Evidence as Arguments {#fpil-evidence-passing}

In some cases, safely indexing into a list requires that the list have some minimum size, but the list itself is a variable rather than a concrete value.
For this lookup to be safe, there must be some evidence that the list is long enough.
One of the easiest ways to make indexing safe is to have the function that performs a lookup into a data structure take the required evidence of safety as an argument.
For instance, a function that returns the third entry in a list is not generally safe because lists might contain zero, one, or two entries:

```lean
def [third]](#fpil-third) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : α := xs[2]
```

```lean
failed to prove index is valid, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the index is valid
  - Use `a[i]!` notation instead, runtime check is performed, and 'Panic' error message is produced if index is not valid
  - Use `a[i]?` notation instead, result is an `Option` type
  - Use `a[i]'h` notation instead, where `h` is a proof that index is valid
α:Type ?u.3xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ 2 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

However, the obligation to show that the list has at least three entries can be imposed on the caller by adding an argument that consists of evidence that the indexing operation is safe:

```lean
def third (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (ok : xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2) : α := xs[2]
```

In this example, `xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2` is not a program that checks *whether* `xs` has more than 2 entries.
It is a proposition that could be true or false, and the argument `ok` must be evidence that it is true.

When the function is called on a concrete list, its length is known.
In these cases, `by [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` can construct the evidence automatically:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [third]](#fpil-third) woodlandCritters (by⊢ woodlandCritters.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙)
```

```lean
"snail"
```

### Indexing Without Evidence {#fpil-indexing-without-evidence}

In cases where it's not practical to prove that an indexing operation is in bounds, there are other alternatives.
Adding a question mark results in an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, where the result is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` if the index is in bounds, and `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` otherwise.
For example:

```lean
def thirdOption (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α := xs[2]?
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [thirdOption]](#fpil-thirdOption) woodlandCritters
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "snail"
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [thirdOption]](#fpil-thirdOption) ["only", "two"]
```

```lean
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

There is also a version that crashes the program when the index is out of bounds, rather than returning an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) woodlandCritters[1]!
```

```lean
"deer"
```

### Messages You May Meet {#fpil-props-proofs-indexing-messages}

In addition to proving that a statement is true, the `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactic can also prove that it is false.
When asked to prove that a one-element list has more than two elements, it returns an error that indicates that the statement is indeed false:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [third]](#fpil-third) ["rabbit"] (by⊢ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)"rabbit"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)⊢ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)"rabbit"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2)
```

```lean
Tactic `decide` proved that the proposition
  [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)"rabbit"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 2
is false
```

The `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` and `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactics do not automatically unfold definitions with `def`.
Attempting to prove `[OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)` using `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` fails:

```lean
theorem [onePlusOneIsStillTwo]](#fpil-Foo___onePlusOneIsStillTwo) : [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo) := by⊢ [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo) [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)⊢ [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)
```

The error messages simply states that it could do nothing, because without unfolding `[OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)`, no progress can be made:

```lean
`simp` made no progress
```

Using `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` also fails:

```lean
theorem onePlusOneIsStillTwo : [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo) := by⊢ [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo) [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)⊢ [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)
```

This is also due to it not unfolding `[OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)`:

```lean
failed to synthesize
  [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)

Hint: Additional diagnostic information may be available using the `set_option diagnostics true` command.
```

Defining `[OnePlusOneIsTwo]](#fpil-Foo___OnePlusOneIsTwo)` with [`abbrev` fixes the problem]](#fpil-abbrev-vs-def) by marking the definition for unfolding.

In addition to the error that occurs when Lean is unable to find compile-time evidence that an indexing operation is safe, polymorphic functions that use unsafe indexing may produce the following message:

```lean
def unsafeThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : α := xs[2]!
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

This is due to a technical restriction that is part of keeping Lean usable as both a logic for proving theorems and a programming language.
In particular, only programs whose types contain at least one value are allowed to crash.
This is because a proposition in Lean is a kind of type that classifies evidence of its truth.
False propositions have no such evidence.
If a program with an empty type could crash, then that crashing program could be used as a kind of fake evidence for a false proposition.

Internally, Lean contains a table of types that are known to have at least one value.
This error is saying that some arbitrary type `α` is not necessarily in that table.
The next chapter describes how to add to this table, and how to successfully write functions like `unsafeThird`.

Adding whitespace between a list and the brackets used for lookup can cause another message:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) woodlandCritters [1]
```

```lean
Function expected at
  woodlandCritters
but this term has type
  [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)

Note: Expected a function because this term is being applied to the argument
  [1]
```

Adding a space causes Lean to treat the expression as a function application, and the index as a list that contains a single number.
This error message results from having Lean attempt to treat `woodlandCritters` as a function.

#### Exercises {#fpil-props-proofs-indexing-exercises}

- Prove the following theorems using `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`: `2 + 3 = 5`, `15 - 8 = 7`, `"Hello, ".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "world" = "Hello, world"`. What happens if `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` is used to prove `5 < 18`? Why?
- Prove the following theorems using `by [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)`: `2 + 3 = 5`, `15 - 8 = 7`, `"Hello, ".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "world" = "Hello, world"`, `5 < 18`.
- Write a function that looks up the fifth entry in a list. Pass the evidence that this lookup is safe as an argument to the function.

## Overloading and Type Classes {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/

In many languages, the built-in datatypes get special treatment.
For example, in C and Java, `+` can be used to add `float`s and `int`s, but not arbitrary-precision numbers from a third-party library.
Similarly, numeric literals can be used directly for the built-in types, but not for user-defined number types.
Other languages provide an *overloading* mechanism for operators, where the same operator can be given a meaning for a new type.
In these languages, such as C++ and C#, a wide variety of built-in operators can be overloaded, and the compiler uses the type checker to select a particular implementation.

In addition to numeric literals and operators, many languages allow overloading of functions or methods.
In C++, Java, C# and Kotlin, multiple implementations of a method are allowed, with differing numbers and types of arguments.
The compiler uses the number of arguments and their types to determine which overload was intended.

Function and operator overloading has a key limitation: polymorphic functions can't restrict their type arguments to types for which a given overload exists.
For example, an overloaded method might be defined for strings, byte arrays, and file pointers, but there's no way to write a second method that works for any of these.
Instead, this second method must itself be overloaded for each type that has an overload of the original method, resulting in many boilerplate definitions instead of a single polymorphic definition.
Another consequence of this restriction is that some operators (such as equality in Java) end up being defined for *every* combination of arguments, even when it is not necessarily sensible to do so.
If programmers are not very careful, this can lead to programs that crash at runtime or silently compute an incorrect result.

Lean implements overloading using a mechanism called *type classes*, pioneered in Haskell, that allows overloading of operators, functions, and literals in a manner that works well with polymorphism.
A type class describes a collection of overloadable operations.
To overload these operations for a new type, an *instance* is created that contains an implementation of each operation for the new type.
For example, a type class named `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` describes types that allow addition, and an instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` provides an implementation of addition for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

The terms *class* and *instance* can be confusing for those who are used to object-oriented languages, because they are not closely related to classes and instances in object-oriented languages.
However, they do share common roots: in everyday language, the term “class” refers to a group that shares some common attributes.
While classes in object-oriented programming certainly describe groups of objects with common attributes, the term additionally refers to a specific mechanism in a programming language for describing such a group.
Type classes are also a means of describing types that share common attributes (namely, implementations of certain operations), but they don't really have anything else in common with classes as found in object-oriented programming.

A Lean type class is much more analogous to a Java or C# *interface*.
Both type classes and interfaces describe a conceptually related set of operations that are implemented for a type or collection of types.
Similarly, an instance of a type class is akin to the code in a Java or C# class that is prescribed by the implemented interfaces, rather than an instance of a Java or C# class.
Unlike Java or C#'s interfaces, types can be given instances for type classes that the author of the type does not have access to.
In this way, they are very similar to Rust traits.
