## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.1. Positive Numbers {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-31-positive-numbers}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Positive-Numbers/

In some applications, only positive numbers make sense.
For example, compilers and interpreters typically use one-indexed line and column numbers for source positions, and a datatype that represents only non-empty lists will never report a length of zero.
Rather than relying on natural numbers, and littering the code with assertions that the number is not zero, it can be useful to design a datatype that represents only positive numbers.

One way to represent positive numbers is very similar to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, except with `one` as the base case instead of `[zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
inductive Pos : Type where
| one : Pos
| succ : Pos → Pos
```

This datatype represents exactly the intended set of values, but it is not very convenient to use.
For example, numeric literals are rejected:

```lean
def [seven]](#fpil-seven) : Pos := 7
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Pos 7
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `7` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  Pos
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Instead, the constructors must be used directly:

```lean
def seven : Pos :=
[Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) Pos.one)))))
```

Similarly, addition and multiplication are not easy to use:

```lean
def [fourteen]](#fpil-fourteen) : Pos := [seven]](#fpil-seven) + [seven]](#fpil-seven)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) Pos Pos ?m.3

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

```lean
def fortyNine : Pos := [seven]](#fpil-seven) * [seven]](#fpil-seven)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) Pos Pos ?m.3

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Each of these error messages begins with `failed to synthesize`.
This indicates that the error is due to an overloaded operation that has not been implemented, and it describes the type class that must be implemented.

### 3.1.1. Classes and Instances {#fpil-classes-and-instances}

A type class consists of a name, some parameters, and a collection of *methods*.
The parameters describe the types for which overloadable operations are being defined, and the methods are the names and type signatures of the overloadable operations.
Once again, there is a terminology clash with object-oriented languages.
In object-oriented programming, a method is essentially a function that is connected to a particular object in memory, with special access to the object's private state.
Objects are interacted with via their methods.
In Lean, the term “method” refers to an operation that has been declared to be overloadable, with no special connection to objects or values or private fields.

One way to overload addition is to define a type class named `Plus`, with an addition method named `plus`.
Once an instance of `Plus` for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` has been defined, it becomes possible to add two `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s using `Plus.plus`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) Plus.plus 5 3
```

```lean
8
```

Adding more instances allows `Plus.plus` to take more types of arguments.

In the following type class declaration, `Plus` is the name of the class, `α : Type` is the only argument, and `plus : α → α → α` is the only method:

```lean
class Plus (α : Type) where
plus : α → α → α
```

This declaration says that there is a type class `Plus` that overloads operations with respect to a type `α`.
In particular, there is one overloaded operation called `plus` that takes two `α`s and returns an `α`.

Type classes are first class, just as types are first class.
In particular, a type class is another kind of type.
The type of `Plus` is `Type → Type`, because it takes a type as an argument (`α`) and results in a new type that describes the overloading of `Plus`'s operation for `α`.

To overload `plus` for a particular type, write an instance:

```lean
instance : Plus [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
plus := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
```

The colon after `instance` indicates that `Plus [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is indeed a type.
Each method of class `Plus` should be assigned a value using `:=`.
In this case, there is only one method: `plus`.

By default, type class methods are defined in a namespace with the same name as the type class.
It can be convenient to `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open)` the namespace so that users don't need to type the name of the class first.
Parentheses in an `open` command indicate that only the indicated names from the namespace are to be made accessible:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Plus (plus)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) plus 5 3
```

```lean
8
```

Defining an addition function for `Pos` and an instance of `Plus Pos` allows `[plus]](#fpil-Pos___plus)` to be used to add both `Pos` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` values:

```lean
def Pos.plus : Pos → Pos → Pos
| Pos.one, k => [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) k
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n, k => [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) (n.[plus]](#fpil-Pos___plus) k)
instance : Plus Pos where
plus := [Pos.plus]](#fpil-Pos___plus)
def fourteen : Pos := plus [seven]](#fpil-seven) [seven]](#fpil-seven)
```

Because there is not yet an instance of `Plus [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)`, attempting to add two floating-point numbers with `plus` fails with a familiar message:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) plus 5.2 917.25861
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  Plus [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

These errors mean that Lean was unable to find an instance for a given type class.

### 3.1.2. Overloaded Addition {#fpil-overloaded-addition}

Lean's built-in addition operator is syntactic sugar for a type class called `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`, which flexibly allows the arguments to addition to have different types.
`[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` is short for *heterogeneous addition*.
For example, an `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` instance can be written to allow a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to be added to a `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)`, resulting in a new `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)`.
When a programmer writes `x + y`, it is interpreted as meaning `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x y`.

While an understanding of the full generality of `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` relies on features that are discussed in [another section in this chapter](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Controlling-Instance-Search/#out-params), there is a simpler type class called `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` that does not allow the types of the arguments to be mixed.
The Lean libraries are set up so that an instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` will be found when searching for an instance of `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` in which both arguments have the same type.

Defining an instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) Pos` allows `Pos` values to use ordinary addition syntax:

```lean
instance : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) Pos where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) := [Pos.plus]](#fpil-Pos___plus)
```

```lean
def fourteen : Pos := [seven]](#fpil-seven) + [seven]](#fpil-seven)
```

### 3.1.3. Conversion to Strings {#fpil-conversion-to-strings}

Another useful built-in class is called `ToString`.
Instances of `ToString` provide a standard way of converting values from a given type into strings.
For example, a `ToString` instance is used when a value occurs in an interpolated string, and it determines how the `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` function used at the [beginning of the description of `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Hello___-World___/Running-a-Program/#running-a-program) will display a value.

For example, one way to convert a `Pos` into a `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` is to reveal its inner structure.
The function `posToString` takes a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` that determines whether to parenthesize uses of `[Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ)`, which should be `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` in the initial call to the function and `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` in all recursive calls.

```lean
def posToString (atTop : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (p : Pos) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
let paren s := [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) atTop [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) s [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "(" ++ s ++ ")"
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) p [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| Pos.one => "Pos.one"
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n => paren s!"Pos.succ {posToString [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) n}"
```

Using this function for a `ToString` instance:

```lean
instance : ToString Pos where
toString := posToString [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

results in informative, yet overwhelming, output:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) s!"There are {[seven]](#fpil-seven)}"
```

```lean
"There are Pos.succ (Pos.succ (Pos.succ (Pos.succ (Pos.succ (Pos.succ Pos.one)))))"
```

On the other hand, every positive number has a corresponding `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Converting it to a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and then using the `ToString [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance (that is, the overloading of `ToString` for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`) is a quick way to generate much shorter output:

```lean
def Pos.toNat : Pos → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| Pos.one => 1
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n => n.toNat + 1
```

```lean
instance : ToString Pos where
toString x := toString (x.toNat)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) s!"There are {[seven]](#fpil-seven)}"
```

```lean
"There are 7"
```

When more than one instance is defined, the most recent takes precedence.
Additionally, if a type has a `ToString` instance, then it can be used to display the result of `#eval` so `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [seven]](#fpil-seven)` outputs `7`.

### 3.1.4. Overloaded Multiplication {#fpil-overloaded-multiplication}

For multiplication, there is a type class called `[HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)` that allows mixed argument types, just like `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`.
Just as `x + y` is interpreted as `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x y`, `x * y` is interpreted as `[HMul.hMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) x y`.
For the common case of multiplication of two arguments with the same type, a `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)` instance suffices.

An instance of `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)` allows ordinary multiplication syntax to be used with `Pos`:

```lean
def Pos.mul : Pos → Pos → Pos
| Pos.one, k => k
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n, k => n.[mul]](#fpil-Pos___mul) k + k
instance : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) Pos where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) := [Pos.mul]](#fpil-Pos___mul)
```

With this instance, multiplication works as expected:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [[seven]](#fpil-seven) * Pos.one,
[seven]](#fpil-seven) * [seven]](#fpil-seven),
[Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) Pos.one * [seven]](#fpil-seven)]
```

```lean
[7, 49, 14]
```

### 3.1.5. Literal Numbers {#fpil-literal-numbers}

It is quite inconvenient to write out a sequence of constructors for positive numbers.
One way to work around the problem would be to provide a function to convert a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` into a `Pos`.
However, this approach has downsides.
First off, because `Pos` cannot represent `0`, the resulting function would either convert a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to a bigger number, or it would return `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Pos`.
Neither is particularly convenient for users.
Secondly, the need to call the function explicitly would make programs that use positive numbers much less convenient to write than programs that use `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Having a trade-off between precise types and convenient APIs means that the precise types become less useful.

There are three type classes that are used to overload numeric literals: `Zero`, `One`, and `OfNat`.
Because many types have values that are naturally written with `0`, the `Zero` class allow these specific values to be overridden.
It is defined as follows:

```lean
class Zero (α : Type) where
zero : α
```

Because `0` is not a positive number, there should be no instance of `[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) Pos`.

Similarly, many types have values that are naturally written with `1`.
The `One` class allows these to be overridden:

```lean
class One (α : Type) where
one : α
```

An instance of `One Pos` makes perfect sense:

```lean
instance : One Pos where
one := Pos.one
```

With this instance, `1` can be used for `Pos.one`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (1 : Pos)
```

```lean
1
```

In Lean, natural number literals are interpreted using a type class called `OfNat`:

```lean
class OfNat (α : Type) (_ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
ofNat : α
```

This type class takes two arguments: `α` is the type for which a natural number is overloaded, and the unnamed `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` argument is the actual literal number that was encountered in the program.
The method `ofNat` is then used as the value of the numeric literal.
Because the class contains the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` argument, it becomes possible to define only instances for those values where the number makes sense.

`OfNat` demonstrates that the arguments to type classes do not need to be types.
Because types in Lean are first-class participants in the language that can be passed as arguments to functions and given definitions with `def` and `abbrev`, there is no barrier that prevents non-type arguments in positions where a less-flexible language could not permit them.
This flexibility allows overloaded operations to be provided for particular values as well as particular types.
Additionally, it allows the Lean standard library to arrange for there to be a `[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) α` instance whenever there's an `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 0` instance, and vice versa.
Similarly, an instance of `One α` implies an instance of `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 1`, just as an instance of `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 1` implies an instance of `One α`.

A sum type that represents natural numbers less than four can be defined as follows:

```lean
inductive LT4 where
| zero
| one
| two
| three
```

While it would not make sense to allow *any* literal number to be used for this type, numbers less than four clearly make sense:

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [LT4]](#fpil-LT4) 0 where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [LT4.zero]](#fpil-LT4___zero)
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [LT4]](#fpil-LT4) 1 where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [LT4.one]](#fpil-LT4___one)
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [LT4]](#fpil-LT4) 2 where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [LT4.two]](#fpil-LT4___two)
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [LT4]](#fpil-LT4) 3 where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := [LT4.three]](#fpil-LT4___three)
```

With these instances, the following examples work:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3 : [LT4]](#fpil-LT4))
```

```lean
LT4.three
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (0 : [LT4]](#fpil-LT4))
```

```lean
LT4.zero
```

On the other hand, out-of-bounds literals are still not allowed:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (4 : [LT4]](#fpil-LT4))
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [LT4]](#fpil-LT4) 4
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `4` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [LT4]](#fpil-LT4)
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

For `Pos`, the `OfNat` instance should work for *any* `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` other than `[Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Another way to phrase this is to say that for all natural numbers `n`, the instance should work for `n + 1`.
Just as names like `α` automatically become implicit arguments to functions that Lean fills out on its own, instances can take automatic implicit arguments.
In this instance, the argument `n` stands for any `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and the instance is defined for a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that's one greater:

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Pos (n + 1) where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) :=
let rec natPlusOne : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Pos
| 0 => Pos.one
| k + 1 => [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) (natPlusOne k)
natPlusOne n
```

Because `n` stands for a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that's one less than what the user wrote, the helper function `natPlusOne` returns a `Pos` that's one greater than its argument.
This makes it possible to use natural number literals for positive numbers, but not for zero:

```lean
def eight : Pos := 8
```

```lean
def zero : Pos := 0
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Pos 0
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `0` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  Pos
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

### 3.1.6. Exercises {#fpil-positive-numbers-exercises}

#### 3.1.6.1. Another Representation {#fpil-positive-numbers-another-representation}

An alternative way to represent a positive number is as the successor of some `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Replace the definition of `Pos` with a structure whose constructor is named `succ` that contains a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
structure Pos where
succ ::
pred : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Define instances of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)`, `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)`, `ToString`, and `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` that allow this version of `Pos` to be used conveniently.

#### 3.1.6.2. Even Numbers {#fpil-even-numbers-ex}

Define a datatype that represents only even numbers. Define instances of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)`, `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)`, and `ToString` that allow it to be used conveniently.
`[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` requires a feature that is introduced in [the next section](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Type-Classes-and-Polymorphism/#tc-polymorphism).

#### 3.1.6.3. HTTP Requests {#fpil-http-request-ex}

An HTTP request begins with an identification of a HTTP method, such as `GET` or `POST`, along with a URI and an HTTP version.
Define an inductive type that represents an interesting subset of the HTTP methods, and a structure that represents HTTP responses.
Responses should have a `ToString` instance that makes it possible to debug them.
Use a type class to associate different `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions with each HTTP method, and write a test harness as an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action that calls each method and prints the result.

---



## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.2. Type Classes and Polymorphism {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-32-type-classes-and-polymorphism}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Type-Classes-and-Polymorphism/

It can be useful to write functions that work for *any* overloading of a given function.
For example, `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` works for any type that has an instance of `ToString`.
This is indicated using square brackets around the required instance: the type of `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` is `{α : Type} → [ToString α] → α → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`.
This type says that `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` accepts an argument of type `α`, which Lean should determine automatically, and that there must be a `ToString` instance available for `α`.
It returns an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action.

### 3.2.1. Checking Polymorphic Functions' Types {#fpil-checking-polymorphic-types}

Checking the type of a function that takes implicit arguments or uses type classes requires the use of some additional syntax.
Simply writing

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println))
```

yields a type with metavariables:

```lean
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) : ?m.1 → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
```

This is because Lean does its best to discover implicit arguments, and the presence of metavariables indicates that it did not yet discover enough type information to do so.
To understand the signature of a function, this feature can be suppressed with an at-sign (`@`) before the function's name:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) : {α : Type u_1} → [ToString α] → α → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
```

There is a `u_1` after `Type`, which uses a feature of Lean that has not yet been introduced.
For now, ignore these parameters to `Type`.

### 3.2.2. Defining Polymorphic Functions with Instance Implicits {#fpil-defining-polymorphic-functions-with-instance-implicits}

A function that sums all entries in a list needs two instances: `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` allows the entries to be added, and an `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance for `0` provides a sensible value to return for the empty list:

```lean
def [List.sumOfContents]](#fpil-List___sumOfContents) [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] [[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 0] : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → α
| [] => 0
| x :: xs => x + xs.[sumOfContents]](#fpil-List___sumOfContents)
```

This function can be also defined with a `[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) α` requirement instead of `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 0`.
Both are equivalent, but `[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) α` can be easier to read:

```lean
def List.sumOfContents [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] [[Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) α] : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → α
| [] => 0
| x :: xs => x + xs.[sumOfContents]](#fpil-List___sumOfContents)
```

This function can be used for a list of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s:

```lean
def fourNats : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [fourNats]](#fpil-fourNats).[sumOfContents]](#fpil-List___sumOfContents)
```

```lean
10
```

but not for a list of `Pos` numbers:

```lean
def fourPos : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Pos := [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [fourPos]](#fpil-fourPos).[sumOfContents]](#fpil-List___sumOfContents)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Zero___mk) Pos

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

The Lean standard library includes this function, where it is called `[List.sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___sum)`.

Specifications of required instances in square brackets are called *instance implicits*.
Behind the scenes, every type class defines a structure that has a field for each overloaded operation.
Instances are values of that structure type, with each field containing an implementation.
At a call site, Lean is responsible for finding an instance value to pass for each instance implicit argument.
The most important difference between ordinary implicit arguments and instance implicits is the strategy that Lean uses to find an argument value.
In the case of ordinary implicit arguments, Lean uses a technique called *unification* to find a single unique argument value that would allow the program to pass the type checker.
This process relies only on the specific types involved in the function's definition and the call site.
For instance implicits, Lean instead consults a built-in table of instance values.

Just as the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance for `Pos` took a natural number `n` as an automatic implicit argument, instances may also take instance implicit arguments themselves.
The [section on polymorphism]](#fpil-polymorphism) presented a polymorphic point type:

```lean
structure PPoint (α : Type) where
x : α
y : α
```

Addition of points should add the underlying `x` and `y` fields.
Thus, an `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance for `PPoint` requires an `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance for whatever type these fields have.
In other words, the `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance for `PPoint` requires a further `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance for `α`:

```lean
instance [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) (PPoint α) where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) p1 p2 := { x := p1.x + p2.x, y := p1.y + p2.y }
```

When Lean encounters an addition of two points, it searches for and finds this instance.
It then performs a further search for the `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α` instance.

The instance values that are constructed in this way are values of the type class's structure type.
A successful recursive instance search results in a structure value that has a reference to another structure value.
An instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) (PPoint [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))` contains a reference to the instance of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that was found.

This recursive search process means that type classes offer significantly more power than plain overloaded functions.
A library of polymorphic instances is a set of code building blocks that the compiler will assemble on its own, given nothing but the desired type.
Polymorphic functions that take instance arguments are latent requests to the type class mechanism to assemble helper functions behind the scenes.
The API's clients are freed from the burden of plumbing together all of the necessary parts by hand.

### 3.2.3. Methods and Implicit Arguments {#fpil-method-implicit-params}

The type of `[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` may be surprising.
It is `: {α : Type} → (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α n] → α`, in which the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` argument `n` occurs as an explicit function parameter.
In the declaration of the method, however, `ofNat` simply has type `α`.
This seeming discrepancy is because declaring a type class really results in the following:

- A structure type to contain the implementation of each overloaded operation
- A namespace with the same name as the class
- For each method, a function in the class's namespace that retrieves its implementation from an instance

This is analogous to the way that declaring a new structure also declares accessor functions.
The primary difference is that a structure's accessors take the structure value as an explicit parameter, while the type class methods take the instance value as an instance implicit to be found automatically by Lean.

In order for Lean to find an instance, its parameters must be available.
This means that each parameter to the type class must be a parameter to the method that occurs before the instance.
It is most convenient when these parameters are implicit, because Lean does the work of discovering their values.
For example, `[Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` has the type `{α : Type} → [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] → α → α → α`.
In this case, the type parameter `α` can be implicit because the arguments to `[Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` provide information about which type the user intended.
This type can then be used to search for the `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance.

In the case of `[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)`, however, the particular `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` literal to be decoded does not appear as part of any other parameter's type.
This means that Lean would have no information to use when attempting to figure out the implicit parameter `n`.
The result would be a very inconvenient API.
Thus, in these cases, Lean uses an explicit parameter for the class's method.

### 3.2.4. Exercises {#fpil-type-class-polymorphism-exercises}

#### 3.2.4.1. Even Number Literals {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Type-Classes-and-Polymorphism--Exercises--Even-Number-Literals}

Write an instance of `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` for the even number datatype from the [previous section's exercises]](#fpil-even-numbers-ex) that uses recursive instance search.

#### 3.2.4.2. Recursive Instance Search Depth {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Type-Classes-and-Polymorphism--Exercises--Recursive-Instance-Search-Depth}

There is a limit to how many times the Lean compiler will attempt a recursive instance search.
This places a limit on the size of even number literals defined in the previous exercise.
Experimentally determine what the limit is.

## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.3. Controlling Instance Search {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-33-controlling-instance-search}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Controlling-Instance-Search/

An instance of the `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` class is sufficient to allow two expressions with type `Pos` to be conveniently added, producing another `Pos`.
However, in many cases, it can be useful to be more flexible and allow *heterogeneous* operator overloading, where the arguments may have different types.
For example, adding a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to a `Pos` or a `Pos` to a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` will always yield a `Pos`:

```lean
def addNatPos : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Pos → Pos
| 0, p => p
| n + 1, p => [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([addNatPos]](#fpil-addNatPos) n p)
def addPosNat : Pos → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Pos
| p, 0 => p
| p, n + 1 => [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) ([addPosNat]](#fpil-addPosNat) p n)
```

These functions allow natural numbers to be added to positive numbers, but they cannot be used with the `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` type class, which expects both arguments to `[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` to have the same type.

### 3.3.1. Heterogeneous Overloadings {#fpil-heterogeneous-operators}

As mentioned in the section on [overloaded addition]](#fpil-overloaded-addition), Lean provides a type class called `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` for overloading addition heterogeneously.
The `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` class takes three type parameters: the two argument types and the return type.
Instances of `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos Pos` and `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos` allow ordinary addition notation to be used to mix the types:

```lean
instance : [HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos Pos where
[hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) := [addNatPos]](#fpil-addNatPos)
instance : [HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos where
[hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) := [addPosNat]](#fpil-addPosNat)
```

Given the above two instances, the following examples work:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3 : Pos) + (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
8
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) + (5 : Pos)
```

```lean
8
```

The definition of the `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` type class is very much like the following definition of `HPlus` with the corresponding instances:

```lean
class HPlus (α : Type) (β : Type) (γ : Type) where
hPlus : α → β → γ
```

```lean
instance : HPlus [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos Pos where
[hPlus]](#fpil-ProblematicHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) := [addNatPos]](#fpil-addNatPos)
instance : HPlus Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos where
[hPlus]](#fpil-ProblematicHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) := [addPosNat]](#fpil-addPosNat)
```

However, instances of `HPlus` are significantly less useful than instances of `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`.
When attempting to use these instances with `#eval`, an error occurs:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) toString ([HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-ProblematicHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (3 : Pos) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))
```

```lean
typeclass instance problem is stuck
  HPlus Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ?m.6

Note: Lean will not try to resolve this typeclass instance problem because the third type argument to `HPlus` is a metavariable. This argument must be fully determined before Lean will try to resolve the typeclass.

Hint: Adding type annotations and supplying implicit arguments to functions can give Lean more information for typeclass resolution. For example, if you have a variable `x` that you intend to be a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but Lean reports it as having an unresolved type like `?m`, replacing `x` with `(x : Nat)` can get typeclass resolution un-stuck.
```

The message indicates that this happens because there is a metavariable in the type, and Lean has no way to solve it.

As discussed in [the initial description of polymorphism]](#fpil-polymorphism), metavariables represent unknown parts of a program that could not be inferred.
When an expression is written following `#eval`, Lean attempts to determine its type automatically.
In this case, it could not.
Because the third type parameter for `HPlus` was unknown, Lean couldn't carry out type class instance search, but instance search is the only way that Lean could determine the expression's type.
That is, the `HPlus Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) Pos` instance can only apply if the expression should have type `Pos`, but there's nothing in the program other than the instance itself to indicate that it should have this type.

One solution to the problem is to ensure that all three types are available by adding a type annotation to the whole expression:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-ProblematicHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (3 : Pos) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Pos)
```

```lean
8
```

However, this solution is not very convenient for users of the positive number library.

### 3.3.2. Output Parameters {#fpil-output-parameters}

This problem can also be solved by declaring `γ` to be an *output parameter*.
Most type class parameters are inputs to the search algorithm: they are used to select an instance.
For example, in an `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance, both the type and the natural number are used to select a particular interpretation of a natural number literal.
However, in some cases, it can be convenient to start the search process even when some of the type parameters are not yet known, and use the instances that are discovered in the search to determine values for metavariables.
The parameters that aren't needed to start instance search are outputs of the process, which is declared with the `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` modifier:

```lean
class HPlus (α : Type) (β : Type) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) Type) where
hPlus : α → β → γ
```

With this output parameter, type class instance search is able to select an instance without knowing `γ` in advance.
For instance:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (3 : Pos) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
8
```

It might be helpful to think of output parameters as defining a kind of function.
Any given instance of a type class that has one or more output parameters provides Lean with instructions for determining the outputs from the inputs.
The process of searching for an instance, possibly recursively, ends up being more powerful than mere overloading.
Output parameters can determine other types in the program, and instance search can assemble a collection of underlying instances into a program that has this type.

### 3.3.3. Default Instances {#fpil-default-instances}

Deciding whether a parameter is an input or an output controls the circumstances under which Lean will initiate type class search.
In particular, type class search does not occur until all inputs are known.
However, in some cases, output parameters are not enough, and instance search should also occur when some inputs are unknown.
This is a bit like default values for optional function arguments in Python or Kotlin, except default *types* are being selected.

*Default instances* are instances that are available for instance search *even when not all their inputs are known*.
When one of these instances can be used, it will be used.
This can cause programs to successfully type check, rather than failing with errors related to unknown types and metavariables.
On the other hand, default instances can make instance selection less predictable.
In particular, if an undesired default instance is selected, then an expression may have a different type than expected, which can cause confusing type errors to occur elsewhere in the program.
Be selective about where default instances are used!

One example of where default instances can be useful is an instance of `HPlus` that can be derived from an `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` instance.
In other words, ordinary addition is a special case of heterogeneous addition in which all three types happen to be the same.
This can be implemented using the following instance:

```lean
instance [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : HPlus α α α where
[hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) := [Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)
```

With this instance, `[hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus)` can be used for any addable type, like `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (3 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
8
```

However, this instance will only be used in situations where the types of both arguments are known.
For example,

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (3 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

yields the type

```lean
[HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) 5 3 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

as expected, but

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

yields a type that contains two metavariables, one for the remaining argument and one for the return type:

```lean
[HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) 5 : ?m.2 → ?m.3
```

In the vast majority of cases, when someone supplies one argument to addition, the other argument will have the same type.
To make this instance into a default instance, apply the `[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance)` attribute:

```lean
@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance)]
instance [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : HPlus α α α where
[hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) := [Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)
```

With this default instance, the example has a more useful type:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) (5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

yields

```lean
[HPlus.hPlus]](#fpil-BetterHPlus___HPlus___hPlus) 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Each operator that exists in overloadable heterogeneous and homogeneous versions follows the pattern of a default instance that allows the homogeneous version to be used in contexts where the heterogeneous is expected.
The infix operator is replaced with a call to the heterogeneous version, and the homogeneous default instance is selected when possible.

Similarly, simply writing `5` gives a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` rather than a type with a metavariable that is waiting for more information in order to select an `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance.
This is because the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is a default instance.

Default instances can also be assigned *priorities* that affect which will be chosen in situations where more than one might apply.
For more information on default instance priorities, please consult the Lean manual.

### 3.3.4. Exercises {#fpil-out-params-exercises}

Define an instance of `[HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) (PPoint α) α (PPoint α)` that multiplies both projections by the scalar.
It should work for any type `α` for which there is a `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) α` instance.
For example,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) {x := 2.5, y := 3.7 : PPoint [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)} * 2.0
```

should yield

```lean
{ x := 5.000000, y := 7.400000 }
```

---



## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.4. Arrays and Indexing {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-34-arrays-and-indexing}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Arrays-and-Indexing/

The [Interlude]](#fpil-props-proofs-indexing) describes how to use indexing notation in order to look up entries in a list by their position.
This syntax is also governed by a type class, and it can be used for a variety of different types.

### 3.4.1. Arrays {#fpil-array-indexing}

For instance, Lean arrays are much more efficient than linked lists for most purposes.
In Lean, the type `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α` is a dynamically-sized array holding values of type `α`, much like a Java `ArrayList`, a C++ `std::vector`, or a Rust `Vec`.
Unlike `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, which has a pointer indirection on each use of the `[cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` constructor, arrays occupy a contiguous region of memory, which is much better for processor caches.
Also, looking up a value in an array takes constant time, while lookup in a linked list takes time proportional to the index being accessed.

In pure functional languages like Lean, it is not possible to mutate a given position in a data structure.
Instead, a copy is made that has the desired modifications.
However, copying is not always necessary: the Lean compiler and runtime contain an optimization that can allow modifications to be implemented as mutations behind the scenes when there is only a single unique reference to an array.

Arrays are written similarly to lists, but with a leading `#`:

```lean
def northernTrees : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
#["sloe", "birch", "elm", "oak"]
```

The number of values in an array can be found using `[Array.size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`.
For instance, `[northernTrees]](#fpil-northernTrees).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)` evaluates to `4`.
For indices that are smaller than an array's size, indexing notation can be used to find the corresponding value, just as with lists.
That is, `[northernTrees]](#fpil-northernTrees)[2]` evaluates to `"elm"`.
Similarly, the compiler requires a proof that an index is in bounds, and attempting to look up a value outside the bounds of the array results in a compile-time error, just as with lists.
For instance, `[northernTrees]](#fpil-northernTrees)[8]` results in:

```lean
failed to prove index is valid, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the index is valid
  - Use `a[i]!` notation instead, runtime check is performed, and 'Panic' error message is produced if index is not valid
  - Use `a[i]?` notation instead, result is an `Option` type
  - Use `a[i]'h` notation instead, where `h` is a proof that index is valid
⊢ 8 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) [northernTrees]](#fpil-northernTrees).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
```

### 3.4.2. Non-Empty Lists {#fpil-non-empty-list-indexing}

A datatype that represents non-empty lists can be defined as a structure with a field for the head of the list and a field for the tail, which is an ordinary, potentially empty list:

```lean
structure NonEmptyList (α : Type) : Type where
head : α
tail : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

For example, the non-empty list `idahoSpiders` (which contains some spider species native to the US state of Idaho) consists of `"Banded Garden Spider"` followed by four other spiders, for a total of five spiders:

```lean
def idahoSpiders : NonEmptyList [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := {
[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "Banded Garden Spider",
[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [
"Long-legged Sac Spider",
"Wolf Spider",
"Hobo Spider",
"Cat-faced Spider"
]
}
```

Looking up the value at a specific index in this list with a recursive function should consider three possibilities:

1. The index is `0`, in which case the head of the list should be returned.
2. The index is `n + 1` and the tail is empty, in which case the index is out of bounds.
3. The index is `n + 1` and the tail is non-empty, in which case the function can be called recursively on the tail and `n`.

For example, a lookup function that returns an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` can be written as follows:

```lean
def NonEmptyList.get? : NonEmptyList α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| xs, 0 => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head)
| {[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := _, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := []}, _ + 1 => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| {[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := _, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := h :: t}, n + 1 => [get?]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___get___) {[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := h, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := t} n
```

Each case in the pattern match corresponds to one of the possibilities above.
The recursive call to `[get?]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___get___)` does not require a `NonEmptyList` namespace qualifier because the body of the definition is implicitly in the definition's namespace.
Another way to write this function uses a list lookup `xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail)[n]?` when the index is greater than zero:

```lean
def NonEmptyList.get? : NonEmptyList α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| xs, 0 => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head)
| xs, n + 1 => xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail)[n]?
```

If the list contains one entry, then only `0` is a valid index.
If it contains two entries, then both `0` and `1` are valid indices.
If it contains three entries, then `0`, `1`, and `2` are valid indices.
In other words, the valid indices into a non-empty list are natural numbers that are strictly less than the length of the list, which are less than or equal to the length of the tail.

The definition of what it means for an index to be in bounds should be written as an `abbrev` because the tactics used to find evidence that indices are acceptable are able to solve inequalities of numbers, but they don't know anything about the name `NonEmptyList.inBounds`:

```lean
abbrev NonEmptyList.inBounds (xs : NonEmptyList α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Prop :=
i ≤ xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

This function returns a proposition that might be true or false.
For instance, `2` is in bounds for `idahoSpiders`, while `5` is not:

```lean
theorem atLeastThreeSpiders : idahoSpiders.inBounds 2 := by⊢ idahoSpiders.inBounds 2 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
theorem notSixSpiders : ¬idahoSpiders.inBounds 5 := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)idahoSpiders.inBounds 5 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The logical negation operator has a very low precedence, which means that `¬idahoSpiders.inBounds 5` is equivalent to `¬(idahoSpiders.inBounds 5)`.

This fact can be used to write a lookup function that requires evidence that the index is valid, and thus need not return `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, by delegating to the version for lists that checks the evidence at compile time:

```lean
def NonEmptyList.get (xs : NonEmptyList α)
(i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (ok : xs.inBounds i) : α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) i [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head)
| n + 1 => xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail)[n]
```

It is, of course, possible to write this function to use the evidence directly, rather than delegating to a standard library function that happens to be able to use the same evidence.
This requires techniques for working with proofs and propositions that are described later in this book.

### 3.4.3. Overloading Indexing {#fpil-overloading-indexing}

Indexing notation for a collection type can be overloaded by defining an instance of the `GetElem` type class.
For the sake of flexibility, `GetElem` has four parameters:

- The type of the collection
- The type of the index
- The type of elements that are extracted from the collection
- A function that determines what counts as evidence that the index is in bounds

The element type and the evidence function are both output parameters.
`GetElem` has a single method, `getElem`, which takes a collection value, an index value, and evidence that the index is in bounds as arguments, and returns an element:

```lean
class GetElem
(coll : Type)
(idx : Type)
(item : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) Type)
(inBounds : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (coll → idx → Prop)) where
getElem : (c : coll) → (i : idx) → inBounds c i → item
```

In the case of `NonEmptyList α`, these parameters are:

- The collection is `NonEmptyList α`
- Indices have type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`
- The type of elements is `α`
- An index is in bounds if it is less than or equal to the length of the tail

In fact, the `[GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk)` instance can delegate directly to `[NonEmptyList.get]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___get)`:

```lean
instance : [GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) (NonEmptyList α) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) α NonEmptyList.inBounds where
[getElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) := [NonEmptyList.get]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___get)
```

With this instance, `NonEmptyList` becomes just as convenient to use as `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`.
Evaluating `idahoSpiders.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head)` yields `"Banded Garden Spider"`, while `idahoSpiders[9]` leads to the compile-time error:

```lean
failed to prove index is valid, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the index is valid
  - Use `a[i]!` notation instead, runtime check is performed, and 'Panic' error message is produced if index is not valid
  - Use `a[i]?` notation instead, result is an `Option` type
  - Use `a[i]'h` notation instead, where `h` is a proof that index is valid
⊢ idahoSpiders.inBounds 9
```

Because both the collection type and the index type are input parameters to the `[GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk)` type class, new types can be used to index into existing collections.
The positive number type `Pos` is a perfectly reasonable index into a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, with the caveat that it cannot point at the first entry.
The following instance of `[GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk)` allows `Pos` to be used just as conveniently as `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to find a list entry:

```lean
instance : [GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) Pos α
(fun list n => list.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > n.toNat) where
[getElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (i : Pos) ok := xs[i.toNat]
```

Indexing can also make sense for non-numeric indices.
For example, `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` can be used to select between the fields in a point, with `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` corresponding to `x` and `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` corresponding to `y`:

```lean
instance : [GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) (PPoint α) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) α (fun _ _ => [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)) where
[getElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk) (p : PPoint α) (i : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) _ :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p.x [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p.y
```

In this case, both Booleans are valid indices.
Because every possible `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` is in bounds, the evidence is simply the true proposition `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`.

---



## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.5. Standard Classes {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-35-standard-classes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Standard-Classes/

This section presents a variety of operators and functions that can be overloaded using type classes in Lean.
Each operator or function corresponds to a method of a type class.
Unlike C++, infix operators in Lean are defined as abbreviations for named functions; this means that overloading them for new types is not done using the operator itself, but rather using the underlying name (such as `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`).

### 3.5.1. Arithmetic {#fpil-arithmetic-classes}

Most arithmetic operators are available in a heterogeneous form, where the arguments may have different type and an output parameter decides the type of the resulting expression.
For each heterogeneous operator, there is a corresponding homogeneous version that can be found by removing the letter `h`, so that `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` becomes `[Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)`.
The following arithmetic operators are overloaded:

| Expression | Desugaring | Class Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x + y` | `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x y` | `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` |
| `x - y` | `[HSub.hSub](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) x y` | `[HSub](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk)` |
| `x * y` | `[HMul.hMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) x y` | `[HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)` |
| `x / y` | `[HDiv.hDiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HDiv___mk) x y` | `[HDiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HDiv___mk)` |
| `x % y` | `[HMod.hMod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMod___mk) x y` | `[HMod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMod___mk)` |
| `x ^ y` | `[HPow.hPow](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HPow___mk) x y` | `[HPow](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HPow___mk)` |
| `- x` | `[Neg.neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk) x` | `[Neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk)` |

### 3.5.2. Bitwise Operators {#fpil-bitwise-classes}

Lean contains a number of standard bitwise operators that are overloaded using type classes.
There are instances for fixed-width types such as `[UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt16](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt16___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)`, and `[USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)`.
The latter is the size of words on the current platform, typically 32 or 64 bits.
The following bitwise operators are overloaded:

| Expression | Desugaring | Class Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x &&& y` | `[HAnd.hAnd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAnd___mk) x y` | `[HAnd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAnd___mk)` |
| `x ||| y` | `[HOr.hOr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HOr___mk) x y` | `[HOr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HOr___mk)` |
| `x ^^^ y` | `[HXor.hXor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HXor___mk) x y` | `[HXor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HXor___mk)` |
| `~~~x` | `Complement.complement x` | `Complement` |
| `x >>> y` | `[HShiftRight.hShiftRight](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HShiftRight___mk) x y` | `[HShiftRight](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HShiftRight___mk)` |
| `x <<< y` | `[HShiftLeft.hShiftLeft](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HShiftLeft___mk) x y` | `[HShiftLeft](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HShiftLeft___mk)` |

Because the names `[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` and `[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)` are already taken as the names of logical connectives, the homogeneous versions of `[HAnd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAnd___mk)` and `[HOr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HOr___mk)` are called `[AndOp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#AndOp___mk)` and `[OrOp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#OrOp___mk)` rather than `[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` and `[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)`.

### 3.5.3. Equality and Ordering {#fpil-equality-and-ordering}

Testing equality of two values typically uses the `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` class, which is short for “Boolean equality”.
Due to Lean's use as a theorem prover, there are really two kinds of equality operators in Lean:

- *Boolean equality* is the same kind of equality that is found in other programming languages. It is a function that takes two values and returns a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`. Boolean equality is written with two equals signs, just as in Python and C#. Because Lean is a pure functional language, there's no separate notions of reference vs value equality—pointers cannot be observed directly.
- *Propositional equality* is the mathematical statement that two things are equal. Propositional equality is not a function; rather, it is a mathematical statement that admits proof. It is written with a single equals sign. A statement of propositional equality is like a type that classifies evidence of this equality.

Both notions of equality are important, and used for different purposes.
Boolean equality is useful in programs, when a decision needs to be made about whether two values are equal.
For example, `"Octopus" == "Cuttlefish"` evaluates to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, and `"Octopodes" == "Octo".[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) "podes"` evaluates to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Some values, such as functions, cannot be checked for equality.
For example, `(fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => 1 + x) == ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ·)` yields the error:

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

As this message indicates, `==` is overloaded using a type class.
The expression `x == y` is actually shorthand for `[BEq.beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) x y`.

Propositional equality is a mathematical statement rather than an invocation of a program.
