Because propositions are like types that describe evidence for some statement, propositional equality has more in common with types like `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` than it does with Boolean equality.
This means that it can't automatically be checked.
However, the equality of any two expressions can be stated in Lean, so long as they have the same type.
The statement `(fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => 1 + x) = ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ·)` is a perfectly reasonable statement.
From the perspective of mathematics, two functions are equal if they map equal inputs to equal outputs, so this statement is even true, though it requires a one-line proof to convince Lean of this fact.

Generally speaking, when using Lean as a programming language, it's easiest to stick to Boolean functions rather than propositions.
However, as the names `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` and `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` for `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`'s constructors suggest, this difference is sometimes blurred.
Some propositions are *decidable*, which means that they can be checked just like a Boolean function.
The function that checks whether the proposition is true or false is called a *decision procedure*, and it returns *evidence* of the truth or falsity of the proposition.
Some examples of decidable propositions include equality and inequality of natural numbers, equality of strings, and “ands” and “ors” of propositions that are themselves decidable.

In Lean, `if` works with decidable propositions.
For example, `2 < 4` is a proposition:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) 2 < 4
```

```lean
2 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 4 : Prop
```

Nonetheless, it is perfectly acceptable to write it as the condition in an `if`.
For example, `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 2 < 4 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 2` has type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and evaluates to `1`.

Not all propositions are decidable.
If they were, then computers would be able to prove any true proposition just by running the decision procedure, and mathematicians would be out of a job.
More specifically, decidable propositions have an instance of the `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` type class, which contains the decision procedure.
Trying to use a proposition that isn't decidable as if it were a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` results in a failure to find the `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` instance.
For example, `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => 1 + x) = ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ·) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "yes" [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "no"` results in:

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)(fun x => 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) fun x => x.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

The following propositions, that are usually decidable, are overloaded with type classes:

| Expression | Desugaring | Class Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x < y` | `[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) x y` | `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` |
| `x ≤ y` | `[LE.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x y` | `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` |
| `x > y` | `[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) y x` | `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` |
| `x ≥ y` | `[LE.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) y x` | `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` |

Because defining new propositions hasn't yet been demonstrated, it may be difficult to define completely new instances of `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` and `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)`.
However, they can be defined in terms of existing instances.
`[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` and `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` instances for `Pos` can use the existing instances for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
instance : [LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) Pos where
[lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) x y := [LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) x.toNat y.toNat
```

```lean
instance : [LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) Pos where
[le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x y := [LE.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x.toNat y.toNat
```

These propositions are not decidable by default because Lean doesn't unfold the definitions of propositions while synthesizing an instance.
This can be bridged using the `[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)` operator, which finds an instance if it exists.
The type annotations direct `[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)` to infer instances of `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x.toNat < y.toNat)` and `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x.toNat ≤ y.toNat)`, which are the unfolded versions:

```lean
instance {x : Pos} {y : Pos} : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x < y) :=
([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x.toNat < y.toNat))
instance {x : Pos} {y : Pos} : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x ≤ y) :=
([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x.toNat ≤ y.toNat))
```

The type checker confirms that the definitions of the propositions match.
Confusing them results in an error:

```lean
instance {x : Pos} {y : Pos} : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x ≤ y) :=
([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (x.toNat < y.toNat))
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  [inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)
has type
  [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)x.toNat [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) y.toNat[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)
but is expected to have type
  [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)x [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) y[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)
```

Comparing values using `<`, `==`, and `>` can be inefficient.
Checking first whether one value is less than another, and then whether they are equal, can require two traversals over large data structures.
To solve this problem, Java and C# have standard `compareTo` and `CompareTo` methods (respectively) that can be overridden by a class in order to implement all three operations at the same time.
These methods return a negative integer if the receiver is less than the argument, zero if they are equal, and a positive integer if the receiver is greater than the argument.
Rather than overloading the meaning of integers, Lean has a built-in inductive type that describes these three possibilities:

```lean
inductive Ordering where
| lt
| eq
| gt
```

The `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)` type class can be overloaded to produce these comparisons.
For `Pos`, an implementation can be:

```lean
def Pos.comp : Pos → Pos → [Ordering](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt)
| Pos.one, Pos.one => [Ordering.eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt)
| Pos.one, [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) _ => [Ordering.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt)
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) _, Pos.one => [Ordering.gt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt)
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n, [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) k => [comp]](#fpil-Pos___comp) n k
instance : [Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) Pos where
[compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) := [Pos.comp]](#fpil-Pos___comp)
```

In situations where `compareTo` would be the right approach in Java, use `[Ord.compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)` in Lean.

### 3.5.4. Hashing {#fpil-hashing}

Java and C# have `hashCode` and `GetHashCode` methods, respectively, that compute a hash of a value for use in data structures such as hash tables.
The Lean equivalent is a type class called `Hashable`:

```lean
class Hashable (α : Type) where
hash : α → [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)
```

If two values are considered equal according to a `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` instance for their type, then they should have the same hashes.
In other words, if `x == y` then `[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) x == [hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) y`.
If `x ≠ y`, then `[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) x` won't necessarily differ from `[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) y` (after all, there are infinitely more `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` values than there are `[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)` values), but data structures built on hashing will have better performance if unequal values are likely to have unequal hashes.
This is the same expectation as in Java and C#.

The standard library contains a function `[mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash)` with type `[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec) → [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec) → [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)` that can be used to combine hashes for different fields for a constructor.
A reasonable hash function for an inductive datatype can be written by assigning a unique number to each constructor, and then mixing that number with the hashes of each field.
For example, a `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)` instance for `Pos` can be written:

```lean
def hashPos : Pos → [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)
| Pos.one => 0
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n => [mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash) 1 ([hashPos]](#fpil-hashPos) n)
instance : [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) Pos where
[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) := [hashPos]](#fpil-hashPos)
```

`[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)` instances for polymorphic types can use recursive instance search.
Hashing a `NonEmptyList α` is only possible when `α` can be hashed:

```lean
instance [[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) α] : [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) (NonEmptyList α) where
[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) xs := [mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash) ([hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head)) ([hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail))
```

Binary trees use both recursion and recursive instance search in the implementations of `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` and `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)`:

```lean
inductive BinTree (α : Type) where
| leaf : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α
| branch : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → α → [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α
def eqBinTree [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf), [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) =>
[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r, [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l2 x2 r2 =>
x == x2 && [eqBinTree]](#fpil-eqBinTree) l l2 && [eqBinTree]](#fpil-eqBinTree) r r2
| _, _ =>
[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
instance [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] : [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) ([BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α) where
[beq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) := [eqBinTree]](#fpil-eqBinTree)
def hashBinTree [[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) α] : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) =>
0
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) left x right =>
[mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash) 1
([mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash) ([hashBinTree]](#fpil-hashBinTree) left)
([mixHash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#mixHash) ([hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) x)
([hashBinTree]](#fpil-hashBinTree) right)))
instance [[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) α] : [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) ([BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α) where
[hash](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) := [hashBinTree]](#fpil-hashBinTree)
```

### 3.5.5. Deriving Standard Classes {#fpil-deriving-standard-classes}

Instance of classes like `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` and `Hashable` are often quite tedious to implement by hand.
Lean includes a feature called *instance deriving* that allows the compiler to automatically construct well-behaved instances of many type classes.
In fact, the `[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)` phrase in the definition of `Firewood` in the [first section on polymorphism]](#fpil-polymorphism) is an example of instance deriving.

Instances can be derived in two ways.
The first can be used when defining a structure or inductive type.
In this case, add `deriving` to the end of the type declaration followed by the names of the classes for which instances should be derived.
For a type that is already defined, a standalone `deriving` command can be used.
Write `deriving instance`` C1, C2, ... ``for`` T` to derive instances of `C1, C2, ...` for the type `T` after the fact.

`[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` and `Hashable` instances can be derived for `Pos` and `NonEmptyList` using a very small amount of code:

```lean
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk), [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) [for](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) Pos
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk), [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk) [for](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) NonEmptyList
```

Instances can be derived for at least the following classes:

- `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)`
- `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)`
- `[Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)`
- `Hashable`
- `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)`

In some cases, however, the derived `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)` instance may not produce precisely the ordering desired in an application.
When this is the case, it's fine to write an `[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk)` instance by hand.
The collection of classes for which instances can be derived can be extended by advanced users of Lean.

Aside from the clear advantages in programmer productivity and code readability, deriving instances also makes code easier to maintain, because the instances are updated as the definitions of types evolve.
When reviewing changes to code, modifications that involve updates to datatypes are much easier to read without line after line of formulaic modifications to equality tests and hash computation.

### 3.5.6. Appending {#fpil-append-class}

Many datatypes have some sort of append operator.
In Lean, appending two values is overloaded with the type class `HAppend`, which is a heterogeneous operation like that used for arithmetic operations:

```lean
class HAppend (α : Type) (β : Type) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) Type) where
hAppend : α → β → γ
```

The syntax `xs ++ ys` desugars to `[HAppend.hAppend](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) xs ys`.
For homogeneous cases, it's enough to implement an instance of `[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk)`, which follows the usual pattern:

```lean
instance : [Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) (NonEmptyList α) where
[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) xs ys :=
{ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head), [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) ++ ys.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) :: ys.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) }
```

After defining the above instance,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) idahoSpiders ++ idahoSpiders
```

has the following output:

```lean
{ head := "Banded Garden Spider",
  tail := ["Long-legged Sac Spider",
           "Wolf Spider",
           "Hobo Spider",
           "Cat-faced Spider",
           "Banded Garden Spider",
           "Long-legged Sac Spider",
           "Wolf Spider",
           "Hobo Spider",
           "Cat-faced Spider"] }
```

Similarly, a definition of `HAppend` allows non-empty lists to be appended to ordinary lists:

```lean
instance : [HAppend](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) (NonEmptyList α) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (NonEmptyList α) where
[hAppend](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) xs ys :=
{ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head), [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) ++ ys }
```

With this instance available,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) idahoSpiders ++ ["Trapdoor Spider"]
```

results in

```lean
{ head := "Banded Garden Spider",
  tail := ["Long-legged Sac Spider", "Wolf Spider", "Hobo Spider", "Cat-faced Spider", "Trapdoor Spider"] }
```

### 3.5.7. Functors {#fpil-Functor}

A polymorphic type is a *functor* if it has an overload for a function named `map` that transforms every element contained in it by a function.
While most languages use this terminology, C#'s equivalent of `map` is called `System.Linq.Enumerable.Select`.
For example, mapping a function over a list constructs a new list in which each entry from the starting list has been replaced by the result of the function on that entry.
Mapping a function `f` over an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` leaves `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` untouched, and replaces `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x` with `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f x)`.

Here are some examples of functors and how their `Functor` instances overload `map`:

- `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) (· + 5) [1, 2, 3]` evaluates to `[6, 7, 8]`
- `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) toString ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 5 [List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)))` evaluates to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "[5]"`
- `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) [List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]` evaluates to `[[3, 2, 1], [6, 5, 4]]`

Because `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` is a bit of a long name for this common operation, Lean also provides an infix operator for mapping a function, namely `<$>`.
The prior examples can be rewritten as follows:

- `(· + 5) <$> [1, 2, 3]` evaluates to `[6, 7, 8]`
- `toString <$> ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 5 [List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)))` evaluates to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "[5]"`
- `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) <$> [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]` evaluates to `[[3, 2, 1], [6, 5, 4]]`

An instance of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` for `NonEmptyList` requires specifying the `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` function.

```lean
instance : [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) NonEmptyList where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f xs := { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := f xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head), [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := f <$> xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) }
```

Here, `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` uses the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` to map the function over the tail.
This instance is defined for `NonEmptyList` rather than for `NonEmptyList α` because the argument type `α` plays no role in resolving the type class.
A `NonEmptyList` can have a function mapped over it *no matter what the type of entries is*.
If `α` were a parameter to the class, then it would be possible to make versions of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` that only worked for `NonEmptyList [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but part of being a functor is that `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` works for any entry type.

Here is an instance of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` for `PPoint`:

```lean
instance : [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) PPoint where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f p := { x := f p.x, y := f p.y }
```

In this case, `f` has been applied to both `x` and `y`.

Even when the type contained in a functor is itself a functor, mapping a function only goes down one layer.
That is, when using `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` on a `NonEmptyList (PPoint [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`, the function being mapped should take `PPoint [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` as its argument rather than `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

The definition of the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` class uses one more language feature that has not yet been discussed: default method definitions.
Normally, a class will specify some minimal set of overloadable operations that make sense together, and then use polymorphic functions with instance implicit arguments that build on the overloaded operations to provide a larger library of features.
For example, the function `concat` can concatenate any non-empty list whose entries are appendable:

```lean
def concat [[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) α] (xs : NonEmptyList α) : α :=
let rec catList (start : α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → α
| [] => start
| (z :: zs) => [catList]](#fpil-concat___catList) (start ++ z) zs
[catList]](#fpil-concat___catList) xs.[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) xs.[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail)
```

However, for some classes, there are operations that can be more efficiently implemented with knowledge of the internals of a datatype.

In these cases, a default method definition can be provided.
A default method definition provides a default implementation of a method in terms of the other methods.
However, instance implementors may choose to override this default with something more efficient.
Default method definitions contain `:=` in a `class` definition.

In the case of `Functor`, some types have a more efficient way of implementing `map` when the function being mapped ignores its argument.
Functions that ignore their arguments are called *constant functions* because they always return the same value.
Here is the definition of `Functor`, in which `mapConst` has a default implementation:

```lean
class Functor (f : Type → Type) where
map : {α β : Type} → (α → β) → f α → f β
mapConst {α β : Type} (x : α) (coll : f β) : f α :=
map (fun _ => x) coll
```

Just as a `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)` instance that doesn't respect `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` is buggy, a `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance that moves around the data as it maps the function is also buggy.
For example, a buggy `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` might throw away its argument and always return the empty list, or it might reverse the list.
A bad `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance for `PPoint` might place `f x` in both the `x` and the `y` fields, or swap them.
Specifically, `Functor` instances should follow two rules:

1. Mapping the identity function should result in the original argument.
2. Mapping two composed functions should have the same effect as composing their mapping.

More formally, the first rule says that `id <$> x` equals `x`.
The second rule says that `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) (fun y => f (g y)) x` equals `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f ([map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) g x)`.
The composition `f ∘ g` can also be written `fun y => f (g y)`.
These rules prevent implementations of `map` that move the data around or delete some of it.

### 3.5.8. Messages You May Meet {#fpil-standard-classes-messages}

Lean is not able to derive instances for all classes.
For example, the code

```lean
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) ToString [for](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) NonEmptyList
```

results in the following error:

```lean
No deriving handlers have been implemented for class `ToString`
```

Invoking `[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next)` causes Lean to consult an internal table of code generators for type class instances.
If the code generator is found, then it is invoked on the provided type to create the instance.
This message, however, means that no code generator was found for `ToString`.

### 3.5.9. Exercises {#fpil-standard-classes-exercises}

- Write an instance of `[HAppend](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (NonEmptyList α) (NonEmptyList α)` and test it.
- Implement a `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance for the binary tree datatype.

---



## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.6. Coercions {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-36-coercions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Coercions/

In mathematics, it is common to use the same symbol to stand for different aspects of some object in different contexts.
For example, if a ring is referred to in a context where a set is expected, then it is understood that the ring's underlying set is what's intended.
In programming languages, it is common to have rules to automatically translate values of one type into values of another type.
Java allows a `byte` to be automatically promoted to an `int`, and Kotlin allows a non-nullable type to be used in a context that expects a nullable version of the type.

In Lean, both purposes are served by a mechanism called *coercions*.
When Lean encounters an expression of one type in a context that expects a different type, it will attempt to coerce the expression before reporting a type error.
Unlike Java, C, and Kotlin, the coercions are extensible by defining instances of type classes.

### 3.6.1. Strings and Paths {#fpil-string-path-coercion}

In the [source code to `feline`]](#fpil-handling-input), a `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` is converted to a `[FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)` using the anonymous constructor syntax.
In fact, this was not necessary: Lean defines a coercion from `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` to `[FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)`, so a string can be used in a position where a path is expected.
Even though the function `[IO.FS.readFile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___readFile)` has type `[System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk) → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, the following code is accepted by Lean:

```lean
def fileDumper : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[putStr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) "Which file? "
stdout.[flush](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
let f := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii.[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"'The file {f}' contains:"
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) (← [IO.FS.readFile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___readFile) f)
```

`String.trimAscii` removes leading and trailing whitespace from a string, returning a [string slice]](#fpil---tech-term-string-slices) that is converted back to a string using `[String.Slice.copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)`.
On the last line of `fileDumper`, the coercion from `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` to `[FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)` automatically converts `f`, so it is not necessary to write `IO.FS.readFile ⟨f⟩`.

### 3.6.2. Positive Numbers {#fpil-positive-number-coercion}

Every positive number corresponds to a natural number.
The function `Pos.toNat` that was defined earlier converts a `Pos` to the corresponding `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
def Pos.toNat : Pos → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| Pos.one => 1
| [Pos.succ]](#fpil-Pos___succ) n => n.toNat + 1
```

The function `[List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop)`, with type `{α : Type} → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, removes a prefix of a list.
Applying `[List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop)` to a `Pos`, however, leads to a type error:

```lean
[1, 2, 3, 4].[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) (2 : Pos)
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  2
has type
  Pos
but is expected to have type
  [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
in the application
  [List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) 2
```

Because the author of `[List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop)` did not make it a method of a type class, it can't be overridden by defining a new instance.

The type class `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` describes overloaded ways of coercing from one type to another:

```lean
class Coe (α : Type) (β : Type) where
coe : α → β
```

An instance of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is enough to allow the prior code to work:

```lean
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) x := x.toNat
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [1, 2, 3, 4].[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) (2 : Pos)
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

Using `#check` shows the result of the instance search that was used behind the scenes:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [1, 2, 3, 4].[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) (2 : Pos)
```

```lean
[List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) (Pos.toNat 2) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

### 3.6.3. Chaining Coercions {#fpil-chaining-coercions}

When searching for coercions, Lean will attempt to assemble a coercion out of a chain of smaller coercions.
For example, there is already a coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`.
Because of that instance, combined with the `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) Pos [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` instance, the following code is accepted:

```lean
def oneInt : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) := Pos.one
```

This definition uses two coercions: from `Pos` to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and then from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`.

The Lean compiler does not get stuck in the presence of circular coercions.
For example, even if two types `A` and `B` can be coerced to one another, their mutual coercions can be used to find a path:

```lean
inductive A where
| a
inductive B where
| b
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) A B where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) _ := [B.b]](#fpil-B___b)
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) B A where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) _ := [A.a]](#fpil-A___a)
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) A where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) _ := [A.a]](#fpil-A___a)
def coercedToB : B := ()
```

Remember: the double parentheses `()` is short for the constructor `[Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)`.
After deriving a `[Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk) B` instance with `[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk) [for](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___deriving-next) B`,

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [coercedToB]](#fpil-coercedToB)
```

results in:

```lean
B.b
```

The `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` type can be used similarly to nullable types in C# and Kotlin: the `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` constructor represents the absence of a value.
The Lean standard library defines a coercion from any type `α` to `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α` that wraps the value in `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
This allows option types to be used in a manner even more similar to nullable types, because `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` can be omitted.
For instance, the function `List.last?` that finds the last entry in a list can be written without a `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` around the return value `x`:

```lean
def List.last? : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [x] => x
| _ :: x :: xs => last? (x :: xs)
```

Instance search finds the coercion, and inserts a call to `coe`, which wraps the argument in `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
These coercions can be chained, so that nested uses of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` don't require nested `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` constructors:

```lean
def perhapsPerhapsPerhaps : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))) :=
"Please don't tell me"
```

Coercions are only activated automatically when Lean encounters a mismatch between an inferred type and a type that is imposed from the rest of the program.
In cases with other errors, coercions are not activated.
For example, if the error is that an instance is missing, coercions will not be used:

```lean
def [perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat]](#fpil-perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) :=
392
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))) 392
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `392` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

This can be worked around by manually indicating the desired type to be used for `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)`:

```lean
def perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) :=
(392 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

Additionally, coercions can be manually inserted using an up arrow:

```lean
def perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) :=
↑(392 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

In some cases, this can be used to ensure that Lean finds the right instances.
It can also make the programmer's intentions more clear.

### 3.6.4. Non-Empty Lists and Dependent Coercions {#fpil-CoeDep}

An instance of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) α β` makes sense when the type `β` has a value that can represent each value from the type `α`.
Coercing from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` makes sense, because the type `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` contains all the natural numbers, but a coercion from `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is a poor idea because `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` does not contain the negative numbers.
Similarly, a coercion from non-empty lists to ordinary lists makes sense because the `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` type can represent every non-empty list:

```lean
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) (NonEmptyList α) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)
| { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := x, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := xs } => x :: xs
```

This allows non-empty lists to be used with the entire `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` API.

On the other hand, it is impossible to write an instance of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (NonEmptyList α)`, because there's no non-empty list that can represent the empty list.
This limitation can be worked around by using another version of coercions, which are called *dependent coercions*.
Dependent coercions can be used when the ability to coerce from one type to another depends on which particular value is being coerced.
Just as the `OfNat` type class takes the particular `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` being overloaded as a parameter, dependent coercion takes the value being coerced as a parameter:

```lean
class CoeDep (α : Type) (x : α) (β : Type) where
coe : β
```

This is a chance to select only certain values, either by imposing further type class constraints on the value or by writing certain constructors directly.
For example, any `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` that is not actually empty can be coerced to a `NonEmptyList`:

```lean
instance : [CoeDep](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeDep___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (x :: xs) (NonEmptyList α) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeDep___mk) := { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := x, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := xs }
```

### 3.6.5. Coercing to Types {#fpil-CoeSort}

In mathematics, it is common to have a concept that consists of a set equipped with additional structure.
For example, a monoid is some set `S`, an element `s` of `S`, and an associative binary operator on `S`, such that `s` is neutral on the left and right of the operator.
`S` is referred to as the “carrier set” of the monoid.
The natural numbers with zero and addition form a monoid, because addition is associative and adding zero to any number is the identity.
Similarly, the natural numbers with one and multiplication also form a monoid.
Monoids are also widely used in functional programming: lists, the empty list, and the append operator form a monoid, as do strings, the empty string, and string append:

```lean
structure Monoid where
Carrier : Type
neutral : Carrier
op : Carrier → Carrier → Carrier
def natMulMonoid : Monoid :=
{ [Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier) := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), [neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) := 1, [op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) := (· * ·) }
def natAddMonoid : Monoid :=
{ [Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier) := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), [neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) := 0, [op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) := (· + ·) }
def stringMonoid : Monoid :=
{ [Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier) := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray), [neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) := "", [op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) := [String.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___append) }
def listMonoid (α : Type) : Monoid :=
{ [Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier) := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α, [neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) := [], [op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) := [List.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append) }
```

Given a monoid, it is possible to write the `foldMap` function that, in a single pass, transforms the entries in a list into a monoid's carrier set and then combines them using the monoid's operator.
Because monoids have a neutral element, there is a natural result to return when the list is empty, and because the operator is associative, clients of the function don't have to care whether the recursive function combines elements from left to right or from right to left.

```lean
def foldMap (M : Monoid) (f : α → M.[Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : M.[Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier) :=
let rec go (soFar : M.[Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → M.[Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier)
| [] => soFar
| y :: ys => [go]](#fpil-MMM___foldMap___go) (M.[op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) soFar (f y)) ys
[go]](#fpil-MMM___foldMap___go) M.[neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) xs
```

Even though a monoid consists of three separate pieces of information, it is common to just refer to the monoid's name in order to refer to its set.
Instead of saying “Let A be a monoid and let *x* and *y* be elements of its carrier set”, it is common to say “Let *A* be a monoid and let *x* and *y* be elements of *A*”.
This practice can be encoded in Lean by defining a new kind of coercion, from the monoid to its carrier set.

The `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk)` class is just like the `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` class, with the exception that the target of the coercion must be a *sort*, namely `Type` or `Prop`.
The term *sort* in Lean refers to these types that classify other types—`Type` classifies types that themselves classify data, and `Prop` classifies propositions that themselves classify evidence of their truth.
Just as `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` is checked when a type mismatch occurs, `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk)` is used when something other than a sort is provided in a context where a sort would be expected.

The coercion from a monoid into its carrier set extracts the carrier:

```lean
instance : [CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) Monoid Type where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) m := m.[Carrier]](#fpil-Monoid___Carrier)
```

With this coercion, the type signatures become less bureaucratic:

```lean
def foldMap (M : Monoid) (f : α → M) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : M :=
let rec go (soFar : M) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → M
| [] => soFar
| y :: ys => [go]](#fpil-foldMap___go) (M.[op]](#fpil-Monoid___op) soFar (f y)) ys
[go]](#fpil-foldMap___go) M.[neutral]](#fpil-Monoid___neutral) xs
```

Another useful example of `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk)` is used to bridge the gap between `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` and `Prop`.
As discussed in [the section on ordering and equality]](#fpil-equality-and-ordering), Lean's `if` expression expects the condition to be a decidable proposition rather than a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Programs typically need to be able to branch based on Boolean values, however.
Rather than have two kinds of `if` expression, the Lean standard library defines a coercion from `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` to the proposition that the `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` in question is equal to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`:

```lean
instance : [CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) Prop where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) b := b = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

In this case, the sort in question is `Prop` rather than `Type`.

### 3.6.6. Coercing to Functions {#fpil-CoeFun}

Many datatypes that occur regularly in programming consist of a function along with some extra information about it.
For example, a function might be accompanied by a name to show in logs or by some configuration data.
Additionally, putting a type in a field of a structure, similarly to the `Monoid` example, can make sense in contexts where there is more than one way to implement an operation and more manual control is needed than type classes would allow.
For example, the specific details of values emitted by a JSON serializer may be important because another application expects a particular format.
Sometimes, the function itself may be derivable from just the configuration data.

A type class called `CoeFun` can transform values from non-function types to function types.
`CoeFun` has two parameters: the first is the type whose values should be transformed into functions, and the second is an output parameter that determines exactly which function type is being targeted.

```lean
class CoeFun (α : Type) (makeFunctionType : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (α → Type)) where
coe : (x : α) → makeFunctionType x
```

The second parameter is itself a function that computes a type.
In Lean, types are first-class and can be passed to functions or returned from them, just like anything else.

For example, a function that adds a constant amount to its argument can be represented as a wrapper around the amount to add, rather than by defining an actual function:

```lean
structure Adder where
howMuch : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

A function that adds five to its argument has a `5` in the `howMuch` field:

```lean
def add5 : Adder := ⟨5⟩
```

This `Adder` type is not a function, and applying it to an argument results in an error:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [add5]](#fpil-add5) 3
```

```lean
Function expected at
  [add5]](#fpil-add5)
but this term has type
  Adder

Note: Expected a function because this term is being applied to the argument
  3
```

Defining a `[CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk)` instance causes Lean to transform the adder into a function with type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
instance : [CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) Adder (fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) a := (· + a.howMuch)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [add5]](#fpil-add5) 3
```

```lean
8
```

Because all `Adder`s should be transformed into `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` functions, the argument to `[CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk)`'s second parameter was ignored.

When the value itself is needed to determine the right function type, then `[CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk)`'s second parameter is no longer ignored.
For example, given the following representation of JSON values:

```lean
inductive JSON where
| true : JSON
| false : JSON
| null : JSON
| string : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → JSON
| number : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next) → JSON
| object : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ([String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) × JSON) → JSON
| array : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) JSON → JSON
```

a JSON serializer is a structure that tracks the type it knows how to serialize along with the serialization code itself:

```lean
structure Serializer where
Contents : Type
serialize : Contents → JSON
```

A serializer for strings need only wrap the provided string in the `[JSON.string]](#fpil-JSON___string)` constructor:

```lean
def Str : [Serializer]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer) :=
{ [Contents]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer___Contents) := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray),
[serialize]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer___serialize) := [JSON.string]](#fpil-JSON___string)
}
```

Viewing JSON serializers as functions that serialize their argument requires extracting the inner type of serializable data:

```lean
instance : [CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) [Serializer]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer) (fun s => s.[Contents]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer___Contents) → JSON) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) s := s.[serialize]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer___serialize)
```

Given this instance, a serializer can be applied directly to an argument:

```lean
def buildResponse (title : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (R : [Serializer]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer))
(record : R.[Contents]](#fpil-Ser___Serializer___Contents)) : JSON :=
[JSON.object]](#fpil-JSON___object) [
("title", [JSON.string]](#fpil-JSON___string) title),
("status", [JSON.number]](#fpil-JSON___number) 200),
("record", R record)
]
```

The serializer can be passed directly to `[buildResponse]](#fpil-Ser___buildResponse)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [buildResponse]](#fpil-Ser___buildResponse) "Functional Programming in Lean" [Str]](#fpil-Ser___Str) "Programming is fun!"
```

```lean
JSON.object
  [("title", JSON.string "Functional Programming in Lean"),
   ("status", JSON.number 200.000000),
   ("record", JSON.string "Programming is fun!")]
```

#### 3.6.6.1. Aside: JSON as a String {#fpil-json-string}

It can be a bit difficult to understand JSON when encoded as Lean objects.
To help make sure that the serialized response was what was expected, it can be convenient to write a simple converter from `JSON` to `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`.
The first step is to simplify the display of numbers.
`JSON` doesn't distinguish between integers and floating point numbers, and the type `[Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)` is used to represent both.
In Lean, `[Float.toString](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___toString)` includes a number of trailing zeros:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (5 : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)).[toString](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___toString)
```

```lean
"5.000000"
```

The solution is to write a little function that cleans up the presentation by dropping all trailing zeros, followed by a trailing decimal point:

```lean
def dropDecimals (numString : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) numString.[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) '.' [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
let noTrailingZeros := numString.dropEndWhile (· == '0')
(noTrailingZeros.[dropEndWhile](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___dropEndWhile) (· == '.')).[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) numString
```

With this definition, `[dropDecimals]](#fpil-dropDecimals) (5 : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)).[toString](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___toString)` yields `5`, and `[dropDecimals]](#fpil-dropDecimals) (5.2 : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float-next)).[toString](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___toString)` yields `5.2`.

The next step is to define a helper function to append a list of strings with a separator in between them:

```lean
def String.separate (sep : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (strings : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) strings [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => ""
| x :: xs => [String.join](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___join) (x :: xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (sep ++ ·))
```

This function is useful to account for comma-separated elements in JSON arrays and objects.
`", ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) ["1", "2"]` yields `"1, 2"`, `", ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) ["1"]` yields `"1"`, and `", ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) []` yields `""`.
In the Lean standard library, this function is called `[String.intercalate](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___intercalate)`.

Finally, a string escaping procedure is needed for JSON strings, so that the Lean string containing `"Hello!"` can be output as `"\"Hello!\""`.
Fortunately, the Lean compiler contains an internal function for escaping JSON strings already, called `Lean.Json.escape`.
To access this function, add `import Lean` to the beginning of your file.

The function that emits a string from a `JSON` value is declared `partial` because Lean cannot see that it terminates.
This is because recursive calls to `[asString]](#fpil-JSON___asString)` occur in functions that are being applied by `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)`, and this pattern of recursion is complicated enough that Lean cannot see that the recursive calls are actually being performed on smaller values.
In an application that just needs to produce JSON strings and doesn't need to mathematically reason about the process, having the function be `partial` is not likely to cause problems.

```lean
partial def JSON.asString (val : JSON) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) val [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true]](#fpil-JSON___true) => "true"
| [false]](#fpil-JSON___false) => "false"
| [null]](#fpil-JSON___null) => "null"
| [string]](#fpil-JSON___string) s => "\"" ++ Lean.Json.escape s ++ "\""
| [number]](#fpil-JSON___number) n => [dropDecimals]](#fpil-dropDecimals) n.[toString](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___toString)
| [object]](#fpil-JSON___object) members =>
let memberToString mem :=
"\"" ++ Lean.Json.escape mem.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ++ "\": " ++ [asString]](#fpil-JSON___asString) mem.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
"{" ++ ", ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) (members.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) memberToString) ++ "}"
| [array]](#fpil-JSON___array) elements =>
"[" ++ ", ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) (elements.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) [asString]](#fpil-JSON___asString)) ++ "]"
```

With this definition, the output of serialization is easier to read:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([buildResponse]](#fpil-Ser___buildResponse) "Functional Programming in Lean" [Str]](#fpil-Ser___Str) "Programming is fun!").[asString]](#fpil-JSON___asString)
```

```lean
"{\"title\": \"Functional Programming in Lean\", \"status\": 200, \"record\": \"Programming is fun!\"}"
```

### 3.6.7. Messages You May Meet {#fpil-coercion-messages}

Natural number literals are overloaded with the `OfNat` type class.
Because coercions fire in cases where types don't match, rather than in cases of missing instances, a missing `OfNat` instance for a type does not cause a coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to be applied:

```lean
def [perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat]](#fpil-perhapsPerhapsPerhapsNat) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))) :=
392
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))) 392
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `392` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)))
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

### 3.6.8. Design Considerations {#fpil-coercion-design-considerations}

Coercions are a powerful tool that should be used responsibly.
On the one hand, they can allow an API to naturally follow the everyday rules of the domain being modeled.
This can be the difference between a bureaucratic mess of manual conversion functions and a clear program.
