As Abelson and Sussman wrote in the preface to *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* (MIT Press, 1996),

> Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute.

Coercions, used wisely, are a valuable means of achieving readable code that can serve as the basis for communication with domain experts.
APIs that rely heavily on coercions have a number of important limitations, however.
Think carefully about these limitations before using coercions in your own libraries.

First off, coercions are only applied in contexts where enough type information is available for Lean to know all of the types involved, because there are no output parameters in the coercion type classes. This means that a return type annotation on a function can be the difference between a type error and a successfully applied coercion.
For example, the coercion from non-empty lists to lists makes the following program work:

```lean
def lastSpider : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[List.getLast?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast___) idahoSpiders
```

On the other hand, if the type annotation is omitted, then the result type is unknown, so Lean is unable to find the coercion:

```lean
def lastSpider :=
[List.getLast?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast___) idahoSpiders
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  idahoSpiders
has type
  NonEmptyList [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
but is expected to have type
  [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ?m.3
in the application
  [List.getLast?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast___) idahoSpiders
```

More generally, when a coercion is not applied for some reason, the user receives the original type error, which can make it difficult to debug chains of coercions.

Finally, coercions are not applied in the context of field accessor notation.
This means that there is still an important difference between expressions that need to be coerced and those that don't, and this difference is visible to users of your API.

## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.7. Additional Conveniences {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-37-additional-conveniences}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Additional-Conveniences/

### 3.7.1. Constructor Syntax for Instances {#fpil-instance-constructor-syntax}

Behind the scenes, type classes are structure types and instances are values of these types.
The only differences are that Lean stores additional information about type classes, such as which parameters are output parameters, and that instances are registered for searching.
While values that have structure types are typically defined using either `⟨...⟩` syntax or with braces and fields, and instances are typically defined using `where`, both syntaxes work for both kinds of definition.

For example, a forestry application might represent trees as follows:

```lean
structure Tree : Type where
latinName : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
commonNames : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
def oak : [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) :=
⟨"Quercus robur", ["common oak", "European oak"]⟩
def birch : [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) :=
{ [latinName]](#fpil-Tree___latinName) := "Betula pendula",
[commonNames]](#fpil-Tree___commonNames) := ["silver birch", "warty birch"]
}
def sloe : [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) where
[latinName]](#fpil-Tree___latinName) := "Prunus spinosa"
[commonNames]](#fpil-Tree___commonNames) := ["sloe", "blackthorn"]
```

All three syntaxes are equivalent.

Similarly, type class instances can be defined using all three syntaxes:

```lean
class Display (α : Type) where
displayName : α → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
instance : [Display]](#fpil-Display) [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) :=
⟨[Tree.latinName]](#fpil-Tree___latinName)⟩
instance : [Display]](#fpil-Display) [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) :=
{ [displayName]](#fpil-Display___displayName) := [Tree.latinName]](#fpil-Tree___latinName) }
instance : [Display]](#fpil-Display) [Tree]](#fpil-Tree) where
[displayName]](#fpil-Display___displayName) t := t.[latinName]](#fpil-Tree___latinName)
```

The `where` syntax is typically used for instances, while structures use either the curly-brace syntax or the `where` syntax.
The `⟨...⟩` syntax can be useful when emphasizing that a structure type is very much like a tuple in which the fields happen to be named, but the names are not important at the moment.
However, there are situations where it can make sense to use other alternatives.
In particular, a library might provide a function that constructs an instance value.
Placing a call to this function after `:=` in an instance declaration is the easiest way to use such a function.

### 3.7.2. Examples {#fpil-example-command}

When experimenting with Lean code, definitions can be more convenient to use than `#eval` or `#check` commands.
First off, definitions don't produce any output, which can help keep the reader's focus on the most interesting output.
Secondly, it's easiest to write most Lean programs by starting with a type signature, allowing Lean to provide more assistance and better error messages while writing the program itself.
On the other hand, `#eval` and `#check` are easiest to use in contexts where Lean is able to determine the type from the provided expression.
Thirdly, `#eval` cannot be used with expressions whose types don't have `ToString` or `[Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)` instances, such as functions.
Finally, multi-step `do` blocks, `let`-expressions, and other syntactic forms that take multiple lines are particularly difficult to write with a type annotation in `#eval` or `#check`, simply because the required parenthesization can be difficult to predict.

To work around these issues, Lean supports the explicit indication of examples in a source file.
An example is like a definition without a name.
For instance, a non-empty list of birds commonly found in Copenhagen's green spaces can be written:

```lean
example : NonEmptyList [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
{ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "Sparrow",
[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := ["Duck", "Swan", "Magpie", "Eurasian coot", "Crow"]
}
```

Examples may define functions by accepting arguments:

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
n + k == k + n
```

While this creates a function behind the scenes, this function has no name and cannot be called.
Nonetheless, this is useful for demonstrating how a library can be used with arbitrary or unknown values of some given type.
In source files, `example` declarations are best paired with comments that explain how the example illustrates the concepts of the library.

## Overloading and Type Classes — 3.8. Summary {#fpil-overloading-and-type-classes-38-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Summary/

### 3.8.1. Type Classes and Overloading {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Summary--Type-Classes-and-Overloading}

Type classes are Lean's mechanism for overloading functions and operators.
A polymorphic function can be used with multiple types, but it behaves in the same manner no matter which type it is used with.
For example, a polymorphic function that appends two lists can be used no matter the type of the entries in the list, but it is unable to have different behavior depending on which particular type is found.
An operation that is overloaded with type classes, on the other hand, can also be used with multiple types.
However, each type requires its own implementation of the overloaded operation.
This means that the behavior can vary based on which type is provided.

A *type class* has a name, parameters, and a body that consists of a number of names with types.
The name is a way to refer to the overloaded operations, the parameters determine which aspects of the definitions can be overloaded, and the body provides the names and type signatures of the overloadable operations.
Each overloadable operation is called a *method* of the type class.
Type classes may provide default implementations of some methods in terms of the others, freeing implementors from defining each overload by hand when it is not needed.

An *instance* of a type class provides implementations of the methods for given parameters.
Instances may be polymorphic, in which case they can work for a variety of parameters, and they may optionally provide more specific implementations of default methods in cases where a more efficient version exists for some particular type.

Type class parameters are either *input parameters* (the default), or *output parameters* (indicated by an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` modifier).
Lean will not begin searching for an instance until all input parameters are no longer metavariables, while output parameters may be solved while searching for instances.
Parameters to a type class need not be types—they may also be ordinary values.
The `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` type class, used to overload natural number literals, takes the overloaded `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` itself as a parameter, which allows instances to restrict the allowed numbers.

Instances may be marked with a `@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance)]` attribute.
When an instance is a default instance, then it will be chosen as a fallback when Lean would otherwise fail to find an instance due to the presence of metavariables in the type.

### 3.8.2. Type Classes for Common Syntax {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Summary--Type-Classes-for-Common-Syntax}

Most infix operators in Lean are overridden with a type class.
For instance, the addition operator corresponds to a type class called `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)`.
Most of these operators have a corresponding heterogeneous version, in which the two arguments need not have the same type.
These heterogeneous operators are overloaded using a version of the class whose name starts with `H`, such as `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`.

Indexing syntax is overloaded using a type class called `GetElem`, which involves proofs.
`GetElem` has two output parameters, which are the type of elements to be extracted from the collection and a function that can be used to determine what counts as evidence that the index value is in bounds for the collection.
This evidence is described by a proposition, and Lean attempts to prove this proposition when array indexing is used.
When Lean is unable to check that list or array access operations are in bounds at compile time, the check can be deferred to run time by appending a `?` to the indexing syntax.

### 3.8.3. Functors {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Summary--Functors}

A functor is a polymorphic type that supports a mapping operation.
This mapping operation transforms all elements “in place”, changing no other structure.
For instance, lists are functors and the mapping operation may neither drop, duplicate, nor mix up entries in the list.

While functors are defined by having `map`, the `Functor` type class in Lean contains an additional default method that is responsible for mapping the constant function over a value, replacing all values whose type are given by polymorphic type variable with the same new value.
For some functors, this can be done more efficiently than traversing the entire structure.

### 3.8.4. Deriving Instances {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Summary--Deriving-Instances}

Many type classes have very standard implementations.
For instance, the Boolean equality class `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` is usually implemented by first checking whether both arguments are built with the same constructor, and then checking whether all their arguments are equal.
Instances for these classes can be created *automatically*.

When defining an inductive type or a structure, a `deriving` clause at the end of the declaration will cause instances to be created automatically.
Additionally, the `deriving instance`﻿` ... `﻿`for`﻿` ...` command can be used outside of the definition of a datatype to cause an instance to be generated.
Because each class for which instances can be derived requires special handling, not all classes are derivable.

### 3.8.5. Coercions {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Overloading-and-Type-Classes--Summary--Coercions}

Coercions allow Lean to recover from what would normally be a compile-time error by inserting a call to a function that transforms data from one type to another.
For example, the coercion from any type `α` to the type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α` allows values to be written directly, rather than with the `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` constructor, making `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` work more like nullable types from object-oriented languages.

There are multiple kinds of coercion.
They can recover from different kinds of errors, and they are represented by their own type classes.
The `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)` class is used to recover from type errors.
When Lean has an expression of type `α` in a context that expects something with type `β`, Lean first attempts to string together a chain of coercions that can transform `α`s into `β`s, and only displays the error when this cannot be done.
The `CoeDep` class takes the specific value being coerced as an extra parameter, allowing either further type class search to be done on the value or allowing constructors to be used in the instance to limit the scope of the conversion.
The `CoeFun` class intercepts what would otherwise be a “not a function” error when compiling a function application, and allows the value in the function position to be transformed into an actual function if possible.

## Monads {#fpil-monads}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/

In C# and Kotlin, the `?.` operator is a way to look up a property or call a method on a potentially-null value.
If the receiver is `null`, the whole expression is null.
Otherwise, the underlying non-`null` value receives the call.
Uses of `?.` can be chained, in which case the first `null` result terminates the chain of lookups.
Chaining null-checks like this is much more convenient than writing and maintaining deeply nested `if`s.

Similarly, exceptions are significantly more convenient than manually checking and propagating error codes.
At the same time, logging is easiest to accomplish by having a dedicated logging framework, rather than having each function return both its log results and its return value.
Chained null checks and exceptions typically require language designers to anticipate this use case, while logging frameworks typically make use of side effects to decouple code that logs from the accumulation of the logs.

## Monads — 4.1. One API, Many Applications {#fpil-monads-41-one-api-many-applications}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/One-API___-Many-Applications/

All these features and more can be implemented in library code as instances of a common API called `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`.
Lean provides dedicated syntax that makes this API convenient to use, but can also get in the way of understanding what is going on behind the scenes.
This chapter begins with the nitty-gritty presentation of manually nesting null checks, and builds from there to the convenient, general API.
Please suspend your disbelief in the meantime.

### 4.1.1. Checking for `none`: Don't Repeat Yourself {#fpil-example-option-monad}

In Lean, pattern matching can be used to chain checks for null.
Getting the first entry from a list can just use the optional indexing notation:

```lean
def first (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α :=
xs[0]?
```

The result must be an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` because empty lists have no first entry.
Extracting the first and third entries requires a check that each is not `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
def firstThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[0]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[2]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) third =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third)
```

Similarly, extracting the first, third, and fifth entries requires more checks that the values are not `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
def firstThirdFifth (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[0]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[2]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) third =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[4]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) fifth =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third, fifth)
```

And adding the seventh entry to this sequence begins to become quite unmanageable:

```lean
def firstThirdFifthSeventh (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α × α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[0]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[2]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) third =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[4]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) fifth =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[6]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) seventh =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third, fifth, seventh)
```

The fundamental problem with this code is that it addresses two concerns: extracting the numbers and checking that all of them are present.
The second concern is addressed by copying and pasting the code that handles the `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` case.
It is often good style to lift a repetitive segment into a helper function:

```lean
def andThen (opt : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α) (next : α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) β) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) β :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) opt [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => next x
```

This helper, which is used similarly to `?.` in C# and Kotlin, takes care of propagating `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` values.
It takes two arguments: an optional value and a function to apply when the value is not `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
If the first argument is `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, then the helper returns `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
If the first argument is not `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, then the function is applied to the contents of the `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` constructor.

Now, `firstThird` can be rewritten to use `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)` instead of pattern matching:

```lean
def firstThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α) :=
[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen) xs[0]? fun first =>
[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen) xs[2]? fun third =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third)
```

In Lean, functions don't need to be enclosed in parentheses when passed as arguments.
The following equivalent definition uses more parentheses and indents the bodies of functions:

```lean
def firstThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α) :=
[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen) xs[0]? (fun first =>
[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen) xs[2]? (fun third =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third)))
```

The `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)` helper provides a sort of “pipeline” through which values flow, and the version with the somewhat unusual indentation is more suggestive of this fact.
Improving the syntax used to write `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)` can make these computations even easier to understand.

#### 4.1.1.1. Infix Operators {#fpil-defining-infix-operators}

In Lean, infix operators can be declared using the `infix`, `infixl`, and `infixr` commands, which create (respectively) non-associative, left-associative, and right-associative operators.
When used multiple times in a row, a *left associative* operator stacks up the opening parentheses on the left side of the expression.
The addition operator `+` is left associative, so `w + x + y + z` is equivalent to `(((w + x) + y) + z)`.
The exponentiation operator `^` is right associative, so `w ^ x ^ y ^ z` is equivalent to `w ^ (x ^ (y ^ z))`.
Comparison operators such as `<` are non-associative, so `x < y < z` is a syntax error and requires manual parentheses.

The following declaration makes `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)` into an infix operator:

```lean
infixl:55 " ~~> " => [andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)
```

The number following the colon declares the *precedence* of the new infix operator.
In ordinary mathematical notation, `x + y * z` is equivalent to `x + (y * z)` even though both `+` and `*` are left associative.
In Lean, `+` has precedence 65 and `*` has precedence 70.
Higher-precedence operators are applied before lower-precedence operators.
According to the declaration of `~~>`, both `+` and `*` have higher precedence, and thus apply first.
Typically, figuring out the most convenient precedences for a group of operators requires some experimentation and a large collection of examples.

Following the new infix operator is a double arrow `=>`, which specifies the named function to be used for the infix operator.
Lean's standard library uses this feature to define `+` and `*` as infix operators that point at `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)` and `[HMul.hMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)`, respectively, allowing type classes to be used to overload the infix operators.
Here, however, `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)` is just an ordinary function.

Having defined an infix operator for `[andThen]](#fpil-Monads___Option___M___andThen)`, `firstThird` can be rewritten in a way that brings the “pipeline” feeling of `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`-checks front and center:

```lean
def firstThirdInfix (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α) :=
xs[0]? ~~> fun first =>
xs[2]? ~~> fun third =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third)
```

This style is much more concise when writing larger functions:

```lean
def firstThirdFifthSeventh (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (α × α × α × α) :=
xs[0]? ~~> fun first =>
xs[2]? ~~> fun third =>
xs[4]? ~~> fun fifth =>
xs[6]? ~~> fun seventh =>
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (first, third, fifth, seventh)
```

### 4.1.2. Propagating Error Messages {#fpil-example-except-monad}

Pure functional languages such as Lean have no built-in exception mechanism for error handling, because throwing or catching an exception is outside of the step-by-step evaluation model for expressions.
However, functional programs certainly need to handle errors.
In the case of `firstThirdFifthSeventh`, it is likely relevant for a user to know just how long the list was and where the lookup failed.

This is typically accomplished by defining a datatype that can be either an error or a result, and translating functions with exceptions into functions that return this datatype:

```lean
inductive Except (ε : Type) (α : Type) where
| error : ε → Except ε α
| ok : α → Except ε α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk), [Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk), [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

The type variable `ε` stands for the type of errors that can be produced by the function.
Callers are expected to handle both errors and successes, which makes the type variable `ε` play a role that is a bit like that of a list of checked exceptions in Java.

Similarly to `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `Except` can be used to indicate a failure to find an entry in a list.
In this case, the error type is a `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`:

```lean
def get (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[i]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) s!"Index {i} not found (maximum is {xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) - 1})"
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x
```

Looking up an in-bounds value yields an `[Except.ok]](#fpil-FakeExcept___Except___ok)`:

```lean
def ediblePlants : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
["ramsons", "sea plantain", "sea buckthorn", "garden nasturtium"]
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) [ediblePlants]](#fpil-Monads___Err___ediblePlants) 2
```

```lean
Except.ok "sea buckthorn"
```

Looking up an out-of-bounds value yields an `[Except.error]](#fpil-FakeExcept___Except___error)`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) [ediblePlants]](#fpil-Monads___Err___ediblePlants) 4
```

```lean
Except.error "Index 4 not found (maximum is 3)"
```

A single list lookup can conveniently return a value or an error:

```lean
def first (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0
```

However, performing two list lookups requires handling potential failures:

```lean
def firstThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) third =>
[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) (first, third)
```

Adding another list lookup to the function requires still more error handling:

```lean
def firstThirdFifth (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) third =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 4 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) fifth =>
[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) (first, third, fifth)
```

And one more list lookup begins to become quite unmanageable:

```lean
def firstThirdFifthSeventh (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α × α × α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) first =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) third =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 4 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) fifth =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 6 [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) seventh =>
[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) (first, third, fifth, seventh)
```

Once again, a common pattern can be factored out into a helper.
Each step through the function checks for an error, and only proceeds with the rest of the computation if the result was a success.
A new version of `andThen` can be defined for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`:

```lean
def andThen (attempt : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e α) (next : α → [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e β) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e β :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) attempt [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) msg
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x => next x
```

Just as with `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, this version of `andThen` allows a more concise definition of `firstThird'`:

```lean
def firstThird' (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α) :=
andThen ([get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0) fun first =>
andThen ([get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2) fun third =>
[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) (first, third)
```

In both the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` case, there are two repeating patterns: there is the checking of intermediate results at each step, which has been factored out into `andThen`, and there is the final successful result, which is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` or `[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, respectively.
For the sake of convenience, success can be factored out into a helper called `ok`:

```lean
def ok (x : α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α := [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x
```

Similarly, failure can be factored out into a helper called `fail`:

```lean
def fail (err : ε) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α := [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) err
```

Using `ok` and `fail` makes `get` a little more readable:

```lean
def get (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[i]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => fail s!"Index {i} not found (maximum is {xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) - 1})"
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => ok x
```

After adding the infix declaration for `andThen`, `firstThird` can be just as concise as the version that returns an `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
infixl:55 " ~~> " => andThen
```

```lean
def firstThird (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α) :=
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0 ~~> fun first =>
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2 ~~> fun third =>
ok (first, third)
```

The technique scales similarly to larger functions:

```lean
def firstThirdFifthSeventh (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) (α × α × α × α) :=
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 0 ~~> fun first =>
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 2 ~~> fun third =>
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 4 ~~> fun fifth =>
[get]](#fpil-Monads___Err___get) xs 6 ~~> fun seventh =>
ok (first, third, fifth, seventh)
```

### 4.1.3. Logging {#fpil-logging}

A number is even if dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder:

```lean
def isEven (i : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
i % 2 == 0
```

The function `sumAndFindEvens` computes the sum of a list while remembering the even numbers encountered along the way:

```lean
def sumAndFindEvens : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) × [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [] => ([], 0)
| i :: is =>
let (moreEven, sum) := sumAndFindEvens is
([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [isEven]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___isEven) i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) i :: moreEven [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) moreEven, sum + i)
```

This function is a simplified example of a common pattern.
Many programs need to traverse a data structure once, while both computing a main result and accumulating some kind of tertiary extra result.
One example of this is logging: a program that is an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action can always log to a file on disk, but because the disk is outside of the mathematical world of Lean functions, it becomes much more difficult to prove things about logs based on `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`.
Another example is a function that computes the sum of all the nodes in a tree with an inorder traversal, while simultaneously recording each nodes visited:

```lean
def inorderSum : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) × [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => ([], 0)
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r =>
let (leftVisited, leftSum) := inorderSum l
let (hereVisited, hereSum) := ([x], x)
let (rightVisited, rightSum) := inorderSum r
(leftVisited ++ hereVisited ++ rightVisited,
leftSum + hereSum + rightSum)
```

Both `sumAndFindEvens` and `inorderSum` have a common repetitive structure.
Each step of computation returns a pair that consists of a list of data that have been saved along with the primary result.
The lists are then appended, and the primary result is computed and paired with the appended lists.
The common structure becomes more apparent with a small rewrite of `sumAndFindEvens` that more cleanly separates the concerns of saving even numbers and computing the sum:

```lean
def sumAndFindEvens : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) × [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [] => ([], 0)
| i :: is =>
let (moreEven, sum) := sumAndFindEvens is
let (evenHere, ()) := ([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [isEven]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___isEven) i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [i] [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [], ())
(evenHere ++ moreEven, sum + i)
```

For the sake of clarity, a pair that consists of an accumulated result together with a value can be given its own name:

```lean
structure WithLog (logged : Type) (α : Type) where
log : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) logged
val : α
```

Similarly, the process of saving a list of accumulated results while passing a value on to the next step of a computation can be factored out into a helper, once again named `andThen`:

```lean
def andThen (result : WithLog α β) (next : β → WithLog α γ) : WithLog α γ :=
let {[log]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___log) := thisOut, [val]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___val) := thisRes} := result
let {[log]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___log) := nextOut, [val]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___val) := nextRes} := next thisRes
{[log]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___log) := thisOut ++ nextOut, [val]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___val) := nextRes}
```

In the case of errors, `ok` represents an operation that always succeeds.
Here, however, it is an operation that simply returns a value without logging anything:

```lean
def ok (x : β) : WithLog α β := {[log]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___log) := [], [val]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___val) := x}
```

Just as `Except` provides `fail` as a possibility, `WithLog` should allow items to be added to a log.
This has no interesting return value associated with it, so it returns `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`:

```lean
def save (data : α) : WithLog α [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
{[log]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___log) := [data], [val]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithLog___val) := ()}
```

`WithLog`, `andThen`, `ok`, and `save` can be used to separate the logging concern from the summing concern in both programs:

```lean
def sumAndFindEvens : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → WithLog [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [] => ok 0
| i :: is =>
andThen ([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [isEven]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___isEven) i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) save i [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) ok ()) fun () =>
andThen ([sumAndFindEvens]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithAndThen___sumAndFindEvens) is) fun sum =>
ok (i + sum)
```

```lean
def inorderSum : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → WithLog [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => ok 0
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r =>
andThen ([inorderSum]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithAndThen___inorderSum) l) fun leftSum =>
andThen (save x) fun () =>
andThen ([inorderSum]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithAndThen___inorderSum) r) fun rightSum =>
ok (leftSum + x + rightSum)
```

And, once again, the infix operator helps put focus on the correct steps:

```lean
infixl:55 " ~~> " => andThen
```

```lean
def sumAndFindEvens : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → WithLog [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [] => ok 0
| i :: is =>
([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [isEven]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___isEven) i [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) save i [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) ok ()) ~~> fun () =>
[sumAndFindEvens]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithInfix___sumAndFindEvens) is ~~> fun sum =>
ok (i + sum)
def inorderSum : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → WithLog [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => ok 0
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r =>
[inorderSum]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithInfix___inorderSum) l ~~> fun leftSum =>
save x ~~> fun () =>
[inorderSum]](#fpil-Monads___Writer___WithInfix___inorderSum) r ~~> fun rightSum =>
ok (leftSum + x + rightSum)
```

### 4.1.4. Numbering Tree Nodes {#fpil-numbering-tree-nodes}

An *inorder numbering* of a tree associates each data point in the tree with the step it would be visited at in an inorder traversal of the tree.
For example, consider `aTree`:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) BinTree [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___in)
def aTree :=
[branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch)
([branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch)
([branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) [leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) "a" ([branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) [leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) "b" [leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf)))
"c"
[leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf))
"d"
([branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) [leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) "e" [leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf))
```

Its inorder numbering is:

```lean
BinTree.branch
  (BinTree.branch
    (BinTree.branch (BinTree.leaf) (0, "a") (BinTree.branch (BinTree.leaf) (1, "b") (BinTree.leaf)))
    (2, "c")
    (BinTree.leaf))
  (3, "d")
  (BinTree.branch (BinTree.leaf) (4, "e") (BinTree.leaf))
```

Trees are most naturally processed with recursive functions, but the usual pattern of recursion on trees makes it difficult to compute an inorder numbering.
This is because the highest number assigned anywhere in the left subtree is used to determine the numbering of a node's data value, and then again to determine the starting point for numbering the right subtree.
In an imperative language, this issue can be worked around by using a mutable variable that contains the next number to be assigned.
The following Python program computes an inorder numbering using a mutable variable:

```
class Branch:
    def __init__(self, value, left=None, right=None):
        self.left = left
        self.value = value
        self.right = right
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Branch({self.value!r}, left={self.left!r}, right={self.right!r})'

def number(tree):
    num = 0
    def helper(t):
        nonlocal num
        if t is None:
            return None
        else:
            new_left = helper(t.left)
            new_value = (num, t.value)
            num += 1
            new_right = helper(t.right)
            return Branch(left=new_left, value=new_value, right=new_right)

    return helper(tree)
```

The numbering of the Python equivalent of `aTree` is:

```
a_tree = Branch("d",
                left=Branch("c",
                            left=Branch("a", left=None, right=Branch("b")),
                            right=None),
                right=Branch("e"))
```

and its numbering is:

``>>> `number(a_tree)`

```
Branch((3, 'd'), left=Branch((2, 'c'), left=Branch((0, 'a'), left=None, right=Branch((1, 'b'), left=None, right=None)), right=None), right=Branch((4, 'e'), left=None, right=None))
```

Even though Lean does not have mutable variables, a workaround exists.
From the point of view of the rest of the world, the mutable variable can be thought of as having two relevant aspects: its value when the function is called, and its value when the function returns.
In other words, a function that uses a mutable variable can be seen as a function that takes the mutable variable's starting value as an argument, returning a pair of the variable's final value and the function's result.
This final value can then be passed as an argument to the next step.

Just as the Python example uses an outer function that establishes a mutable variable and an inner helper function that changes the variable, a Lean version of the function uses an outer function that provides the variable's starting value and explicitly returns the function's result along with an inner helper function that threads the variable's value while computing the numbered tree:

```lean
def number (t : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α) : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) :=
let rec helper (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α))
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => (n, [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf))
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) left x right =>
let (k, numberedLeft) := [helper]](#fpil-Monads___State___number___helper) n left
let (i, numberedRight) := [helper]](#fpil-Monads___State___number___helper) (k + 1) right
(i, [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) numberedLeft (k, x) numberedRight)
([helper]](#fpil-Monads___State___number___helper) 0 t).[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

This code, like the `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`-propagating `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` code, the `[error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`-propagating `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` code, and the log-accumulating `WithLog` code, commingles two concerns: propagating the value of the counter, and actually traversing the tree to find the result.
Just as in those cases, an `andThen` helper can be defined to propagate state from one step of a computation to another.
The first step is to give a name to the pattern of taking an input state as an argument and returning an output state together with a value:

```lean
def State (σ : Type) (α : Type) : Type :=
σ → (σ × α)
```

In the case of `State`, `ok` is a function that returns the input state unchanged, along with the provided value:

```lean
def ok (x : α) : State σ α :=
fun s => (s, x)
```

When working with a mutable variable, there are two fundamental operations: reading the value and replacing it with a new one.
Reading the current value is accomplished with a function that places the input state unmodified into the output state, and also places it into the value field:

```lean
def get : State σ σ :=
fun s => (s, s)
```

Writing a new value consists of ignoring the input state, and placing the provided new value into the output state:

```lean
def set (s : σ) : State σ [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
fun _ => (s, ())
```

Finally, two computations that use state can be sequenced by finding both the output state and return value of the first function, then passing them both into the next function:

```lean
def andThen (first : State σ α) (next : α → State σ β) : State σ β :=
fun s =>
let (s', x) := first s
next x s'
infixl:55 " ~~> " => andThen
```

Using `State` and its helpers, local mutable state can be simulated:

```lean
def number (t : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α) : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) :=
let rec helper : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → State [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α))
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => ok [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf)
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) left x right =>
helper left ~~> fun numberedLeft =>
get ~~> fun n =>
set (n + 1) ~~> fun () =>
helper right ~~> fun numberedRight =>
ok ([BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) numberedLeft (n, x) numberedRight)
(helper t 0).snd
```

Because `State` simulates only a single local variable, `get` and `set` don't need to refer to any particular variable name.

### 4.1.5. Monads: A Functional Design Pattern {#fpil-monad-as-design-pattern}

Each of these examples has consisted of:

- A polymorphic type, such as `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε`, `WithLog α`, or `State σ`
- An operator `andThen` that takes care of some repetitive aspect of sequencing programs that have this type
- An operator `ok` that is (in some sense) the most boring way to use the type
- A collection of other operations, such as `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `fail`, `save`, and `get`, that name ways of using the type

This style of API is called a *monad*.
While the idea of monads is derived from a branch of mathematics called category theory, no understanding of category theory is needed in order to use them for programming.
The key idea of monads is that each monad encodes a particular kind of side effect using the tools provided by the pure functional language Lean.
For example, `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` represents programs that can fail by returning `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` represents programs that can throw exceptions, `WithLog` represents programs that accumulate a log while running, and `State` represents programs with a single mutable variable.

---



## Monads — 4.2. The Monad Type Class {#fpil-monads-42-the-monad-type-class}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/The-Monad-Type-Class/

Rather than having to import an operator like `ok` or `andThen` for each type that is a monad, the Lean standard library contains a type class that allow them to be overloaded, so that the same operators can be used for *any* monad.
Monads have two operations, which are the equivalent of `ok` and `andThen`:

```lean
class Monad (m : Type → Type) where
pure : α → m α
bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β
```

This definition is slightly simplified.
The actual definition in the Lean library is somewhat more involved, and will be presented later.

The `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instances for `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε` can be created by adapting the definitions of their respective `andThen` operations:

```lean
instance : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) opt next :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) opt [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => next x
instance : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) attempt next :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) attempt [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e => [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x => next x
```

As an example, `firstThirdFifthSeventh` was defined separately for `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α` and `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α` return types.
Now, it can be defined polymorphically for *any* monad.
It does, however, require a lookup function as an argument, because different monads might fail to find a result in different ways.
The infix version of `bind` is `>>=`, which plays the same role as `~~>` in the examples.

```lean
def firstThirdFifthSeventh [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (lookup : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → m α)
(xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : m (α × α × α × α) :=
lookup xs 0 >>= fun first =>
lookup xs 2 >>= fun third =>
lookup xs 4 >>= fun fifth =>
lookup xs 6 >>= fun seventh =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (first, third, fifth, seventh)
```

Given example lists of slow mammals and fast birds, this implementation of `firstThirdFifthSeventh` can be used with `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
def slowMammals : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
["Three-toed sloth", "Slow loris"]
def fastBirds : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := [
"Peregrine falcon",
"Saker falcon",
"Golden eagle",
"Gray-headed albatross",
"Spur-winged goose",
"Swift",
"Anna's hummingbird"
]
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) firstThirdFifthSeventh (fun xs i => xs[i]?) [slowMammals]](#fpil-slowMammals)
```

```lean
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) firstThirdFifthSeventh (fun xs i => xs[i]?) [fastBirds]](#fpil-fastBirds)
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)"Peregrine falcon"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) "Golden eagle"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) "Spur-winged goose"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) "Anna's hummingbird"[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

After renaming `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`'s lookup function `get` to something more specific, the very same implementation of `firstThirdFifthSeventh` can be used with `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` as well:

```lean
def getOrExcept (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs[i]? [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) =>
[Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) s!"Index {i} not found (maximum is {xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) - 1})"
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x =>
[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) firstThirdFifthSeventh [getOrExcept]](#fpil-Errs___getOrExcept) [slowMammals]](#fpil-slowMammals)
```

```lean
Except.error "Index 2 not found (maximum is 1)"
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) firstThirdFifthSeventh [getOrExcept]](#fpil-Errs___getOrExcept) [fastBirds]](#fpil-fastBirds)
```

```lean
Except.ok ("Peregrine falcon", "Golden eagle", "Spur-winged goose", "Anna's hummingbird")
```

The fact that `m` must have a `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance means that the `>>=` and `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` operations are available.

### 4.2.1. General Monad Operations {#fpil-monad-class-polymorphism}

Because many different types are monads, functions that are polymorphic over *any* monad are very powerful.
For example, the function `mapM` is a version of `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` that uses a `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` to sequence and combine the results of applying a function:

```lean
def mapM [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (f : α → m β) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → m ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β)
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) []
| x :: xs =>
f x >>= fun hd =>
mapM f xs >>= fun tl =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (hd :: tl)
```

The return type of the function argument `f` determines which `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance will be used.
In other words, `mapM` can be used for functions that produce logs, for functions that can fail, or for functions that use mutable state.
Because `f`'s type determines the available effects, they can be tightly controlled by API designers.

As described in [this chapter's introduction]](#fpil-numbering-tree-nodes), `State σ α` represents programs that make use of a mutable variable of type `σ` and return a value of type `α`.
These programs are actually functions from a starting state to a pair of a value and a final state.
The `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` class requires that its parameter expect a single type argument—that is, it should be a `Type → Type`.
This means that the instance for `State` should mention the state type `σ`, which becomes a parameter to the instance:

