## Monads — 4.5. The IO Monad {#fpil-monads-45-the-io-monad}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/The-IO-Monad/

`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` as a monad can be understood from two perspectives, which were described in the section on [running programs]](#fpil-running-a-program).
Each can help to understand the meanings of `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` and `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` for `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`.

From the first perspective, an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action is an instruction to Lean's run-time system.
For example, the instruction might be “read a string from this file descriptor, then re-invoke the pure Lean code with the string”.
This perspective is an *exterior* one, viewing the program from the perspective of the operating system.
In this case, `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action that does not request any effects from the RTS, and `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` instructs the RTS to first carry out one potentially-effectful operation and then invoke the rest of the program with the resulting value.

From the second perspective, an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action transforms the whole world.
`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions are actually pure, because they receive a unique world as an argument and then return the changed world.
This perspective is an *interior* one that matches how `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` is represented inside of Lean.
The world is represented in Lean as a token, and the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad is structured to make sure that each token is used exactly once.

To see how this works, it can be helpful to peel back one definition at a time.
The `#print` command reveals the internals of Lean datatypes and definitions.
For example,

```lean
#print [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

results in

```lean
inductive Nat : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
Nat.zero : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
Nat.succ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

and

```lean
#print [String.toLower](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___toLower)
```

results in

```lean
def String.toLower : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
fun s => [String.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___map) [Char.toLower](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___toLower) s
```

Sometimes, the output of `#print` includes Lean features that have not yet been presented in this book.
For example,

```lean
#print [List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___)
```

produces

```lean
def List.head?.{u} : {α : Type u} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α :=
fun {α} x =>
  match x with
  | [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
  | a [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) tail => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) a
```

which includes a `.{u}` after the definition's name, and annotates types as `Type u` rather than just `Type`.
This can be safely ignored for now.

Printing the definition of `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` shows that it's defined in terms of simpler structures:

```lean
#print [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)
```

```lean
@[reducible] def IO : Type → Type :=
[EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)
```

`[IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)` represents all the errors that could be thrown by an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action:

```lean
#print [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)
```

```lean
inductive IO.Error : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
IO.Error.alreadyExists : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)
IO.Error.otherError : [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)

IO.Error.unexpectedEof : [IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)

```

`[EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO) ε α` represents `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that will either terminate with an error of type `ε` or succeed with a value of type `α`.
This means that, like the `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε` monad, the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad includes the ability to define error handling and exceptions.

Peeling back another layer, `[EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO)` is itself defined in terms of a simpler structure:

```lean
#print [EIO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#EIO)
```

```lean
def EIO : Type → Type → Type :=
fun ε α => [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε IO.RealWorld α
```

The `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST)` monad includes both errors and state—it's similar to a combination of `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` and `State`.
It is defined using another type, `EST.Out`:

```lean
#print [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST)
```

```lean
def EST : Type → Type → Type → Type :=
fun ε σ α => Void σ → EST.Out ε σ α
```

In other words, a program with type `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ α` is a function that accepts an initial state of type `σ` and returns an `EST.Out ε σ α`.
The state is wrapped in the type `Void`, which is an internal primitive that causes a value to be erased from compiled code; `Void σ` has the same representation as `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`.

`EST.Out` is very much like the definition of `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, with one constructor that indicates a successful termination and one constructor that indicates an error:

```lean
#print EST.Out
```

```lean
inductive EST.Out : Type → Type → Type → Type
number of parameters: 3
constructors:
EST.Out.ok : {ε σ α : Type} → α → Void σ → EST.Out ε σ α
EST.Out.error : {ε σ α : Type} → ε → Void σ → EST.Out ε σ α
```

Just like `Except ε α`, the `ok` constructor includes a result of type `α`, and the `error` constructor includes an exception of type `ε`.
Unlike `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, both constructors have an additional state field that includes the final state of the computation.

The `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ` requires `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` and `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)`.
Just as with `State`, the implementation of `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` for `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST)` accepts an initial state and returns it unchanged, and just as with `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, it returns its argument in the `ok` constructor:

```lean
#print EST.pure
```

```lean
protected def EST.pure : {α ε σ : Type} → α → [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ α :=
fun {α ε σ} a s => EST.Out.ok a s
```

`protected` means that the full name `EST.pure` is needed even if the `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST)` namespace has been opened.

Similarly, `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` for `[EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST)` takes an initial state as an argument.
It passes this initial state to its first action.
Like `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, it then checks whether the result is an error.
If so, the error is returned unchanged and the second argument to `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` remains unused.
If the result was a success, then the second argument is applied to both the returned value and to the resulting state.

```lean
#print EST.bind
```

```lean
protected def EST.bind : {ε σ α β : Type} → [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ α → (α → [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ β) → [EST](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Mutable-References/#EST) ε σ β :=
fun {ε σ α β} x f s =>
  match x s with
  | EST.Out.ok a s => f a s
  | EST.Out.error e s => EST.Out.error e s
```

Putting all of this together, `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` is a monad that tracks state and errors at the same time.
The collection of available errors is that given by the datatype `[IO.Error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO___Error___alreadyExists)`, which has constructors that describe many things that can go wrong in a program.
The state is a type that represents the real world, called `IO.RealWorld`.
Each basic `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action receives this real world and returns another one, paired either with an error or a result.
In `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`, `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` returns the world unchanged, while `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` passes the modified world from one action into the next action.

Because the entire universe doesn't fit in a computer's memory, the world being passed around is just a representation.
So long as world tokens are not re-used, the representation is safe.
The type `IO.RealWorld` is a trivial primitive type that does not need any representation at all, because it is only used inside of `Void`.

---



## Monads — 4.6. Additional Conveniences {#fpil-monads-46-additional-conveniences}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/Additional-Conveniences/

### 4.6.1. Shared Argument Types {#fpil-shared-argument-types}

When defining a function that takes multiple arguments that have the same type, both can be written before the same colon.
For example,

```lean
def equal? [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] (x : α) (y : α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x == y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

can be written

```lean
def equal? [[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk) α] (x y : α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x == y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

This is especially useful when the type signature is large.

### 4.6.2. Leading Dot Notation {#fpil-leading-dot-notation}

The constructors of an inductive type are in a namespace.
This allows multiple related inductive types to use the same constructor names, but it can lead to programs becoming verbose.
In contexts where the inductive type in question is known, the namespace can be omitted by preceding the constructor's name with a dot, and Lean uses the expected type to resolve the constructor names.
For example, a function that mirrors a binary tree can be written:

```lean
def BinTree.mirror : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α
| [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => [BinTree.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf)
| [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r => [BinTree.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) ([mirror]](#fpil-Old___BinTree___mirror) r) x ([mirror]](#fpil-Old___BinTree___mirror) l)
```

Omitting the namespaces makes it significantly shorter, at the cost of making the program harder to read in contexts like code review tools that don't include the Lean compiler:

```lean
def BinTree.mirror : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α → [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α
| [.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf) => .leaf
| [.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) l x r => [.branch]](#fpil-BinTree___branch) (mirror r) x (mirror l)
```

Using the expected type of an expression to disambiguate a namespace is also applicable to names other than constructors.
If `BinTree.empty` is defined as an alternative way of creating `[BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree)`s, then it can also be used with dot notation:

```lean
def BinTree.empty : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) α := [.leaf]](#fpil-BinTree___leaf)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (.empty : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
BinTree.empty : [BinTree]](#fpil-BinTree) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

### 4.6.3. Or-Patterns {#fpil-or-patterns}

In contexts that allow multiple patterns, such as `match`-expressions, multiple patterns may share their result expressions.
The datatype `Weekday` that represents days of the week:

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| monday
| tuesday
| wednesday
| thursday
| friday
| saturday
| sunday
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

Pattern matching can be used to check whether a day is a weekend:

```lean
def Weekday.isWeekend (day : Weekday) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) day [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Weekday.saturday]](#fpil-Weekday___saturday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [Weekday.sunday]](#fpil-Weekday___sunday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

This can already be simplified by using constructor dot notation:

```lean
def Weekday.isWeekend (day : Weekday) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) day [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.saturday]](#fpil-Weekday___saturday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.sunday]](#fpil-Weekday___sunday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Because both weekend patterns have the same result expression (`[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), they can be condensed into one:

```lean
def Weekday.isWeekend (day : Weekday) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) day [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.saturday]](#fpil-Weekday___saturday) | [.sunday]](#fpil-Weekday___sunday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

This can be further simplified into a version in which the argument is not named:

```lean
def Weekday.isWeekend : Weekday → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [.saturday]](#fpil-Weekday___saturday) | [.sunday]](#fpil-Weekday___sunday) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Behind the scenes, the result expression is simply duplicated across each pattern.
This means that patterns can bind variables, as in this example that removes the `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)` and `[inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)` constructors from a sum type in which both contain the same type of value:

```lean
def condense : α ⊕ α → α
| [.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) x | [.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) x => x
```

Because the result expression is duplicated, the variables bound by the patterns are not required to have the same types.
Overloaded functions that work for multiple types may be used to write a single result expression that works for patterns that bind variables of different types:

```lean
def stringy : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ⊕ Weekday → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| [.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) x | [.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) x => s!"It is {[repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#repr-next) x}"
```

In practice, only variables shared in all patterns can be referred to in the result expression, because the result must make sense for each pattern.
In `getTheNat`, only `n` can be accessed, and attempts to use either `x` or `y` lead to errors.

```lean
def getTheNat : ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) ⊕ ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × β) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, x) | [.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, y) => n
```

Attempting to access `x` in a similar definition causes an error because there is no `x` available in the second pattern:

```lean
def getTheAlpha : ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) ⊕ ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) → α
| [.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, x) | [.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, y) => x
```

```lean
Unknown identifier `x`
```

The fact that the result expression is essentially copy-pasted to each branch of the pattern match can lead to some surprising behavior.
For example, the following definitions are acceptable because the `[inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)` version of the result expression refers to the global definition of `str`:

```lean
def str := "Some string"
def getTheString : ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) ⊕ ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × β) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| [.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, str) | [.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (n, y) => str
```

Calling this function on both constructors reveals the confusing behavior.
In the first case, a type annotation is needed to tell Lean which type `β` should be:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [getTheString]](#fpil-getTheString) ([.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (20, "twenty") : ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) ⊕ ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)))
```

```lean
"twenty"
```

In the second case, the global definition is used:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [getTheString]](#fpil-getTheString) ([.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) (20, "twenty"))
```

```lean
"Some string"
```

Using or-patterns can vastly simplify some definitions and increase their clarity, as in `Weekday.isWeekend`.
Because there is a potential for confusing behavior, it's a good idea to be careful when using them, especially when variables of multiple types or disjoint sets of variables are involved.

## Monads — 4.7. Summary {#fpil-monads-47-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/Summary/

### 4.7.1. Encoding Side Effects {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monads--Summary--Encoding-Side-Effects}

Lean is a pure functional language.
This means that it does not include side effects such as mutable variables, logging, or exceptions.
However, most side effects can be *encoded* using a combination of functions and inductive types or structures.
For example, mutable state can be encoded as a function from an initial state to a pair of a final state and a result, and exceptions can be encoded as an inductive type with constructors for successful termination and errors.

Each set of encoded effects is a type.
As a result, if a program uses these encoded effects, then this is apparent in its type.
Functional programming does not mean that programs can't use effects, it simply requires that they be *honest* about which effects they use.
A Lean type signature describes not only the types of arguments that a function expects and the type of result that it returns, but also which effects it may use.

### 4.7.2. The Monad Type Class {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monads--Summary--The-Monad-Type-Class}

It's possible to write purely functional programs in languages that allow effects anywhere.
For example, `2 + 3` is a valid Python program that has no effects at all.
Similarly, combining programs that have effects requires a way to state the order in which the effects must occur.
It matters whether an exception is thrown before or after modifying a variable, after all.

The type class `Monad` captures these two important properties.
It has two methods: `pure` represents programs that have no effects, and `bind` sequences effectful programs.
The contract for `Monad` instances ensures that `bind` and `pure` actually capture pure computation and sequencing.

### 4.7.3. `do`-Notation for Monads {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monads--Summary--do--Notation-for-Monads}

Rather than being limited to `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`, `do`-notation works for any monad.
It allows programs that use monads to be written in a style that is reminiscent of statement-oriented languages, with statements sequenced after one another.
Additionally, `do`-notation enables a number of additional convenient shorthands, such as nested actions.
A program written with `do` is translated to applications of `>>=` behind the scenes.

### 4.7.4. Custom Monads {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monads--Summary--Custom-Monads}

Different languages provide different sets of side effects.
While most languages feature mutable variables and file I/O, not all have features like exceptions.
Other languages offer effects that are rare or unique, like Icon's search-based program execution, Scheme and Ruby's continuations, and Common Lisp's resumable exceptions.
An advantage to encoding effects with monads is that programs are not limited to the set of effects that are provided by the language.
Because Lean is designed to make programming with any monad convenient, programmers are free to choose exactly the set of side effects that make sense for any given application.

### 4.7.5. The `IO` Monad {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monads--Summary--The--IO--Monad}

Programs that can affect the real world are written as `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions in Lean.
`[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` is one monad among many.
The `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad encodes state and exceptions, with the state being used to keep track of the state of the world and the exceptions modeling failure and recovery.

## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/

`[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` both describe operations for types that are still waiting for a type argument.
One way to understand them is that `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` describes containers in which the contained data can be transformed, and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` describes an encoding of programs with side effects.
This understanding is incomplete, however.
After all, `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` has instances for both `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, and simultaneously represents an optional value *and* a computation that might fail to return a value.

From the perspective of data structures, `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` is a bit like a nullable type or like a list that can contain at most one entry.
From the perspective of control structures, `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` represents a computation that might terminate early without a result.
Typically, programs that use the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance are easiest to think of as using `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` as a data structure, while programs that use the `Monad` instance are easiest to think of as using `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` to allow early failure, but learning to use both of these perspectives fluently is an important part of becoming proficient at functional programming.

There is a deeper relationship between functors and monads.
It turns out that *every monad is a functor*.
Another way to say this is that the monad abstraction is more powerful than the functor abstraction, because not every functor is a monad.
Furthermore, there is an additional intermediate abstraction, called *applicative functors*, that has enough power to write many interesting programs and yet permits libraries that cannot use the `Monad` interface.
The type class `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` provides the overloadable operations of applicative functors.
Every monad is an applicative functor, and every applicative functor is a functor, but the converses do not hold.

1. [5.1. Structures and Inheritance](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Structures-and-Inheritance/#structure-inheritance)
2. [5.2. Applicative Functors](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Applicative-Functors/#applicative)
3. [5.3. The Applicative Contract](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/The-Applicative-Contract/#applicative-laws)
4. [5.4. Alternatives](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Alternatives/#alternative)
5. [5.5. Universes](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Universes/#universe-levels)
6. [5.6. The Complete Definitions](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/The-Complete-Definitions/#complete-definitions)
7. [5.7. Summary](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Summary/#structure-applicative-monad-summary)

## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.1. Structures and Inheritance {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-51-structures-and-inheritance}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Structures-and-Inheritance/

In order to understand the full definitions of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`, and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, another Lean feature is necessary: structure inheritance.
Structure inheritance allows one structure type to provide the interface of another, along with additional fields.
This can be useful when modeling concepts that have a clear taxonomic relationship.
For example, take a model of mythical creatures.
Some of them are large, and some are small:

```lean
structure MythicalCreature where
large : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

Behind the scenes, defining the `MythicalCreature` structure creates an inductive type with a single constructor called `mk`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) MythicalCreature.mk
```

```lean
MythicalCreature.mk (large : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : MythicalCreature
```

Similarly, a function `MythicalCreature.large` is created that actually extracts the field from the constructor:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) MythicalCreature.large
```

```lean
MythicalCreature.large (self : MythicalCreature) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

In most old stories, each monster can be defeated in some way.
A description of a monster should include this information, along with whether it is large:

```lean
structure Monster extends MythicalCreature where
vulnerability : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

The `extends MythicalCreature` in the heading states that every monster is also mythical.
To define a `Monster`, both the fields from `MythicalCreature` and the fields from `Monster` should be provided.
A troll is a large monster that is vulnerable to sunlight:

```lean
def troll : Monster where
large := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[vulnerability]](#fpil-Monster___vulnerability) := "sunlight"
```

Behind the scenes, inheritance is implemented using composition.
The constructor `Monster.mk` takes a `MythicalCreature` as its argument:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Monster.mk
```

```lean
Monster.mk (toMythicalCreature : MythicalCreature) (vulnerability : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : Monster
```

In addition to defining functions to extract the value of each new field, a function `Monster.toMythicalCreature` is defined with type `Monster → MythicalCreature`.
This can be used to extract the underlying creature.

Moving up the inheritance hierarchy in Lean is not the same thing as upcasting in object-oriented languages.
An upcast operator causes a value from a derived class to be treated as an instance of the parent class, but the value retains its identity and structure.
In Lean, however, moving up the inheritance hierarchy actually erases the underlying information.
To see this in action, consider the result of evaluating `[troll]](#fpil-troll).toMythicalCreature`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [troll]](#fpil-troll).toMythicalCreature
```

```lean
{ large := true }
```

Only the fields of `MythicalCreature` remain.

Just like the `where` syntax, curly-brace notation with field names also works with structure inheritance:

```lean
def troll : Monster := {large := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), [vulnerability]](#fpil-Monster___vulnerability) := "sunlight"}
```

However, the anonymous angle-bracket notation that delegates to the underlying constructor reveals the internal details:

```lean
def [troll]](#fpil-Foo___troll) : Monster := ⟨[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), "sunlight"⟩
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
has type
  [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
but is expected to have type
  MythicalCreature
in the application
  Monster.mk [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

An extra set of angle brackets is required, which invokes `MythicalCreature.mk` on `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`:

```lean
def troll : Monster := ⟨⟨[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)⟩, "sunlight"⟩
```

Lean's dot notation is capable of taking inheritance into account.
In other words, the existing `MythicalCreature.large` can be used with a `Monster`, and Lean automatically inserts the call to `Monster.toMythicalCreature` before the call to `MythicalCreature.large`.
However, this only occurs when using dot notation, and applying the field lookup function using normal function call syntax results in a type error:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) MythicalCreature.large [troll]](#fpil-troll)
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  [troll]](#fpil-troll)
has type
  Monster
but is expected to have type
  MythicalCreature
in the application
  MythicalCreature.large [troll]](#fpil-troll)
```

Dot notation can also take inheritance into account for user-defined functions.
A small creature is one that is not large:

```lean
def MythicalCreature.small (c : MythicalCreature) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := !c.large
```

Evaluating `[troll]](#fpil-troll).[small]](#fpil-MythicalCreature___small)` yields `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, while attempting to evaluate `[MythicalCreature.small]](#fpil-MythicalCreature___small) [troll]](#fpil-troll)` results in:

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  [troll]](#fpil-troll)
has type
  Monster
but is expected to have type
  MythicalCreature
in the application
  [MythicalCreature.small]](#fpil-MythicalCreature___small) [troll]](#fpil-troll)
```

### 5.1.1. Multiple Inheritance {#fpil-multiple-structure-inheritance}

A helper is a mythical creature that can provide assistance when given the correct payment:

```lean
structure Helper extends MythicalCreature where
assistance : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
payment : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

For example, a *nisse* is a kind of small elf that's known to help around the house when provided with tasty porridge:

```lean
def nisse : Helper where
large := [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[assistance]](#fpil-Helper___assistance) := "household tasks"
[payment]](#fpil-Helper___payment) := "porridge"
```

If domesticated, trolls make excellent helpers.
They are strong enough to plow a whole field in a single night, though they require model goats to keep them satisfied with their lot in life.
A monstrous assistant is a monster that is also a helper:

```lean
structure MonstrousAssistant extends Monster, Helper where
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

A value of this structure type must fill in all of the fields from both parent structures:

```lean
def domesticatedTroll : MonstrousAssistant where
large := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
assistance := "heavy labor"
payment := "toy goats"
[vulnerability]](#fpil-Monster___vulnerability) := "sunlight"
```

Both of the parent structure types extend `MythicalCreature`.
If multiple inheritance were implemented naïvely, then this could lead to a “diamond problem”, where it would be unclear which path to `large` should be taken from a given `MonstrousAssistant`.
Should it take `large` from the contained `Monster` or from the contained `Helper`?
In Lean, the answer is that the first specified path to the grandparent structure is taken, and the additional parent structures' fields are copied rather than having the new structure include both parents directly.

This can be seen by examining the signature of the constructor for `MonstrousAssistant`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) MonstrousAssistant.mk
```

```lean
MonstrousAssistant.mk (toMonster : Monster) (assistance payment : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : MonstrousAssistant
```

It takes a `Monster` as an argument, along with the two fields that `Helper` introduces on top of `MythicalCreature`.
Similarly, while `MonstrousAssistant.toMonster` merely extracts the `Monster` from the constructor, `MonstrousAssistant.toHelper` has no `Helper` to extract.
The `#print` command exposes its implementation:

```lean
#print MonstrousAssistant.toHelper
```

```lean
@[reducible] def MonstrousAssistant.toHelper : MonstrousAssistant → Helper :=
fun self => { toMythicalCreature := self.toMythicalCreature, [assistance]](#fpil-Helper___assistance) := self.assistance, [payment]](#fpil-Helper___payment) := self.payment }
```

This function constructs a `Helper` from the fields of `MonstrousAssistant`.
The `@[reducible]` attribute has the same effect as writing `abbrev`.

#### 5.1.1.1. Default Declarations {#fpil-inheritance-defaults}

When one structure inherits from another, default field definitions can be used to instantiate the parent structure's fields based on the child structure's fields.
If more size specificity is required than whether a creature is large or not, a dedicated datatype describing sizes can be used together with inheritance, yielding a structure in which the `large` field is computed from the contents of the `size` field:

```lean
inductive Size where
| small
| medium
| large
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)
structure SizedCreature extends MythicalCreature where
size : [Size]](#fpil-Size)
large := size == [Size.large]](#fpil-Size___large)
```

This default definition is only a default definition, however.
Unlike property inheritance in a language like C# or Scala, the definitions in the child structure are only used when no specific value for `large` is provided, and nonsensical results can occur:

```lean
def nonsenseCreature : [SizedCreature]](#fpil-SizedCreature) where
large := [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
size := [.large]](#fpil-Size___large)
```

If the child structure should not deviate from the parent structure, there are a few options:

1. Documenting the relationship, as is done for `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` and `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)`
2. Defining a proposition that the fields are related appropriately, and designing the API to require evidence that the proposition is true where it matters
3. Not using inheritance at all

The second option could look like this:

```lean
abbrev SizesMatch (sc : [SizedCreature]](#fpil-SizedCreature)) : Prop :=
sc.large = (sc.size == [Size.large]](#fpil-Size___large))
```

Note that a single equality sign is used to indicate the equality *proposition*, while a double equality sign is used to indicate a function that checks equality and returns a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
`SizesMatch` is defined as an `abbrev` because it should automatically be unfolded in proofs, so that `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` can see the equality that should be proven.

A *huldre* is a medium-sized mythical creature—in fact, they are the same size as humans.
The two sized fields on `huldre` match one another:

```lean
def huldre : [SizedCreature]](#fpil-SizedCreature) where
size := [.medium]](#fpil-Size___medium)
example : SizesMatch huldre := by⊢ SizesMatch huldre
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

#### 5.1.1.2. Type Class Inheritance {#fpil-type-class-inheritance}

Behind the scenes, type classes are structures.
Defining a new type class defines a new structure, and defining an instance creates a value of that structure type.
They are then added to internal tables in Lean that allow it to find the instances upon request.
A consequence of this is that type classes may inherit from other type classes.

Because it uses precisely the same language features, type class inheritance supports all the features of structure inheritance, including multiple inheritance, default implementations of parent types' methods, and automatic collapsing of diamonds.
This is useful in many of the same situations that multiple interface inheritance is useful in languages like Java, C# and Kotlin.
By carefully designing type class inheritance hierarchies, programmers can get the best of both worlds: a fine-grained collection of independently-implementable abstractions, and automatic construction of these specific abstractions from larger, more general abstractions.

---



## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.2. Applicative Functors {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-52-applicative-functors}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Applicative-Functors/

An *applicative functor* is a functor that has two additional operations available: `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` and `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)`.
`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is the same operator used in `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, because `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` in fact inherits from `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`.
`[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` is much like `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`: it allows a function to be used in order to transform the contents of a datatype.
However, with `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)`, the function is itself contained in the datatype: `f (α → β) → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f α) → f β`.
Having the function under the type `f` allows the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` instance to control how the function is applied, while `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` unconditionally applies a function.
The second argument has a type that begins with `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) →` to allow the definition of `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` to short-circuit in cases where the function will never be applied.

The value of this short-circuiting behavior can be seen in the instance of `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
instance : [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) f x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) f [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g => g <$> x ()
```

In this case, if there is no function for `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` to apply, then there is no need to compute its argument, so `x` is never called.
The same consideration informs the instance of `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`:

```lean
instance : [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x
[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) f x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) f [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e => [.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e
| [.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) g => g <$> x ()
```

This short-circuiting behavior depends only on the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` or `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` structures that *surround* the function, rather than on the function itself.

Monads can be seen as a way of capturing the notion of sequentially executing statements into a pure functional language.
The result of one statement can affect which further statements run.
This can be seen in the type of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)`: `m α → (α → m β) → m β`.
The first statement's resulting value is an input into a function that computes the next statement to execute.
Successive uses of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` are like a sequence of statements in an imperative programming language, and `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` is powerful enough to implement control structures like conditionals and loops.

Following this analogy, `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` captures function application in a language that has side effects.
The arguments to a function in languages like Kotlin or C# are evaluated from left to right.
Side effects performed by earlier arguments occur before those performed by later arguments.
A function is not powerful enough to implement custom short-circuiting operators that depend on the specific *value* of an argument, however.

Typically, `seq` is not invoked directly.
Instead, the operator `<*>` is used.
This operator wraps its second argument in `fun () => ...`, simplifying the call site.
In other words, `E1 <*> E2` is syntactic sugar for `[Seq.seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) E1 (fun () => E2)`.

The key feature that allows `seq` to be used with multiple arguments is that a multiple-argument Lean function is really a single-argument function that returns another function that's waiting for the rest of the arguments.
In other words, if the first argument to `seq` is awaiting multiple arguments, then the result of the `seq` will be awaiting the rest.
For example, `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Plus.plus` can have the type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`.
Providing one argument, `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Plus.plus <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 4`, results in the type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`.
This can itself be used with `seq`, so `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Plus.plus <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 4 <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 7` has the type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

Not every functor is applicative.
`Pair` is like the built-in product type `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`:

```lean
structure Pair (α β : Type) : Type where
first : α
second : β
```

Like `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, `Pair` has type `Type → Type → Type`.
This means that `Pair α` has type `Type → Type`, and a `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance is possible:

```lean
instance : [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) (Pair α) where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f x := ⟨x.[first]](#fpil-Pair___first), f x.[second]](#fpil-Pair___second)⟩
```

This instance obeys the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` contract.

The two properties to check are that `id <$> Pair.mk x y`` = ``Pair.mk x y` and that `f <$> g <$> Pair.mk x y`` = ``(f ∘ g) <$> Pair.mk x y`.
The first property can be checked by just stepping through the evaluation of the left side, and noticing that it evaluates to the right side:

```lean
id <$> Pair.mk x y
```

```lean
Pair.mk x (id y)
```

```lean
Pair.mk x y
```

The second can be checked by stepping through both sides, and noting that they yield the same result:

```lean
f <$> g <$> Pair.mk x y
```

```lean
f <$> Pair.mk x (g y)
```

```lean
Pair.mk x (f (g y))
```

```lean
(f ∘ g) <$> Pair.mk x y
```

```lean
Pair.mk x ((f ∘ g) y)
```

```lean
Pair.mk x (f (g y))
```

Attempting to define an `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` instance, however, does not work so well.
It will require a definition of `pure`:

```lean
def Pair.pure (x : β) : Pair α β := _
```

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
β α:Typex:β⊢ Pair α β
```

There is a value with type `β` in scope (namely `x`), and the error message from the underscore suggests that the next step is to use the constructor `Pair.mk`:

```lean
def Pair.pure (x : β) : Pair α β := Pair.mk _ x
```

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder for argument `first`
context:
β α:Typex:β⊢ α
```

Unfortunately, there is no `α` available.
Because `pure` would need to work for *all possible types* `α` to define an instance of `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) (Pair α)`, this is impossible.
After all, a caller could choose `α` to be `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`, which has no values at all.

### 5.2.1. A Non-Monadic Applicative {#fpil-validate}

When validating user input to a form, it's generally considered to be best to provide many errors at once, rather than one error at a time.
This allows the user to have an overview of what is needed to please the computer, rather than feeling badgered as they correct the errors field by field.

Ideally, validating user input will be visible in the type of the function that's doing the validating.
It should return a datatype that is specific—checking that a text box contains a number should return an actual numeric type, for instance.
A validation routine could throw an exception when the input does not pass validation.
Exceptions have a major drawback, however: they terminate the program at the first error, making it impossible to accumulate a list of errors.

On the other hand, the common design pattern of accumulating a list of errors and then failing when it is non-empty is also problematic.
A long nested sequences of `if` statements that validate each sub-section of the input data is hard to maintain, and it's easy to lose track of an error message or two.
Ideally, validation can be performed using an API that enables a new value to be returned yet automatically tracks and accumulates error messages.

An applicative functor called `Validate` provides one way to implement this style of API.
Like the `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` monad, `Validate` allows a new value to be constructed that characterizes the validated data accurately.
Unlike `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, it allows multiple errors to be accumulated, without a risk of forgetting to check whether the list is empty.

#### 5.2.1.1. User Input {#fpil-user-input}

As an example of user input, take the following structure:

```lean
structure RawInput where
name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
birthYear : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

The business logic to be implemented is the following:

1. The name may not be empty
2. The birth year must be numeric and non-negative
3. The birth year must be greater than 1900, and less than or equal to the year in which the form is validated

Representing these as a datatype will require a new feature, called *subtypes*.
With this tool in hand, a validation framework can be written that uses an applicative functor to track errors, and these rules can be implemented in the framework.

#### 5.2.1.2. Subtypes {#fpil-subtypes}

Representing these conditions is easiest with one additional Lean type, called `Subtype`:

```lean
structure Subtype {α : Type} (p : α → Prop) where
val : α
property : p val
```

This structure has two type parameters: an implicit parameter that is the type of data `α`, and an explicit parameter `p` that is a predicate over `α`.
A *predicate* is a logical statement with a variable in it that can be replaced with a value to yield an actual statement, like the [parameter to `[GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk)`](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Overloading-and-Type-Classes/Arrays-and-Indexing/#overloading-indexing) that describes what it means for an index to be in bounds for a lookup.
In the case of `Subtype`, the predicate slices out some subset of the values of `α` for which the predicate holds.
The structure's two fields are, respectively, a value from `α` and evidence that the value satisfies the predicate `p`.
Lean has special syntax for `Subtype`.
If `p` has type `α → Prop`, then the type `Subtype p` can also be written `{x : α // p x}`, or even `{x // p x}` when the type `α` can be inferred automatically.

[Representing positive numbers as inductive types]](#fpil-positive-numbers) is clear and easy to program with.
However, it has a key disadvantage.
While `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` have the structure of ordinary inductive types from the perspective of Lean programs, the compiler treats them specially and uses fast arbitrary-precision number libraries to implement them.
This is not the case for additional user-defined types.
However, a subtype of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that restricts it to non-zero numbers allows the new type to use the efficient representation while still ruling out zero at compile time:

```lean
def FastPos : Type := {x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) // x > 0}
```

The smallest fast positive number is still one.
Now, instead of being a constructor of an inductive type, it's an instance of a structure that's constructed with angle brackets.
The first argument is the underlying `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and the second argument is the evidence that said `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is greater than zero:

```lean
def one : [FastPos]](#fpil-FastPos___FastPos) := ⟨1, by⊢ 1 > 0 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
```

The proposition `1 > 0` is decidable, so the `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` tactic produces the necessary evidence.
The `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance is very much like that for `Pos`, except it uses a short tactic proof to provide evidence that `n + 1 > 0`:

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [FastPos]](#fpil-FastPos___FastPos) (n + 1) where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := ⟨n + 1, byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 > 0 [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
```

Here, `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` is needed because `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)` requires concrete values, but the proposition in question is `n + 1 > 0`.

Subtypes are a two-edged sword.
They allow efficient representation of validation rules, but they transfer the burden of maintaining these rules to the users of the library, who have to *prove* that they are not violating important invariants.
Generally, it's a good idea to use them internally to a library, providing an API to users that automatically ensures that all invariants are satisfied, with any necessary proofs being internal to the library.

Checking whether a value of type `α` is in the subtype `{x : α // p x}` usually requires that the proposition `p x` be decidable.
The [section on equality and ordering classes]](#fpil-equality-and-ordering) describes how decidable propositions can be used with `if`.
When `if` is used with a decidable proposition, a name can be provided.
In the `then` branch, the name is bound to evidence that the proposition is true, and in the `else` branch, it is bound to evidence that the proposition is false.
This comes in handy when checking whether a given `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is positive:

```lean
def Nat.asFastPos? (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [FastPos]](#fpil-FastPos___FastPos) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : n > 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ⟨n, h⟩
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

In the `then` branch, `h` is bound to evidence that `n > 0`, and this evidence can be used as the second argument to `Subtype`'s constructor.

#### 5.2.1.3. Validated Input {#fpil-validated-input}

The validated user input is a structure that expresses the business logic using multiple techniques:

- The structure type itself encodes the year in which it was checked for validity, so that `CheckedInput 2019` is not the same type as `CheckedInput 2020`
- The birth year is represented as a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` rather than a `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`
- Subtypes are used to constrain the allowed values in the name and birth year fields

```lean
structure CheckedInput (thisYear : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Type where
name : {n : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) // n ≠ ""}
birthYear : {y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) // y > 1900 ∧ y ≤ thisYear}
```

An input validator should take the current year and a `RawInput` as arguments, returning either a checked input or at least one validation failure.
This is represented by the `Validate` type:

```lean
inductive Validate (ε α : Type) : Type where
| ok : α → Validate ε α
| errors : NonEmptyList ε → Validate ε α
```

It looks very much like `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`.
The only difference is that the `errors` constructor may contain more than one failure.

`Validate` is a functor.
Mapping a function over it transforms any successful value that might be present, just as in the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instance for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`:

```lean
instance : [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) (Validate ε) where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x => [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) (f x)
| .errors errs => .errors errs
```

The `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` instance for `Validate` has an important difference from the instance for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`: while the instance for `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` terminates at the first error encountered, the instance for `Validate` is careful to accumulate all errors from *both* the function and the argument branches:

```lean
instance : [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) (Validate ε) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) := [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok)
[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) f x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) f [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) g => g <$> (x ())
| .errors errs =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) x () [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) _ => .errors errs
| .errors errs' => .errors (errs ++ errs')
```

Using `.errors` together with the constructor for `NonEmptyList` is a bit verbose.
Helpers like `reportError` make code more readable.
In this application, error reports will consist of field names paired with messages:

```lean
def Field := [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

```lean
def reportError (f : [Field]](#fpil-Field)) (msg : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) α :=
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := (f, msg), [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
```

The `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` instance for `Validate` allows the checking procedures for each field to be written independently and then composed.
Checking a name consists of ensuring that a string is non-empty, then returning evidence of this fact in the form of a `Subtype`.
This uses the evidence-binding version of `if`:

```lean
def checkName (name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) {n : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) // n ≠ ""} :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : name = "" [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
reportError "name" "Required"
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨name, h⟩
```

In the `then` branch, `h` is bound to evidence that `name = ""`, while it is bound to evidence that `¬name = ""` in the `else` branch.

It's certainly the case that some validation errors make other checks impossible.
For example, it makes no sense to check whether the birth year field is greater than 1900 if a confused user wrote the word `"syzygy"` instead of a number.
Checking the allowed range of the number is only meaningful after ensuring that the field in fact contains a number.
This can be expressed using the function `andThen`:

```lean
def Validate.andThen (val : Validate ε α)
(next : α → Validate ε β) : Validate ε β :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) val [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| .errors errs => .errors errs
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x => next x
```

While this function's type signature makes it suitable to be used as `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` in a `Monad` instance, there are good reasons not to do so.
They are described [in the section that describes the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` contract](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/The-Applicative-Contract/#additional-stipulations).

To check that the birth year is a number, a built-in function called `[String.Slice.toNat?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___toNat___-next) : [String.Slice](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___mk) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is useful.
It's most user-friendly to eliminate leading and trailing whitespace first using `String.trimAscii`:

```lean
def checkYearIsNat (year : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) year.trimAscii.[toNat?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___toNat___-next) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => reportError "birth year" "Must be digits"
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) n
```

To check that the provided year is in the expected range, nested uses of the evidence-providing form of `if` are in order:

```lean
def checkBirthYear (thisYear year : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) {y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) // y > 1900 ∧ y ≤ thisYear} :=
```
