```lean
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : year > 1900 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h' : year ≤ thisYear [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨year, bythisYear:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)year:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:year > 1900h':year [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) thisYear⊢ year > 1900 [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) year [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) thisYear [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙⟩
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) reportError "birth year" s!"Must be no later than {thisYear}"
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) reportError "birth year" "Must be after 1900"
```

Finally, these three components can be combined using `<*>`:

```lean
def checkInput (year : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (CheckedInput year) :=
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) CheckedInput.mk <*>
[checkName]](#fpil-checkName) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name) <*>
([checkYearIsNat]](#fpil-checkYearIsNat) input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear)).andThen fun birthYearAsNat =>
[checkBirthYear]](#fpil-checkBirthYear) year birthYearAsNat
```

Testing `checkInput` shows that it can indeed return multiple pieces of feedback:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) checkInput 2023 {[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name) := "David", [birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) := "1984"}
```

```lean
Validate.ok { name := "David", birthYear := 1984 }
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) checkInput 2023 {[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name) := "", [birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) := "2045"}
```

```lean
Validate.errors { head := ("name", "Required"), tail := [("birth year", "Must be no later than 2023")] }
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) checkInput 2023 {[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name) := "David", [birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) := "syzygy"}
```

```lean
Validate.errors { head := ("birth year", "Must be digits"), tail := [] }
```

Form validation with `checkInput` illustrates a key advantage of `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` over `Monad`.
Because `>>=` provides enough power to modify the rest of the program's execution based on the value from the first step, it *must* receive a value from the first step to pass on.
If no value is received (e.g. because an error has occurred), then `>>=` cannot execute the rest of the program.
`Validate` demonstrates why it can be useful to run the rest of the program anyway: in cases where the earlier data isn't needed, running the rest of the program can yield useful information (in this case, more validation errors).
`[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`'s `<*>` may run both of its arguments before recombining the results.
Similarly, `>>=` forces sequential execution.
Each step must complete before the next may run.
This is generally useful, but it makes it impossible to have parallel execution of different threads that naturally emerges from the program's actual data dependencies.
A more powerful abstraction like `Monad` increases the flexibility that's available to the API consumer, but it decreases the flexibility that is available to the API implementor.

---



## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.3. The Applicative Contract {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-53-the-applicative-contract}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/The-Applicative-Contract/

Just like `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, and types that implement `[BEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#BEq___mk)` and `[Hashable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Hashable___mk)`, `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` has a set of rules that all instances should adhere to.

There are four rules that an applicative functor should follow:

1. It should respect identity, so `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) id <*> v = v`
2. It should respect function composition, so `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (· ∘ ·) <*> u <*> v <*> w = u <*> (v <*> w)`
3. Sequencing pure operations should be a no-op, so `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f <*> [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x``=``[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f x)`
4. The ordering of pure operations doesn't matter, so `u <*> [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x = [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (fun f => f x) <*> u`

To check these for the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` instance, start by expanding `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` into `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.

The first rule states that `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) id <*> v = v`.
The definition of `seq` for `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` states that this is the same as `id <$> v = v`, which is one of the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` rules that have already been checked.

The second rule states that `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (· ∘ ·) <*> u <*> v <*> w = u <*> (v <*> w)`.
If any of `u`, `v`, or `w` is `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, then both sides are `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, so the property holds.
Assuming that `u` is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f`, that `v` is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g`, and that `w` is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x`, then this is equivalent to saying that `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (· ∘ ·) <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x)`.
Evaluating the two sides yields the same result:

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (· ∘ ·) <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f ∘ ·) <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f ∘ g) <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ((f ∘ g) x)
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f (g x))
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) g <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x)
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (g x))
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f (g x))
```

The third rule follows directly from the definition of `seq`:

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
```

```lean
f <$> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
```

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f x)
```

In the fourth case, assume that `u` is `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f`, because if it's `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, both sides of the equation are `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
`[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x` evaluates directly to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (f x)`, as does `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (fun g => g x) <*> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) f`.

### 5.3.1. All Applicatives are Functors {#fpil-applicatives-are-functors}

The two operators for `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` are enough to define `map`:

```lean
def map [[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) f] (g : α → β) (x : f α) : f β :=
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) g <*> x
```

This can only be used to implement `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` if the contract for `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` guarantees the contract for `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, however.
The first rule of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` is that `id <$> x = x`, which follows directly from the first rule for `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`.
The second rule of `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` is that `map (f ∘ g) x = map f (map g x)`.
Unfolding the definition of `map` here results in `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f ∘ g) <*> x = [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f <*> ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) g <*> x)`.
Using the rule that sequencing pure operations is a no-op, the left side can be rewritten to `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (· ∘ ·) <*> [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f <*> [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) g <*> x`.
This is an instance of the rule that states that applicative functors respect function composition.

This justifies a definition of `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` that extends `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, with a default definition of `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` given in terms of `pure` and `seq`:

```lean
class Applicative (f : Type → Type) extends [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f where
pure : α → f α
seq : f (α → β) → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f α) → f β
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) g x := seq (pure g) (fun () => x)
```

### 5.3.2. All Monads are Applicative Functors {#fpil-monads-are-applicative}

An instance of `Monad` already requires an implementation of `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`.
Together with `bind`, this is enough to define `seq`:

```lean
def seq [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (f : m (α → β)) (x : [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → m α) : m β := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let g ← f
let y ← x ()
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)
```

Once again, checking that the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` contract implies the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` contract will allow this to be used as a default definition for `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` if `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` extends `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`.

The rest of this section consists of an argument that this implementation of `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` based on `bind` in fact satisfies the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` contract.
One of the beautiful things about functional programming is that this kind of argument can be worked out on a piece of paper with a pencil, using the kinds of evaluation rules from [the initial section on evaluating expressions]](#fpil-evaluating).
Thinking about the meanings of the operations while reading these arguments can sometimes help with understanding.

Replacing `do`-notation with explicit uses of `>>=` makes it easier to apply the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` rules:

```lean
def seq [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (f : m (α → β)) (x : [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → m α) : m β :=
f >>= fun g =>
x () >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)
```

To check that this definition respects identity, check that `seq ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) id) (fun () => v) = v`.
The left hand side is equivalent to `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) id >>= fun g => (fun () => v) () >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)`.
The unit function in the middle can be eliminated immediately, yielding `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) id >>= fun g => v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)`.
Using the fact that `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`, this is the same as `v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (id y)`, which is `v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) y`.
Because `fun x => f x` is the same as `f`, this is the same as `v >>= [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`, and the fact that `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a right identity of `>>=` can be used to get `v`.

This kind of informal reasoning can be made easier to read with a bit of reformatting.
In the following chart, read “`EXPR1 ={ REASON }= EXPR2`” as “`EXPR1` is the same as `EXPR2` because `REASON`”:

```lean
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) id >>= fun g => v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (id y)
```

Reduce the call to `id`

```lean
v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) y
```

`fun x => f x` is the same as `f`

```lean
v >>= [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a right identity of `>>=`

```lean
v
```

To check that it respects function composition, check that `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (· ∘ ·) <*> u <*> v <*> w = u <*> (v <*> w)`.
The first step is to replace `<*>` with this definition of `seq`.
After that, a (somewhat long) series of steps that use the identity and associativity rules from the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` contract is enough to get from one to the other:

```lean
seq (seq (seq ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (· ∘ ·)) (fun _ => u))
(fun _ => v))
(fun _ => w)
```

Definition of `seq`

```lean
(([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (· ∘ ·) >>= fun f =>
u >>= fun x =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f x)) >>= fun g =>
v >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
((u >>= fun x =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x ∘ ·)) >>= fun g =>
v >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

Insertion of parentheses for clarity

```lean
((u >>= fun x =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x ∘ ·)) >>= (fun g =>
v >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y))) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

Associativity of `>>=`

```lean
(u >>= fun x =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x ∘ ·) >>= fun g =>
v >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
(u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x ∘ y)) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

Associativity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x ∘ y) >>= fun h =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h z)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ((x ∘ y) z)
```

Definition of function composition

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x (y z))
```

Time to start moving backwards!
`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
w >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (y z) >>= fun q =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x q)
```

Associativity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
v >>= fun y =>
(w >>= fun p =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (y p)) >>= fun q =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x q)
```

Associativity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
(v >>= fun y =>
w >>= fun q =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (y q)) >>= fun z =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x z)
```

This includes the definition of `seq`

```lean
u >>= fun x =>
seq v (fun () => w) >>= fun q =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x q)
```

This also includes the definition of `seq`

```lean
seq u (fun () => seq v (fun () => w))
```

To check that sequencing pure operations is a no-op:

```lean
seq ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f) (fun () => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x)
```

Replacing `seq` with its definition

```lean
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f >>= fun g =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f >>= fun g =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g x)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f x)
```

And finally, to check that the ordering of pure operations doesn't matter:

```lean
seq u (fun () => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x)
```

Definition of `seq`

```lean
u >>= fun f =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x >>= fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f y)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
u >>= fun f =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f x)
```

Clever replacement of one expression by an equivalent one that makes the rule match

```lean
u >>= fun f =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ((fun g => g x) f)
```

`[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a left identity of `>>=`

```lean
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (fun g => g x) >>= fun h =>
u >>= fun f =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (h f)
```

Definition of `seq`

```lean
seq ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (fun f => f x)) (fun () => u)
```

This justifies a definition of `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` that extends `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`, with a default definition of `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)`:

```lean
class Monad (m : Type → Type) extends [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) m where
bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β
[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) f x :=
bind f fun g =>
bind (x ()) fun y =>
pure (g y)
```

`[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`'s own default definition of `[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` means that every `Monad` instance automatically generates `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` and `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` instances as well.

### 5.3.3. Additional Stipulations {#fpil-additional-stipulations}

In addition to adhering to the individual contracts associated with each type class, combined implementations `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` should work equivalently to these default implementations.
In other words, a type that provides both `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instances should not have an implementation of `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` that works differently from the version that the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance generates as a default implementation.
This is important because polymorphic functions may be refactored to replace a use of `>>=` with an equivalent use of `<*>`, or a use of `<*>` with an equivalent use of `>>=`.
This refactoring should not change the meaning of programs that use this code.

This rule explains why `Validate.andThen` should not be used to implement `bind` in a `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance.
On its own, it obeys the monad contract.
However, when it is used to implement `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)`, the behavior is not equivalent to `[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk)` itself.
To see where they differ, take the example of two computations, both of which return errors.
Start with an example of a case where two errors should be returned, one from validating a function (which could have just as well resulted from a prior argument to the function), and one from validating an argument:

```lean
def notFun : Validate [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) :=
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
def notArg : Validate [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "Second error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
```

Combining them with the version of `<*>` from `Validate`'s `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)` instance results in both errors being reported to the user:

```lean
[notFun]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notFun) <*> [notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg)
```

```lean
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [notFun]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notFun) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) g => g <$> [notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg)
| .errors errs =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) _ => .errors errs
| .errors errs' => .errors (errs ++ errs')
```

```lean
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) _ =>
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
| .errors errs' =>
.errors ({ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] } ++ errs')
```

```lean
.errors
({ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] } ++
{ [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "Second error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := []})
```

```lean
.errors {
[head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error",
[tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := ["Second error"]
}
```

Using the version of `seq` that was implemented with `>>=`, here rewritten to `andThen`, results in only the first error being available:

```lean
seq [notFun]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notFun) (fun () => [notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg))
```

```lean
[notFun]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notFun).andThen fun g =>
[notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg).andThen fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)
```

```lean
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [notFun]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notFun) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| .errors errs => .errors errs
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) val =>
(fun g =>
[notArg]](#fpil-SeqCounterexample___notArg).andThen fun y =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (g y)) val
```

```lean
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := "First error", [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
```

---



## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.4. Alternatives {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-54-alternatives}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Alternatives/

### 5.4.1. Recovery from Failure {#fpil-alternative-recovery}

`Validate` can also be used in situations where there is more than one way for input to be acceptable.
For the input form `RawInput`, an alternative set of business rules that implement conventions from a legacy system might be the following:

1. All human users must provide a birth year that is four digits.
2. Users born prior to 1970 do not need to provide names, due to incomplete older records.
3. Users born after 1970 must provide names.
4. Companies should enter `"FIRM"` as their year of birth and provide a company name.

No particular provision is made for users born in 1970.
It is expected that they will either give up, lie about their year of birth, or call.
The company considers this an acceptable cost of doing business.

The following inductive type captures the values that can be produced from these stated rules:

```lean
abbrev NonEmptyString := {s : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) // s ≠ ""}
inductive LegacyCheckedInput where
| humanBefore1970 :
(birthYear : {y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) // y > 999 ∧ y < 1970}) →
[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) →
LegacyCheckedInput
| humanAfter1970 :
(birthYear : {y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) // y > 1970}) →
[NonEmptyString]](#fpil-NonEmptyString) →
LegacyCheckedInput
| company :
[NonEmptyString]](#fpil-NonEmptyString) →
LegacyCheckedInput
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

A validator for these rules is more complicated, however, as it must address all three cases.
While it can be written as a series of nested `if` expressions, it's easier to design the three cases independently and then combine them.
This requires a means of recovering from failure while preserving error messages:

```lean
def Validate.orElse
(a : Validate ε α)
(b : [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → Validate ε α) :
Validate ε α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) a [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x => [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x
| .errors errs1 =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) b () [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x => [.ok]](#fpil-Validate___ok) x
| .errors errs2 => .errors (errs1 ++ errs2)
```

This pattern of recovery from failures is common enough that Lean has built-in syntax for it, attached to a type class named `OrElse`:

```lean
class OrElse (α : Type) where
orElse : α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → α) → α
```

The expression `E1 <|> E2` is short for `OrElse.orElse E1 (fun () => E2)`.
An instance of `OrElse` for `Validate` allows this syntax to be used for error recovery:

```lean
instance : OrElse (Validate ε α) where
orElse := [Validate.orElse]](#fpil-Validate___orElse)
```

The validator for `LegacyCheckedInput` can be built from a validator for each constructor.
The rules for a company state that the birth year should be the string `"FIRM"` and that the name should be non-empty.
The constructor `[LegacyCheckedInput.company]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___company)`, however, has no representation of the birth year at all, so there's no easy way to carry it out using `<*>`.
The key is to use a function with `<*>` that ignores its argument.

Checking that a Boolean condition holds without recording any evidence of this fact in a type can be accomplished with `checkThat`:

```lean
def checkThat (condition : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(field : [Field]](#fpil-Field)) (msg : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) condition [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) () [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) reportError field msg
```

This definition of `checkCompany` uses `checkThat`, and then throws away the resulting `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` value:

```lean
def checkCompany (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (fun () name => [.company]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___company) name) <*>
checkThat (input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) == "FIRM")
"birth year" "FIRM if a company" <*>
[checkName]](#fpil-checkName) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name)
```

However, this definition is quite noisy.
It can be simplified in two ways.
The first is to replace the first use of `<*>` with a specialized version that automatically ignores the value returned by the first argument, called `*>`.
This operator is also controlled by a type class, called `SeqRight`, and `E1 *> E2` is syntactic sugar for `[SeqRight.seqRight](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqRight___mk) E1 (fun () => E2)`:

```lean
class SeqRight (f : Type → Type) where
seqRight : f α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f β) → f β
```

There is a default implementation of `seqRight` in terms of `seq`: `seqRight (a : f α) (b : Unit → f β) : f β := pure (fun _ x => x) <*> a <*> b ()`.

Using `seqRight`, `checkCompany` becomes simpler:

```lean
def checkCompany (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
checkThat (input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) == "FIRM")
"birth year" "FIRM if a company" *>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [.company]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___company) <*> [checkName]](#fpil-checkName) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name)
```

One more simplification is possible.
For every `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`, `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) f <*> E` is equivalent to `f <$> E`.
In other words, using `seq` to apply a function that was placed into the `Applicative` type using `pure` is overkill, and the function could have just been applied using `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`.
This simplification yields:

```lean
def checkCompany (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
checkThat (input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear) == "FIRM")
"birth year" "FIRM if a company" *>
[.company]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___company) <$> [checkName]](#fpil-checkName) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name)
```

The remaining two constructors of `LegacyCheckedInput` use subtypes for their fields.
A general-purpose tool for checking subtypes will make these easier to read:

```lean
def checkSubtype {α : Type} (v : α) (p : α → Prop) [[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (p v)]
(err : ε) : Validate ε {x : α // p x} :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : p v [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨v, h⟩
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
.errors { [head]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___head) := err, [tail]](#fpil-NonEmptyList___tail) := [] }
```

In the function's argument list, it's important that the type class `[[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) (p v)]` occur after the specification of the arguments `v` and `p`.
Otherwise, it would refer to an additional set of automatic implicit arguments, rather than to the manually-provided values.
The `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` instance is what allows the proposition `p v` to be checked using `if`.

The two human cases do not need any additional tools:

```lean
def checkHumanBefore1970 (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
([checkYearIsNat]](#fpil-checkYearIsNat) input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear)).andThen fun y =>
[.humanBefore1970]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___humanBefore1970) <$>
[checkSubtype]](#fpil-checkSubtype) y (fun x => x > 999 ∧ x < 1970)
("birth year", "less than 1970") <*>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name)
```

```lean
def checkHumanAfter1970 (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
([checkYearIsNat]](#fpil-checkYearIsNat) input.[birthYear]](#fpil-RawInput___birthYear)).andThen fun y =>
[.humanAfter1970]](#fpil-LegacyCheckedInput___humanAfter1970) <$>
[checkSubtype]](#fpil-checkSubtype) y (· > 1970)
("birth year", "greater than 1970") <*>
[checkName]](#fpil-checkName) input.[name]](#fpil-RawInput___name)
```

The validators for the three cases can be combined using `<|>`:

```lean
def checkLegacyInput (input : RawInput) :
Validate ([Field]](#fpil-Field) × [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) LegacyCheckedInput :=
[checkCompany]](#fpil-checkCompany) input <|>
[checkHumanBefore1970]](#fpil-checkHumanBefore1970) input <|>
[checkHumanAfter1970]](#fpil-checkHumanAfter1970) input
```

The successful cases return constructors of `LegacyCheckedInput`, as expected:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [checkLegacyInput]](#fpil-checkLegacyInput) ⟨"Johnny's Troll Groomers", "FIRM"⟩
```

```lean
Validate.ok (LegacyCheckedInput.company "Johnny's Troll Groomers")
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [checkLegacyInput]](#fpil-checkLegacyInput) ⟨"Johnny", "1963"⟩
```

```lean
Validate.ok (LegacyCheckedInput.humanBefore1970 1963 "Johnny")
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [checkLegacyInput]](#fpil-checkLegacyInput) ⟨"", "1963"⟩
```

```lean
Validate.ok (LegacyCheckedInput.humanBefore1970 1963 "")
```

The worst possible input returns all the possible failures:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [checkLegacyInput]](#fpil-checkLegacyInput) ⟨"", "1970"⟩
```

```lean
Validate.errors
  { head := ("birth year", "FIRM if a company"),
    tail := [("name", "Required"),
             ("birth year", "less than 1970"),
             ("birth year", "greater than 1970"),
             ("name", "Required")] }
```

### 5.4.2. The `Alternative` Class {#fpil-Alternative}

Many types support a notion of failure and recovery.
The `Many` monad from the section on [evaluating arithmetic expressions in a variety of monads]](#fpil-nondeterministic-search) is one such type, as is `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
Both support failure without providing a reason (unlike, say, `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` and `Validate`, which require some indication of what went wrong).

The `Alternative` class describes applicative functors that have additional operators for failure and recovery:

```lean
class Alternative (f : Type → Type) extends [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) f where
failure : f α
orElse : f α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f α) → f α
```

Just as implementors of `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α` get `[HAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) α α α` instances for free, implementors of `Alternative` get `OrElse` instances for free:

```lean
instance [Alternative f] : OrElse (f α) where
orElse := [Alternative.orElse]](#fpil-FakeAlternative___Alternative___orElse)
```

The implementation of `Alternative` for `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` keeps the first non-`[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` argument:

```lean
instance : [Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) where
failure := [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
orElse
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x, _ => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none), y => y ()
```

Similarly, the implementation for `Many` follows the general structure of `Many.union`, with minor differences due to the laziness-inducing `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` parameters being placed differently:

```lean
def Many.orElse : Many α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → Many α) → Many α
| [.none]](#fpil-Many___none), ys => ys ()
| .more x xs, ys => .more x (fun () => [orElse]](#fpil-Many___orElse) (xs ()) ys)
instance : [Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk) Many where
failure := [.none]](#fpil-Many___none)
orElse := [Many.orElse]](#fpil-Many___orElse)
```

Like other type classes, `Alternative` enables the definition of a variety of operations that work for *any* applicative functor that implements `Alternative`.
One of the most important is `guard`, which causes `failure` when a decidable proposition is false:

```lean
def guard [[Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk) f] (p : Prop) [[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] : f [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) failure
```

It is very useful in monadic programs to terminate execution early.
In `Many`, it can be used to filter out a whole branch of a search, as in the following program that computes all even divisors of a natural number:

```lean
def Many.countdown : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Many [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => .none
| n + 1 => .more n (fun () => [countdown]](#fpil-Guard___Many___countdown) n)
def evenDivisors (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Many [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let k ← [Many.countdown]](#fpil-Guard___Many___countdown) (n + 1)
guard (k % 2 = 0)
guard (n % k = 0)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) k
```

Running it on `20` yields the expected results:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([evenDivisors]](#fpil-Guard___evenDivisors) 20).[takeAll]](#fpil-Many___takeAll)
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)20[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 10[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

### 5.4.3. Exercises {#fpil-Alternative-exercises}

#### 5.4.3.1. Improve Validation Friendliness {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Alternatives--Exercises--Improve-Validation-Friendliness}

The errors returned from `Validate` programs that use `<|>` can be difficult to read, because inclusion in the list of errors simply means that the error can be reached through *some* code path.
A more structured error report can be used to guide the user through the process more accurately:

- Replace the `NonEmptyList` in `Validate.errors` with a bare type variable, and then update the definitions of the `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) (Validate ε)` and `OrElse (Validate ε α)` instances to require only that there be an `[Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) ε` instance available.
- Define a function `Validate.mapErrors : Validate ε α → (ε → ε') → Validate ε' α` that transforms all the errors in a validation run.
- Using the datatype `TreeError` to represent errors, rewrite the legacy validation system to track its path through the three alternatives.
- Write a function `report : TreeError → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` that outputs a user-friendly view of the `TreeError`'s accumulated warnings and errors.

```lean
inductive TreeError where
| field : [Field]](#fpil-Field) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → TreeError
| path : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → TreeError → TreeError
| both : TreeError → TreeError → TreeError
instance : [Append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) TreeError where
[append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Append___mk) := [.both]](#fpil-TreeError___both)
```

---



## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.5. Universes {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-55-universes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Universes/

In the interests of simplicity, this book has thus far papered over an important feature of Lean: *universes*.
A universe is a type that classifies other types.
Two of them are familiar: `Type` and `Prop`.
`Type` classifies ordinary types, such as `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) × [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)`, and `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`.
`Prop` classifies propositions that may be true or false, such as `"nisse" = "elf"` or `3 > 2`.
The type of `Prop` is `Type`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Prop
```

```lean
Prop : Type
```

For technical reasons, more universes than these two are needed.
In particular, `Type` cannot itself be a `Type`.
This would allow a logical paradox to be constructed and undermine Lean's usefulness as a theorem prover.

The formal argument for this is known as *Girard's Paradox*.
It is related to a better-known paradox known as *Russell's Paradox*, which was used to show that early versions of set theory were inconsistent.
In these set theories, a set can be defined by a property.
For example, one might have the set of all red things, the set of all fruit, the set of all natural numbers, or even the set of all sets.
Given a set, one can ask whether a given element is contained in it.
For instance, a bluebird is not contained in the set of all red things, but the set of all red things is contained in the set of all sets.
Indeed, the set of all sets even contains itself.

What about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves?
It contains the set of all red things, as the set of all red things is not itself red.
It does not contain the set of all sets, because the set of all sets contains itself.
But does it contain itself?
If it does contain itself, then it cannot contain itself.
But if it does not, then it must.

This is a contradiction, which demonstrates that something was wrong with the initial assumptions.
In particular, allowing sets to be constructed by providing an arbitrary property is too powerful.
Later versions of set theory restrict the formation of sets to remove the paradox.

A related paradox can be constructed in versions of dependent type theory that assign the type `Type` to `Type`.
To ensure that Lean has consistent logical foundations and can be used as a tool for mathematics, `Type` needs to have some other type.
This type is called `Type 1`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type
```

```lean
Type : Type 1
```

Similarly, `Type 1` is a `Type 2`,
`Type 2` is a `Type 3`,
`Type 3` is a `Type 4`, and so forth.

Function types occupy the smallest universe that can contain both the argument type and the return type.
This means that `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is a `Type`, `Type → Type` is a `Type 1`, and `Type 1 → Type 2` is a `Type 3`.

There is one exception to this rule.
If the return type of a function is a `Prop`, then the whole function type is in `Prop`, even if the argument is in a larger universe such as `Type` or even `Type 1`.
In particular, this means that predicates over values that have ordinary types are in `Prop`.
For example, the type `(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → n = n + 0` represents a function from a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to evidence that it is equal to itself plus zero.
Even though `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is in `Type`, this function type is in `Prop` due to this rule.
Similarly, even though `Type` is in `Type 1`, the function type `Type → 2 + 2 = 4` is still in `Prop`.

### 5.5.1. User Defined Types {#fpil-inductive-type-universes}

Structures and inductive datatypes can be declared to inhabit particular universes.
Lean then checks whether each datatype avoids paradoxes by being in a universe that's large enough to prevent it from containing its own type.
For instance, in the following declaration, `MyList` is declared to reside in `Type`, and so is its type argument `α`:

```lean
inductive MyList (α : Type) : Type where
| nil : MyList α
| cons : α → MyList α → MyList α
```

`MyList` itself is a `Type → Type`.
This means that it cannot be used to contain actual types, because then its argument would be `Type`, which is a `Type 1`:

```lean
def myListOfNat : MyList Type :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList1___MyList___cons) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.nil]](#fpil-MyList1___MyList___nil)
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  Type
has type
  Type 1
of sort `Type 2` but is expected to have type
  Type
of sort `Type 1` in the application
  MyList Type
```

Updating `MyList` so that its argument is a `Type 1` results in a definition rejected by Lean:

```lean
inductive MyList (α : Type 1) : Type where
| nil : MyList α
| cons : α → MyList α → MyList α
```

```lean
Invalid universe level in constructor `MyList.cons`: Parameter has type
  α
at universe level
  2
which is not less than or equal to the inductive type's resulting universe level
  1
```

This error occurs because the argument to `cons` with type `α` is from a larger universe than `MyList`.
Placing `MyList` itself in `Type 1` solves this issue, but at the cost of `MyList` now being itself inconvenient to use in contexts that expect a `Type`.

The specific rules that govern whether a datatype is allowed are somewhat complicated.
Generally speaking, it's easiest to start with the datatype in the same universe as the largest of its arguments.
Then, if Lean rejects the definition, increase its level by one, which will usually go through.

### 5.5.2. Universe Polymorphism {#fpil-universe-polymorphism}

Defining a datatype in a specific universe can lead to code duplication.
Placing `MyList` in `Type → Type` means that it can't be used for an actual list of types.
Placing it in `Type 1 → Type 1` means that it can't be used for a list of lists of types.
Rather than copy-pasting the datatype to create versions in `Type`, `Type 1`, `Type 2`, and so on, a feature called *universe polymorphism* can be used to write a single definition that can be instantiated in any of these universes.

Ordinary polymorphic types use variables to stand for types in a definition.
This allows Lean to fill in the variables differently, which enables these definitions to be used with a variety of types.
Similarly, universe polymorphism allows variables to stand for universes in a definition, enabling Lean to fill them in differently so that they can be used with a variety of universes.
Just as type arguments are conventionally named with Greek letters, universe arguments are conventionally named `u`, `v`, and `w`.

This definition of `MyList` doesn't specify a particular universe level, but instead uses a variable `u` to stand for any level.
If the resulting datatype is used with `Type`, then `u` is `0`, and if it's used with `Type 3`, then `u` is `3`:

```lean
inductive MyList (α : Type u) : Type u where
| nil : MyList α
| cons : α → MyList α → MyList α
```

With this definition, the same definition of `MyList` can be used to contain both actual natural numbers and the natural number type itself:

```lean
def myListOfNumbers : MyList [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) 0 ([.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) 1 [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil))
def myListOfNat : MyList Type :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil)
```

It can even contain itself:

```lean
def myListOfList : MyList (Type → Type) :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) MyList [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil)
```

It would seem that this would make it possible to write a logical paradox.
After all, the whole point of the universe system is to rule out self-referential types.
Behind the scenes, however, each occurrence of `MyList` is provided with a universe level argument.
In essence, the universe-polymorphic definition of `MyList` created a *copy* of the datatype at each level, and the level argument selects which copy is to be used.
These level arguments are written with a dot and curly braces, so `MyList.{0} : Type → Type`, `MyList.{1} : Type 1 → Type 1`, and `MyList.{2} : Type 2 → Type 2`.

Writing the levels explicitly, the prior example becomes:

```lean
def myListOfNumbers : MyList.{0} [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) 0 ([.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) 1 [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil))
def myListOfNat : MyList.{1} Type :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil)
def myListOfList : MyList.{1} (Type → Type) :=
[.cons]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___cons) MyList.{0} [.nil]](#fpil-MyList3___MyList___nil)
```

When a universe-polymorphic definition takes multiple types as arguments, it's a good idea to give each argument its own level variable for maximum flexibility.
For example, a version of `Sum` with a single level argument can be written as follows:

```lean
inductive Sum (α : Type u) (β : Type u) : Type u where
| inl : α → Sum α β
| inr : β → Sum α β
```

This definition can be used at multiple levels:

```lean
def stringOrNat : Sum [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [.inl]](#fpil-MySum___Inflexible___Sum___inl) "hello"
def typeOrType : Sum Type Type := [.inr]](#fpil-MySum___Inflexible___Sum___inr) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

However, it requires that both arguments be in the same universe:

```lean
def stringOrType : Sum [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) Type := [.inr]](#fpil-MySum___Inflexible___Sum___inr) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  Type
has type
  Type 1
of sort `Type 2` but is expected to have type
  Type
of sort `Type 1` in the application
  Sum [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) Type
```

This datatype can be made more flexible by using different variables for the two type arguments' universe levels, and then declaring that the resulting datatype is in the largest of the two:

```lean
inductive Sum (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v) where
| inl : α → Sum α β
| inr : β → Sum α β
```

This allows `Sum` to be used with arguments from different universes:

```lean
def stringOrType : Sum [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) Type := [.inr]](#fpil-MySum___Sum___inr) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

In positions where Lean expects a universe level, any of the following are allowed:

- A concrete level, like `0` or `1`
- A variable that stands for a level, such as `u` or `v`
- The maximum of two levels, written as `max` applied to the levels
- A level increase, written with `+ 1`

#### 5.5.2.1. Writing Universe-Polymorphic Definitions {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Universes--Universe-Polymorphism--Writing-Universe-Polymorphic-Definitions}

Until now, every datatype defined in this book has been in `Type`, the smallest universe of data.
When presenting polymorphic datatypes from the Lean standard library, such as `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` and `Sum`, this book created non-universe-polymorphic versions of them.
The real versions use universe polymorphism to enable code re-use between type-level and non-type-level programs.

There are a few general guidelines to follow when writing universe-polymorphic types.
First off, independent type arguments should have different universe variables, which enables the polymorphic definition to be used with a wider variety of arguments, increasing the potential for code reuse.
Secondly, the whole type is itself typically either in the maximum of all the universe variables, or one greater than this maximum.
Try the smaller of the two first.
Finally, it's a good idea to put the new type in as small of a universe as possible, which allows it to be used more flexibly in other contexts.
Non-polymorphic types, such as `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`, can be placed directly in `Type 0`.

#### 5.5.2.2. `Prop` and Polymorphism {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Universes--Universe-Polymorphism--Prop--and-Polymorphism}

Just as `Type`, `Type 1`, and so on describe types that classify programs and data, `Prop` classifies logical propositions.
A type in `Prop` describes what counts as convincing evidence for the truth of a statement.
Propositions are like ordinary types in many ways: they can be declared inductively, they can have constructors, and functions can take propositions as arguments.
However, unlike datatypes, it typically doesn't matter *which* evidence is provided for the truth of a statement, only *that* evidence is provided.
On the other hand, it is very important that a program not only return a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but that it's the *correct* `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

`Prop` is at the bottom of the universe hierarchy, and the type of `Prop` is `Type`.
This means that `Prop` is a suitable argument to provide to `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, for the same reason that `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is.
Lists of propositions have type `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Prop`:

```lean
def someTruePropositions : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Prop := [
1 + 1 = 2,
"Hello, " ++ "world!" = "Hello, world!"
]
```

Filling out the universe argument explicitly demonstrates that `Prop` is a `Type`:

```lean
def someTruePropositions : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).{0} Prop := [
1 + 1 = 2,
"Hello, " ++ "world!" = "Hello, world!"
]
```

Behind the scenes, `Prop` and `Type` are united into a single hierarchy called `Sort`.
`Prop` is the same as `Sort 0`, `Type 0` is `Sort 1`, `Type 1` is `Sort 2`, and so forth.
In fact, `Type u` is the same as `Sort (u+1)`.
When writing programs with Lean, this is typically not relevant, but it may occur in error messages from time to time, and it explains the name of the `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk)` class.
Additionally, having `Prop` as `Sort 0` allows one more universe operator to become useful.
The universe level `imax u v` is `0` when `v` is `0`, or the larger of `u` or `v` otherwise.
Together with `Sort`, this allows the special rule for functions that return `Prop`s to be used when writing code that should be as portable as possible between `Prop` and `Type` universes.

### 5.5.3. Polymorphism in Practice {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Universes--Polymorphism-in-Practice}

In the remainder of the book, definitions of polymorphic datatypes, structures, and classes will use universe polymorphism in order to be consistent with the Lean standard library.
This will enable the complete presentation of the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`, and `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` classes to be completely consistent with their actual definitions.

---



## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.6. The Complete Definitions {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-56-the-complete-definitions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/The-Complete-Definitions/

Now that all the relevant language features have been presented, this section describes the complete, honest definitions of `Functor`, `Applicative`, and `Monad` as they occur in the Lean standard library.
For the sake of understanding, no details are omitted.

### 5.6.1. Functor {#fpil-complete-functor-definition}

The complete definition of the `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` class makes use of universe polymorphism and a default method implementation:

```lean
class Functor (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
map : {α β : Type u} → (α → β) → f α → f β
mapConst : {α β : Type u} → α → f β → f α :=
[Function.comp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___comp) map ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _)
```

In this definition, `[Function.comp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___comp)` is function composition, which is typically written with the `∘` operator.
`[Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const)` is the *constant function*, which is a two-argument function that ignores its second argument.
Applying this function to only one argument produces a function that always returns the same value, which is useful when an API demands a function but a program doesn't need to compute different results for different arguments.
A simple version of `[Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const)` can be written as follows:

```lean
def simpleConst (x : α) (_ : β) : α := x
```

Using it with one argument as the function argument to `List.map` demonstrates its utility:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [1, 2, 3].[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) ([simpleConst]](#fpil-simpleConst) "same")
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)"same"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) "same"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) "same"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

The actual function has the following signature:

```lean
[Function.const.{u, v}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) {α : Sort u} (β : Sort v) (a : α) : β → α
```

Here, the type argument `β` is an explicit argument, so the default definition of `mapConst` provides an `_` argument that instructs Lean to find a unique type to pass to `[Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const)` that would cause the program to type check.
`[Function.comp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___comp) map ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _)` is equivalent to `fun (x : α) (y : f β) => map (fun _ => x) y`.

The `Functor` type class inhabits a universe that is the greater of `u+1` and `v`.
Here, `u` is the level of universes accepted as arguments to `f`, while `v` is the universe returned by `f`.
To see why the structure that implements the `Functor` type class must be in a universe that's larger than `u`, begin with a simplified definition of the class:

```lean
class Functor (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
map : {α β : Type u} → (α → β) → f α → f β
```

This type class's structure type is equivalent to the following inductive type:

```lean
inductive Functor (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
| mk : ({α β : Type u} → (α → β) → f α → f β) → Functor f
```

The implementation of the `map` method that is passed as an argument to `mk` contains a function that takes two types in `Type u` as arguments.
This means that the type of the function itself is in `Type (u+1)`, so `Functor` must also be at a level that is at least `u+1`.
Similarly, other arguments to the function have a type built by applying `f`, so it must also have a level that is at least `v`.
All the type classes in this section share this property.

### 5.6.2. Applicative {#fpil-complete-applicative-definition}

The `Applicative` type class is actually built from a number of smaller classes that each contain some of the relevant methods.
The first are `Pure` and `Seq`, which contain `pure` and `seq` respectively:

```lean
class Pure (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
pure {α : Type u} : α → f α
```

