```lean
class Seq (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
seq : {α β : Type u} → f (α → β) → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f α) → f β
```

In addition to these, `Applicative` also depends on `SeqRight` and an analogous `SeqLeft` class:

```lean
class SeqRight (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
seqRight : {α β : Type u} → f α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f β) → f β
```

```lean
class SeqLeft (f : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v) where
seqLeft : {α β : Type u} → f α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f β) → f α
```

The `seqRight` function, which was introduced in the [section about alternatives and validation]](#fpil-alternative), is easiest to understand from the perspective of effects.
`E1 *> E2`, which desugars to `[SeqRight.seqRight](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqRight___mk) E1 (fun () => E2)`, can be understood as first executing `E1`, and then `E2`, resulting only in `E2`'s result.
Effects from `E1` may result in `E2` not being run, or being run multiple times.
Indeed, if `f` has a `Monad` instance, then `E1 *> E2` is equivalent to `do let _ ← E1; E2`, but `seqRight` can be used with types like `Validate` that are not monads.

Its cousin `seqLeft` is very similar, except the leftmost expression's value is returned.
`E1 <* E2` desugars to `[SeqLeft.seqLeft](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqLeft___mk) E1 (fun () => E2)`.
`[SeqLeft.seqLeft](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqLeft___mk)` has type `f α → ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → f β) → f α`, which is identical to that of `seqRight` except for the fact that it returns `f α`.
`E1 <* E2` can be understood as a program that first executes `E1`, and then `E2`, returning the original result for `E1`.
If `f` has a `Monad` instance, then `E1 <* E2` is equivalent to `do let x ← E1; _ ← E2; pure x`.
Generally speaking, `seqLeft` is useful for specifying extra conditions on a value in a validation or parser-like workflow without changing the value itself.

The definition of `Applicative` extends all these classes, along with `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`:

```lean
class Applicative (f : Type u → Type v)
extends [Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f, Pure f, Seq f, SeqLeft f, SeqRight f where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) := fun x y => Seq.seq (pure x) fun _ => y
seqLeft := fun a b => Seq.seq ([Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _) a) b
seqRight := fun a b => Seq.seq ([Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _ id) a) b
```

A complete definition of `Applicative` requires only definitions for `pure` and `seq`.
This is because there are default definitions for all of the methods from `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `SeqLeft`, and `SeqRight`.
The `mapConst` method of `Functor` has its own default implementation in terms of `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`.
These default implementations should only be overridden with new functions that are behaviorally equivalent, but more efficient.
The default implementations should be seen as specifications for correctness as well as automatically-created code.

The default implementation for `seqLeft` is very compact.
Replacing some of the names with their syntactic sugar or their definitions can provide another view on it, so:

```lean
Seq.seq ([Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _) a) b
```

becomes

```lean
fun a b => Seq.seq ((fun x _ => x) <$> a) b
```

How should `(fun x _ => x) <$> a` be understood?
Here, `a` has type `f α`, and `f` is a functor.
If `f` is `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, then `(fun x _ => x) <$> [1, 2, 3]` evaluates to `[fun _ => 1, fun _ => 2, fun _ => 3`.
If `f` is `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, then `(fun x _ => x) <$> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "hello"` evaluates to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (fun _ => "hello")`.
In each case, the values in the functor are replaced by functions that return the original value, ignoring their argument.
When combined with `seq`, this function discards the values from `seq`'s second argument.

The default implementation for `seqRight` is very similar, except `[Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const)` has an additional argument `id`.
This definition can be understood similarly, by first introducing some standard syntactic sugar and then replacing some names with their definitions:

```lean
fun a b => Seq.seq ([Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) ([Function.const](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___const) _ id) a) b
```

```lean
fun a b => Seq.seq ((fun _ => id) <$> a) b
```

```lean
fun a b => Seq.seq ((fun _ => fun x => x) <$> a) b
```

```lean
fun a b => Seq.seq ((fun _ x => x) <$> a) b
```

How should `(fun _ x => x) <$> a` be understood?
Once again, examples are useful.
`fun _ x => x) <$> [1, 2, 3]` is equivalent to `[fun x => x, fun x => x, fun x => x]`, and `(fun _ x => x) <$> [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "hello"` is equivalent to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (fun x => x)`.
In other words, `(fun _ x => x) <$> a` preserves the overall shape of `a`, but each value is replaced by the identity function.
From the perspective of effects, the side effects of `a` occur, but the values are thrown out when it is used with `seq`.

### 5.6.3. Monad {#fpil-complete-monad-definition}

Just as the constituent operations of `Applicative` are split into their own type classes, `Bind` has its own class as well:

```lean
class Bind (m : Type u → Type v) where
bind : {α β : Type u} → m α → (α → m β) → m β
```

`Monad` extends `Applicative` with `Bind`:

```lean
class Monad (m : Type u → Type v) : Type (max (u+1) v)
extends [Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) m, Bind m where
[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) f x := bind x ([Function.comp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#Function___comp) pure f)
[seq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Seq___mk) f x := bind f fun y => [Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) y (x ())
[seqLeft](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqLeft___mk) x y := bind x fun a => bind (y ()) (fun _ => pure a)
[seqRight](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#SeqRight___mk) x y := bind x fun _ => y ()
```

Tracing the collection of inherited methods and default methods from the entire hierarchy shows that a `Monad` instance requires only implementations of `bind` and `pure`.
In other words, `Monad` instances automatically yield implementations of `seq`, `seqLeft`, `seqRight`, `map`, and `mapConst`.
From the perspective of API boundaries, any type with a `Monad` instance gets instances for `Bind`, `Pure`, `Seq`, `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`, `SeqLeft`, and `SeqRight`.

### 5.6.4. Exercises {#fpil-complete-functor-applicative-monad-exercises}

1. Understand the default implementations of `map`, `seq`, `seqLeft`, and `seqRight` in `Monad` by working through examples such as `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`. In other words, substitute their definitions for `bind` and `pure` into the default definitions, and simplify them to recover the versions `map`, `seq`, `seqLeft`, and `seqRight` that would be written by hand.
2. On paper or in a text file, prove to yourself that the default implementations of `map` and `seq` satisfy the contracts for `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` and `Applicative`. In this argument, you're allowed to use the rules from the `Monad` contract as well as ordinary expression evaluation.

## Functors, Applicative Functors, and Monads — 5.7. Summary {#fpil-functors-applicative-functors-and-monads-57-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads/Summary/

### 5.7.1. Type Classes and Structures {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Summary--Type-Classes-and-Structures}

Behind the scenes, type classes are represented by structures.
Defining a class defines a structure, and additionally creates an empty table of instances.
Defining an instance creates a value that either has the structure as its type or is a function that can return the structure, and additionally adds an entry to the table.
Instance search consists of constructing an instance by consulting the instance tables.
Both structures and classes may provide default values for fields (which are default implementations of methods).

### 5.7.2. Structures and Inheritance {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Summary--Structures-and-Inheritance}

Structures may inherit from other structures.
Behind the scenes, a structure that inherits from another structure contains an instance of the original structure as a field.
In other words, inheritance is implemented with composition.
When multiple inheritance is used, only the unique fields from the additional parent structures are used to avoid a diamond problem, and the functions that would normally extract the parent value are instead organized to construct one.
Record dot notation takes structure inheritance into account.

Because type classes are just structures with some additional automation applied, all of these features are available in type classes.
Together with default methods, this can be used to create a fine-grained hierarchy of interfaces that nonetheless does not impose a large burden on clients, because the small classes that the large classes inherit from can be automatically implemented.

### 5.7.3. Applicative Functors {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Summary--Applicative-Functors}

An applicative functor is a functor with two additional operations:

- `pure`, which is the same operator as that for `Monad`
- `seq`, which allows a function to be applied in the context of the functor.

While monads can represent arbitrary programs with control flow, applicative functors can only run function arguments from left to right.
Because they are less powerful, they provide less control to programs written against the interface, while the implementor of the method has a greater degree of freedom.
Some useful types can implement `Applicative` but not `Monad`.

In fact, the type classes `Functor`, `Applicative`, and `Monad` form a hierarchy of power.
Moving up the hierarchy, from `Functor` towards `Monad`, allows more powerful programs to be written, but fewer types implement the more powerful classes.
Polymorphic programs should be written to use as weak of an abstraction as possible, while datatypes should be given instances that are as powerful as possible.
This maximizes code re-use.
The more powerful type classes extend the less powerful ones, which means that an implementation of `Monad` provides implementations of `Functor` and `Applicative` for free.

Each class has a set of methods to be implemented and a corresponding contract that specifies additional rules for the methods.
Programs that are written against these interfaces expect that the additional rules are followed, and may be buggy if they are not.
The default implementations of `Functor`'s methods in terms of `Applicative`'s, and of `Applicative`'s in terms of `Monad`'s, will obey these rules.

### 5.7.4. Universes {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Functors___-Applicative-Functors___-and-Monads--Summary--Universes}

To allow Lean to be used as both a programming language and a theorem prover, some restrictions on the language are necessary.
This includes restrictions on recursive functions that ensure that they all either terminate or are marked as `partial` and written to return types that are not uninhabited.
Additionally, it must be impossible to represent certain kinds of logical paradoxes as types.

One of the restrictions that rules out certain paradoxes is that every type is assigned to a *universe*.
Universes are types such as `Prop`, `Type`, `Type 1`, `Type 2`, and so forth.
These types describe other types—just as `0` and `17` are described by `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is itself described by `Type`, and `Type` is described by `Type 1`.
The type of functions that take a type as an argument must be a larger universe than the argument's universe.

Because each declared datatype has a universe, writing code that uses types like data would quickly become annoying, requiring each polymorphic type to be copy-pasted to take arguments from `Type 1`.
A feature called *universe polymorphism* allows Lean programs and datatypes to take universe levels as arguments, just as ordinary polymorphism allows programs to take types as arguments.
Generally speaking, Lean libraries should use universe polymorphism when implementing libraries of polymorphic operations.

---



## Monad Transformers {#fpil-monad-transformers}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/

A monad is a way to encode some collection of side effects in a pure language.
Different monads provide different effects, such as state and error handling.
Many monads even provide useful effects that aren't available in most languages, such as nondeterministic searches, readers, and even continuations.

A typical application has a core set of easily testable functions written without monads paired with an outer wrapper that uses a monad to encode the necessary application logic.
These monads are constructed from well-known components.
For example:

- Mutable state is encoded with a function parameter and a return value that have the same type
- Error handling is encoded by having a return type that is similar to `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, with constructors for success and failure
- Logging is encoded by pairing the return value with the log

Writing each monad by hand is tedious, however, involving boilerplate definitions of the various type classes.
Each of these components can also be extracted to a definition that modifies some other monad to add an additional effect.
Such a definition is called a *monad transformer*.
A concrete monad can be build from a collection of monad transformers, which enables much more code re-use.

1. [6.1. Combining IO and Reader](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Combining-IO-and-Reader/#io-reader)
2. [6.2. A Monad Construction Kit](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/A-Monad-Construction-Kit/#Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--A-Monad-Construction-Kit)
3. [6.3. Ordering Monad Transformers](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Ordering-Monad-Transformers/#monad-transformer-order)
4. [6.4. More do Features](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/More-do-Features/#more-do-features)
5. [6.5. Additional Conveniences](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Additional-Conveniences/#monad-transformer-conveniences)
6. [6.6. Summary](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Summary/#monad-transformer-summary)

## Monad Transformers — 6.1. Combining IO and Reader {#fpil-monad-transformers-61-combining-io-and-reader}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Combining-IO-and-Reader/

One case where a reader monad can be useful is when there is some notion of the “current configuration” of the application that is passed through many recursive calls.
An example of such a program is `tree`, which recursively prints the files in the current directory and its subdirectories, indicating their tree structure using characters.
The version of `tree` in this chapter, called `doug` after the mighty Douglas Fir tree that adorns the west coast of North America, provides the option of Unicode box-drawing characters or their ASCII equivalents when indicating directory structure.

For example, the following commands create a directory structure and some empty files in a directory called `doug-demo`:

`cd doug-demo``mkdir -p a/b/c``mkdir -p a/d``mkdir -p a/e/f``touch a/b/hello``touch a/d/another-file``touch a/e/still-another-file-again`

Running `doug` results in the following:

`doug``├── doug-demo/
│ ├── a/
│ │ ├── b/
│ │ │ ├── c/
│ │ │ ├── hello
│ │ ├── d/
│ │ │ ├── another-file
│ │ ├── e/
│ │ │ ├── f/
│ │ │ ├── still-another-file-again
`

### 6.1.1. Implementation {#fpil-reader-io-implementation}

Internally, `doug` passes a configuration value downwards as it recursively traverses the directory structure.
This configuration contains two fields: `useASCII` determines whether to use Unicode box-drawing characters or ASCII vertical line and dash characters to indicate structure, and `currentPrefix` contains a string to prepend to each line of output.
As the current directory deepens, the prefix string accumulates indicators of being in a directory.
The configuration is a structure:

```lean
structure Config where
useASCII : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
currentPrefix : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := ""
```

This structure has default definitions for both fields.
The default `Config` uses Unicode display with no prefix.

Users who invoke `doug` will need to be able to provide command-line arguments.
The usage information is as follows:

```lean
def usage : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
"Usage: doug [--ascii]
Options:
\t--ascii\tUse ASCII characters to display the directory structure"
```

Accordingly, a configuration can be constructed by examining a list of command-line arguments:

```lean
def configFromArgs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Config
| [] => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) {} -- both fields default
| ["--ascii"] => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) {useASCII := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)}
| _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

The `main` function is a wrapper around an inner worker, called `dirTree`, that shows the contents of a directory using a configuration.
Before calling `dirTree`, `main` is responsible for processing command-line arguments.
It must also return the appropriate exit code to the operating system:

```lean
def main (args : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match [configFromArgs]](#fpil-DirTree___configFromArgs) args with
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) config =>
dirTree config (← [IO.currentDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___currentDir))
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 0
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) =>
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) s!"Didn't understand argument(s) {" ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) args}\n"
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) [usage]](#fpil-DirTree___usage)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 1
```

`[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln)` is a version of `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` that outputs to standard error.

Not all paths should be shown in the directory tree.
In particular, files named `.` or `..` should be skipped, as they are actually features used for navigation rather than files *per se*.
Of those files that should be shown, there are two kinds: ordinary files and directories:

```lean
inductive Entry where
| file : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Entry]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry)
| dir : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Entry]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry)
```

To determine whether a file should be shown, along with which kind of entry it is, `doug` uses `toEntry`:

```lean
def toEntry (path : [System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [Entry]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match path.[components](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___components).[getLast?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast___) with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.dir]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___dir) ""))
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) "." | [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ".." => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) name =>
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) (← path.[isDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___isDir)) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [.dir]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___dir) name [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [.file]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___file) name))
```

`[System.FilePath.components](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___components)` converts a path into a list of path components, splitting the name at directory separators.
If there is no last component, then the path is the root directory.
If the last component is a special navigation file (`.` or `..`), then the file should be excluded.
Otherwise, directories and files are wrapped in the corresponding constructors.

Lean's logic has no way to know that directory trees are finite.
Indeed, some systems allow the construction of circular directory structures.
Thus, `dirTree` is declared `partial`:

```lean
partial def dirTree (cfg : Config) (path : [System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← toEntry path with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.file]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___file) name) => showFileName cfg name
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.dir]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___dir) name) =>
showDirName cfg name
let contents ← path.[readDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___readDir)
let newConfig := cfg.inDirectory
doList (contents.[qsort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___qsort) dirLT).toList fun d =>
dirTree newConfig d.[path](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___path)
```

The call to `toEntry` is a [nested action]](#fpil-nested-actions)—the parentheses are optional in positions where the arrow couldn't have any other meaning, such as `match`.
When the filename doesn't correspond to an entry in the tree (e.g. because it is `..`), `dirTree` does nothing.
When the filename points to an ordinary file, `dirTree` calls a helper to show it with the current configuration.
When the filename points to a directory, it is shown with a helper, and then its contents are recursively shown in a new configuration in which the prefix has been extended to account for being in a new directory.
The contents of the directory are sorted in order to make the output deterministic, compared according to `dirLT`.

```lean
def dirLT (e1 : [IO.FS.DirEntry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___mk)) (e2 : [IO.FS.DirEntry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___mk)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
e1.[fileName](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___mk) < e2.[fileName](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___mk)
```

Showing the names of files and directories is achieved with `showFileName` and `showDirName`:

```lean
def showFileName (cfg : Config) (file : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) (cfg.[fileName]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___fileName) file)
def showDirName (cfg : Config) (dir : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) (cfg.[dirName]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___dirName) dir)
```

Both of these helpers delegate to functions on `Config` that take the ASCII vs Unicode setting into account:

```lean
def Config.preFile (cfg : Config) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) cfg.useASCII [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "|--" [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "├──"
def Config.preDir (cfg : Config) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) cfg.useASCII [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "| " [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) "│ "
def Config.fileName (cfg : Config) (file : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
s!"{cfg.currentPrefix}{cfg.[preFile]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___preFile)} {file}"
def Config.dirName (cfg : Config) (dir : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
s!"{cfg.currentPrefix}{cfg.[preFile]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___preFile)} {dir}/"
```

Similarly, `Config.inDirectory` extends the prefix with a directory marker:

```lean
def Config.inDirectory (cfg : Config) : Config :=
{cfg with currentPrefix := cfg.[preDir]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___preDir) ++ " " ++ cfg.currentPrefix}
```

Iterating an IO action over a list of directory contents is achieved using `doList`.
Because `doList` carries out all the actions in a list and does not base control-flow decisions on the values returned by any of the actions, the full power of `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` is not necessary, and it will work for any `[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk)`:

```lean
def doList [[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) f] : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → (α → f [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) → f [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
| [], _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| x :: xs, action =>
action x *>
doList xs action
```

### 6.1.2. Using a Custom Monad {#fpil-reader-io-custom-monad}

While this implementation of `doug` works, manually passing the configuration around is verbose and error-prone.
The type system will not catch it if the wrong configuration is passed downwards, for instance.
A reader effect ensures that the same configuration is passed to all recursive calls, unless it is manually overridden, and it helps make the code less verbose.

To create a version of `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` that is also a reader of `Config`, first define the type and its `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance, following the recipe from [the evaluator example]](#fpil-custom-environments):

```lean
def ConfigIO (α : Type) : Type :=
Config → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α
instance : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) ConfigIO where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := fun _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) result next := fun cfg => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let v ← result cfg
next v cfg
```

The difference between this `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance and the one for `Reader` is that this one uses `do`-notation in the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad as the body of the function that `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` returns, rather than applying `next` directly to the value returned from `result`.
Any `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` effects performed by `result` must occur before `next` is invoked, which is ensured by the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad's `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` operator.
`ConfigIO` is not universe polymorphic because the underlying `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` type is also not universe polymorphic.

Running a `ConfigIO` action involves transforming it into an `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` action by providing it with a configuration:

```lean
def ConfigIO.run (action : ConfigIO α) (cfg : Config) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α :=
action cfg
```

This function is not really necessary, as a caller could simply provide the configuration directly.
However, naming the operation can make it easier to see which parts of the code are intended to run in which monad.

The next step is to define a means of accessing the current configuration as part of `ConfigIO`:

```lean
def currentConfig : ConfigIO Config :=
fun cfg => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) cfg
```

This is just like `read` from [the evaluator example]](#fpil-custom-environments), except it uses `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`'s `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` to return its value rather than doing so directly.
Because entering a directory modifies the current configuration for the scope of a recursive call, it will be necessary to have a way to override a configuration:

```lean
def locally (change : Config → Config) (action : ConfigIO α) : ConfigIO α :=
fun cfg => action (change cfg)
```

Much of the code used in `doug` has no need for configurations, and `doug` calls ordinary Lean `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions from the standard library that certainly don't need a `Config`.
Ordinary `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions can be run using `runIO`, which ignores the configuration argument:

```lean
def runIO (action : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α) : ConfigIO α :=
fun _ => action
```

With these components, `showFileName` and `showDirName` can be updated to take their configuration arguments implicitly through the `ConfigIO` monad.
They use [nested actions]](#fpil-nested-actions) to retrieve the configuration, and `runIO` to actually execute the call to `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)`:

```lean
def showFileName (file : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
runIO ([IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) ((← currentConfig).[fileName]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___fileName) file))
def showDirName (dir : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
runIO ([IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) ((← currentConfig).[dirName]](#fpil-DirTree___Config___dirName) dir))
```

In the new version of `dirTree`, the calls to `toEntry` and `[readDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___readDir)` are wrapped in `runIO`.
Additionally, instead of building a new configuration and then requiring the programmer to keep track of which one to pass to recursive calls, it uses `locally` to naturally delimit the modified configuration to only a small region of the program, in which it is the *only* valid configuration:

```lean
partial def dirTree (path : [System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← runIO (toEntry path) with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.file]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___file) name) => showFileName name
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.dir]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___dir) name) =>
showDirName name
let contents ← runIO path.[readDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___readDir)
locally (·.inDirectory)
(doList (contents.[qsort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___qsort) dirLT).toList fun d =>
dirTree d.[path](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___path))
```

The new version of `main` uses `ConfigIO.run` to invoke `dirTree` with the initial configuration:

```lean
def main (args : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match [configFromArgs]](#fpil-DirTree___configFromArgs) args with
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) config =>
(dirTree (← [IO.currentDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___currentDir))).run config
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 0
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) =>
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) s!"Didn't understand argument(s) {" ".[separate]](#fpil-String___separate) args}\n"
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) [usage]](#fpil-DirTree___usage)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 1
```

This custom monad has a number of advantages over passing configurations manually:

1. It is easier to ensure that configurations are passed down unchanged, except when changes are desired
2. The concern of passing the configuration onwards is more clearly separated from the concern of printing directory contents
3. As the program grows, there will be more and more intermediate layers that do nothing with configurations except propagate them, and these layers don't need to be rewritten as the configuration logic changes

However, there are also some clear downsides:

1. As the program evolves and the monad requires more features, each of the basic operators such as `locally` and `currentConfig` will need to be updated
2. Wrapping ordinary `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions in `runIO` is noisy and distracts from the flow of the program
3. Writing monads instances by hand is repetitive, and the technique for adding a reader effect to another monad is a design pattern that requires documentation and communication overhead

Using a technique called *monad transformers*, all of these downsides can be addressed.
A monad transformer takes a monad as an argument and returns a new monad.
Monad transformers consist of:

1. A definition of the transformer itself, which is typically a function from types to types
2. A `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance that assumes the inner type is already a monad
3. An operator to “lift” an action from the inner monad to the transformed monad, akin to `runIO`

### 6.1.3. Adding a Reader to Any Monad {#fpil-ReaderT}

Adding a reader effect to `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` was accomplished in `ConfigIO` by wrapping `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α` in a function type.
The Lean standard library contains a function that can do this to *any* polymorphic type, called `ReaderT`:

```lean
def ReaderT (ρ : Type u) (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) :
Type (max u v) :=
ρ → m α
```

Its arguments are as follows:

- `ρ` is the environment that is accessible to the reader
- `m` is the monad that is being transformed, such as `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`
- `α` is the type of values being returned by the monadic computation
  Both `α` and `ρ` are in the same universe because the operator that retrieves the environment in the monad will have type `m ρ`.

With `ReaderT`, `ConfigIO` becomes:

```lean
abbrev ConfigIO (α : Type) : Type := ReaderT Config [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) α
```

It is an `abbrev` because `ReaderT` has many useful features defined in the standard library that a non-reducible definition would hide.
Rather than taking responsibility for making these work directly for `ConfigIO`, it's easier to simply have `ConfigIO` behave identically to `ReaderT Config [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`.

The manually-written `currentConfig` obtained the environment out of the reader.
This effect can be defined in a generic form for all uses of `ReaderT`, under the name `read`:

```lean
def read [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : ReaderT ρ m ρ :=
fun env => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) env
```

However, not every monad that provides a reader effect is built with `ReaderT`.
The type class `MonadReader` allows any monad to provide a `read` operator:

```lean
class MonadReader (ρ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type u)) (m : Type u → Type v) :
Type (max (u + 1) v) where
read : m ρ
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : MonadReader ρ (ReaderT ρ m) where
read := fun env => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) env
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) MonadReader (read)
```

The type `ρ` is an output parameter because any given monad typically only provides a single type of environment through a reader, so automatically selecting it when the monad is known makes programs more convenient to write.

The `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `ReaderT` is essentially the same as the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `ConfigIO`, except `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` has been replaced by some arbitrary monad argument `m`:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (ReaderT ρ m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := fun _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) result next := fun env => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let v ← result env
next v env
```

The next step is to eliminate uses of `runIO`.
When Lean encounters a mismatch in monad types, it automatically attempts to use a type class called `MonadLift` to transform the actual monad into the expected monad.
This process is similar to the use of coercions.
`MonadLift` is defined as follows:

```lean
class MonadLift (m : Type u → Type v) (n : Type u → Type w) where
monadLift : {α : Type u} → m α → n α
```

The method `monadLift` translates from the monad `m` to the monad `n`.
The process is called “lifting” because it takes an action in the embedded monad and makes it into an action in the surrounding monad.
In this case, it will be used to “lift” from `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` to `ReaderT Config [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`, though the instance works for *any* inner monad `m`:

```lean
instance : [MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) m (ReaderT ρ m) where
[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) action := fun _ => action
```

The implementation of `[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk)` is very similar to that of `runIO`.
Indeed, it is enough to define `showFileName` and `showDirName` without using `runIO`:

```lean
def showFileName (file : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) s!"{(← read).currentPrefix} {file}"
def showDirName (dir : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) s!"{(← read).currentPrefix} {dir}/"
```

One final operation from the original `ConfigIO` remains to be translated to a use of `ReaderT`: `locally`.
The definition can be translated directly to `ReaderT`, but the Lean standard library provides a more general version.
The standard version is called `withReader`, and it is part of a type class called `MonadWithReader`:

```lean
class MonadWithReader (ρ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type u)) (m : Type u → Type v) where
withReader {α : Type u} : (ρ → ρ) → m α → m α
```

Just as in `MonadReader`, the environment `ρ` is an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)`.
The `withReader` operation is exported, so that it doesn't need to be written with the type class name before it:

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) MonadWithReader (withReader)
```

The instance for `ReaderT` is essentially the same as the definition of `locally`:

```lean
instance : MonadWithReader ρ (ReaderT ρ m) where
withReader change action :=
fun cfg => action (change cfg)
```

With these definitions in place, the new version of `dirTree` can be written:

```lean
partial def dirTree (path : [System.FilePath](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___mk)) : ConfigIO [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← toEntry path with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.file]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___file) name) => showFileName name
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([.dir]](#fpil-DirTree___Entry___dir) name) =>
showDirName name
let contents ← path.[readDir](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#System___FilePath___readDir)
withReader (·.inDirectory)
(doList (contents.[qsort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___qsort) dirLT).toList fun d =>
dirTree d.[path](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___DirEntry___path))
```

Aside from replacing `locally` with `withReader`, it is the same as before.

Replacing the custom `ConfigIO` type with `ReaderT` did not save a large number of lines of code in this section.
However, rewriting the code using components from the standard library does have long-term benefits.
First, readers who know about `ReaderT` don't need to take time to understand the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `ConfigIO`, working backwards to the meaning of monad itself.
Instead, they can be confident in their initial understanding.
Next, adding further effects to the monad (such as a state effect to count the files in each directory and display a count at the end) requires far fewer changes to the code, because the monad transformers and `[MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk)` instances provided in the library work well together.
Finally, using a set of type classes included in the standard library, polymorphic code can be written in such a way that it can work with a variety of monads without having to care about details like the order in which the monad transformers were applied.
Just as some functions work in any monad, others can work in any monad that provides a certain type of state, or a certain type of exceptions, without having to specifically describe the *way* in which a particular concrete monad provides the state or exceptions.

### 6.1.4. Exercises {#fpil-reader-io-exercises}

#### 6.1.4.1. Controlling the Display of Dotfiles {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Combining-IO-and-Reader--Exercises--Controlling-the-Display-of-Dotfiles}

Files whose names begin with a dot character (`'.'`) typically represent files that should usually be hidden, such as source-control metadata and configuration files.
Modify `doug` with an option to show or hide filenames that begin with a dot.
This option should be controlled with a `-a` command-line option.

#### 6.1.4.2. Starting Directory as Argument {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Combining-IO-and-Reader--Exercises--Starting-Directory-as-Argument}

Modify `doug` so that it takes a starting directory as an additional command-line argument.

---



## Monad Transformers — 6.2. A Monad Construction Kit {#fpil-monad-transformers-62-a-monad-construction-kit}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/A-Monad-Construction-Kit/

`[ReaderT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT)` is far from the only useful monad transformer.
This section describes a number of additional transformers.
Each monad transformer consists of the following:

1. A definition or datatype `T` that takes a monad as an argument.
   It should have a type like `(Type u → Type v) → Type u → Type v`, though it may accept additional arguments prior to the monad.
2. A `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `T m` that relies on an instance of `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m`. This enables the transformed monad to be used as a monad.
3. A `[MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk)` instance that translates actions of type `m α` into actions of type `T m α`, for arbitrary monads `m`. This enables actions from the underlying monad to be used in the transformed monad.

Furthermore, the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for the transformer should obey the contract for `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, at least if the underlying `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance does.
In addition, `[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk) ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x : m α)` should be equivalent to `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x` in the transformed monad, and `[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk)` should distribute over `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` so that `[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk) (x >>= f : m α)` is the same as `([monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk) x : m α) >>= fun y => [monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk) (f y)`.

Many monad transformers additionally define type classes in the style of `[MonadReader](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadReader___mk)` that describe the actual effects available in the monad.
This can provide more flexibility: it allows programs to be written that rely only on an interface, and don't constrain the underlying monad to be implemented by a given transformer.
The type classes are a way for programs to express their requirements, and monad transformers are a convenient way to meet these requirements.

### 6.2.1. Failure with `OptionT` {#fpil-OptionT}

Failure, represented by the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` monad, and exceptions, represented by the `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` monad, both have corresponding transformers.
In the case of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, failure can be added to a monad by having it contain values of type `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α` where it would otherwise contain values of type `α`.
For example, `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α)` represents `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` actions that don't always return a value of type `α`.
This suggests the definition of the monad transformer `OptionT`:

```lean
def OptionT (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type v :=
m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α)
```

As an example of `OptionT` in action, consider a program that asks the user questions.
The function `getSomeInput` asks for a line of input and removes whitespace from both ends.
If the resulting trimmed input is non-empty, then it is returned, but the function fails if there are no non-whitespace characters:

```lean
def getSomeInput : OptionT [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let input ← (← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)).[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
let trimmed := input.trimAscii
if trimmed.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___isEmpty) then
failure
else [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) trimmed.[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
```

This particular application tracks users with their name and their favorite species of beetle:

```lean
structure UserInfo where
name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
favoriteBeetle : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

Asking the user for input is no more verbose than a function that uses only `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` would be:

```lean
def getUserInfo : OptionT [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UserInfo]](#fpil-Opt___UserInfo) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "What is your name?"
let name ← getSomeInput
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "What is your favorite species of beetle?"
let beetle ← getSomeInput
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ⟨name, beetle⟩
```

However, because the function runs in an `OptionT [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` context rather than just in `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`, failure in the first call to `getSomeInput` causes the whole `getUserInfo` to fail, with control never reaching the question about beetles.
The main function, `interact`, invokes `getUserInfo` in a purely `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` context, which allows it to check whether the call succeeded or failed by matching on the inner `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
def interact : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← getUserInfo with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) =>
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) "Missing info"
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ⟨name, beetle⟩ =>
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) s!"Hello {name}, whose favorite beetle is {beetle}."
```

#### 6.2.1.1. The Monad Instance {#fpil-OptionT-monad-instance}

Writing the monad instance reveals a difficulty.
Based on the types, `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` should use `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` from the underlying monad `m` together with `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
Just as `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` for `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` branches on the first argument, propagating `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` for `OptionT` should run the monadic action that makes up the first argument, branch on the result, and then propagate `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
Following this sketch yields the following definition, which Lean does not accept:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (OptionT m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x)
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) action next := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match (← action) with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => pure none
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v => next v
```

The error message shows a cryptic type mismatch:

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
has type
  [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α✝
but is expected to have type
  α✝
in the application
  [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x)
```

The problem here is that Lean is selecting the wrong `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for the surrounding use of `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`.
Similar errors occur for the definition of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)`.
One solution is to use type annotations to guide Lean to the correct `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (OptionT m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x) : m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) _))
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) action next := ([do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match (← action) with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v => next v : m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) _))
```

While this solution works, it is inelegant and the code becomes a bit noisy.

An alternative solution is to define functions whose type signatures guide Lean to the correct instances.
In fact, `OptionT` could have been defined as a structure:

```lean
structure OptionT (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type v where
run : m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α)
```

This would solve the problem, because the constructor `OptionT.mk` and the field accessor `[OptionT.run]](#fpil-Opt___Structed___OptionT___run)` would guide type class inference to the correct instances.
The downside to doing this is that the resulting code is more complicated, and these structures can make it more difficult to read proofs.
The best of both worlds can be achieved by defining functions that serve the same role as the constructor `OptionT.mk` and the field `[OptionT.run]](#fpil-Opt___Structed___OptionT___run)`, but that work with the direct definition:

```lean
def OptionT.mk (x : m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α)) : OptionT m α := x
def OptionT.run (x : OptionT m α) : m ([Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α) := x
```

Both functions return their inputs unchanged, but they indicate the boundary between code that is intended to present the interface of `OptionT` and code that is intended to present the interface of the underlying monad `m`.
Using these helpers, the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance becomes more readable:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (OptionT m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := OptionT.mk ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x))
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) action next := OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← action with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v => next v
```

Here, the use of `OptionT.mk` indicates that its arguments should be considered as code that uses the interface of `m`, which allows Lean to select the correct `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instances.

After defining the monad instance, it's a good idea to check that the monad contract is satisfied.
The first step is to show that `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) v) f` is the same as `f v`.
Here's the steps:

```lean
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) v) f
```

Unfolding the definitions of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` and `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`

```lean
OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v) with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => f x
```

Desugaring nested action syntax

```lean
OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let y ← [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v)
match y with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => f x
```

Desugaring `[do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)`-notation

```lean
OptionT.mk
([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v) >>= fun y =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) y [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => f x)
```

Using the first monad rule for `m`

```lean
OptionT.mk
([match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x => f x)
```

Reduce `match`

```lean
OptionT.mk (f v)
```

Definition of `OptionT.mk`

```lean
f v
```

The second rule states that `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) w [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is the same as `w`.
To demonstrate this, unfold the definitions of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` and `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`, yielding:

```lean
OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← w with
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) v)
```

In this pattern match, the result of both cases is the same as the pattern being matched, just with `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` around it.
In other words, it is equivalent to `w >>= fun y => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) y`, which is an instance of `m`'s second monad rule.

The final rule states that `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) ([bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) v f) g` is the same as `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) v (fun x => [bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) (f x) g)`.
It can be checked in the same way, by expanding the definitions of `[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk)` and `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` and then delegating to the underlying monad `m`.

#### 6.2.1.2. An `Alternative` Instance {#fpil-OptionT-Alternative-instance}

One convenient way to use `OptionT` is through the `[Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk)` type class.
Successful return is already indicated by `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`, and the `failure` and `orElse` methods of `[Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk)` provide a way to write a program that returns the first successful result from a number of subprograms:

