```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk) (OptionT m) where
failure := OptionT.mk ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none))
orElse x y := OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← x with
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) result => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) result)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => y ()
```

#### 6.2.1.3. Lifting {#fpil-OptionT-lifting}

Lifting an action from `m` to `OptionT m` only requires wrapping `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` around the result of the computation:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) m (OptionT m) where
[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) action := OptionT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (← action))
```

### 6.2.2. Exceptions {#fpil-exceptions}

The monad transformer version of `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` is very similar to the monad transformer version of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
Adding exceptions of type `ε` to some monadic action of type `m`` ``α` can be accomplished by adding exceptions to `α`, yielding type `m ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α)`:

```lean
def ExceptT (ε : Type u) (m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type v :=
m ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α)
```

`OptionT` provides `OptionT.mk` and `OptionT.run` functions to guide the type checker towards the correct `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instances.
This trick is also useful for `ExceptT`:

```lean
def ExceptT.mk {ε α : Type u} (x : m ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α)) : ExceptT ε m α := x
def ExceptT.run {ε α : Type u} (x : ExceptT ε m α) : m ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α) := x
```

The `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance for `ExceptT` is also very similar to the instance for `OptionT`.
The only difference is that it propagates a specific error value, rather than `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`:

```lean
instance {ε : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] :
[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (ExceptT ε m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := ExceptT.mk ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x))
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) result next := ExceptT.mk [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← result with
| [.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) e)
| [.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x => next x
```

The type signatures of `ExceptT.mk` and `ExceptT.run` contain a subtle detail: they annotate the universe levels of `α` and `ε` explicitly.
If they are not explicitly annotated, then Lean generates a more general type signature in which they have distinct polymorphic universe variables.
However, the definition of `ExceptT` expects them to be in the same universe, because they can both be provided as arguments to `m`.
This can lead to a problem in the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance where the universe level solver fails to find a working solution:

```lean
def ExceptT.mk (x : m ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε α)) : ExceptT ε m α := x
```

```lean
instance {ε : Type u} {m : Type u → Type v} [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] :
[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) (ExceptT ε m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := [ExceptT.mk]](#fpil-Ex___Huh___ExceptT___mk) ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ([Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x))
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) result next := [ExceptT.mk]](#fpil-Ex___Huh___ExceptT___mk) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match (← result) with
| .error e => pure (.error e)
| .ok x => next x
```

```lean
stuck at solving universe constraint
  max ?u.26 ?u.27 =?= u
while trying to unify
  ExceptT ε m β✝ : Type v
with
  ExceptT.{max ?u.27 ?u.26, v} ε m β✝ : Type v
```

This kind of error message is typically caused by underconstrained universe variables.
Diagnosing it can be tricky, but a good first step is to look for reused universe variables in some definitions that are not reused in others.

Unlike `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, the `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` datatype is typically not used as a data structure.
It is always used as a control structure with its `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance.
This means that it is reasonable to lift `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε` actions into `ExceptT ε m`, as well as actions from the underlying monad `m`.
Lifting `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` actions into `ExceptT` actions is done by wrapping them in `m`'s `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`, because an action that only has exception effects cannot have any effects from the monad `m`:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) ε) (ExceptT ε m) where
[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) action := ExceptT.mk ([pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) action)
```

Because actions from `m` do not have any exceptions in them, their value should be wrapped in `[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`.
This can be accomplished using the fact that `[Functor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)` is a superclass of `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)`, so applying a function to the result of any monadic computation can be accomplished using `[Functor.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk)`:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) m (ExceptT ε m) where
[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk) action := ExceptT.mk ([.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) <$> action)
```

#### 6.2.2.1. Type Classes for Exceptions {#fpil-exceptions-type-classes}

Exception handling fundamentally consists of two operations: the ability to throw exceptions, and the ability to recover from them.
Thus far, this has been accomplished using the constructors of `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` and pattern matching, respectively.
However, this ties a program that uses exceptions to one specific encoding of the exception handling effect.
Using a type class to capture these operations allows a program that uses exceptions to be used in *any* monad that supports throwing and catching.

Throwing an exception should take an exception as an argument, and it should be allowed in any context where a monadic action is requested.
The “any context” part of the specification can be written as a type by writing `m α`—because there's no way to produce a value of any arbitrary type, the `throw` operation must be doing something that causes control to leave that part of the program.
Catching an exception should accept any monadic action together with a handler, and the handler should explain how to get back to the action's type from an exception:

```lean
class MonadExcept (ε : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type u)) (m : Type v → Type w) where
throw : ε → m α
tryCatch : m α → (ε → m α) → m α
```

The universe levels on `MonadExcept` differ from those of `ExceptT`.
In `ExceptT`, both `ε` and `α` have the same level, while `MonadExcept` imposes no such limitation.
This is because `MonadExcept` never places an exception value inside of `m`.
The most general universe signature recognizes the fact that `ε` and `α` are completely independent in this definition.
Being more general means that the type class can be instantiated for a wider variety of types.

An example program that uses `MonadExcept` is a simple division service.
The program is divided into two parts: a frontend that supplies a user interface based on strings that handles errors, and a backend that actually does the division.
Both the frontend and the backend can throw exceptions, the former for ill-formed input and the latter for division by zero errors.
The exceptions are an inductive type:

```lean
inductive Err where
| divByZero
| notANumber : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Err]](#fpil-Ex___Err)
```

The backend checks for zero, and divides if it can:

```lean
def divBackend [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-Ex___Err) m] (n k : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) : m [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) k == 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [.divByZero]](#fpil-Ex___Err___divByZero)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (n / k)
```

The frontend's helper `asNumber` throws an exception if the string it is passed is not a number.
The overall frontend converts its inputs to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`s and calls the backend, handling exceptions by returning a friendly string error:

```lean
def asNumber [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-Ex___Err) m] (s : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : m [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) s.[toInt?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___toInt___) [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) => [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notANumber]](#fpil-Ex___Err___notANumber) s)
| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) i => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) i
```

```lean
def divFrontend [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-Ex___Err) m] (n k : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : m [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[tryCatch](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (toString (← [divBackend]](#fpil-Ex___divBackend) (← asNumber n) (← asNumber k))))
fun
| [.divByZero]](#fpil-Ex___Err___divByZero) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) "Division by zero!"
| [.notANumber]](#fpil-Ex___Err___notANumber) s => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) s!"Not a number: \"{s}\""
```

Throwing and catching exceptions is common enough that Lean provides a special syntax for using `[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk)`.
Just as `+` is short for `[HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)`, `try` and `catch` can be used as shorthand for the `tryCatch` method:

```lean
def divFrontend [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-Ex___Err) m] (n k : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : m [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
try
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (toString (← [divBackend]](#fpil-Ex___divBackend) (← asNumber n) (← asNumber k)))
catch
| [.divByZero]](#fpil-Ex___Err___divByZero) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) "Division by zero!"
| [.notANumber]](#fpil-Ex___Err___notANumber) s => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) s!"Not a number: \"{s}\""
```

In addition to `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` and `ExceptT`, there are useful `MonadExcept` instances for other types that may not seem like exceptions at first glance.
For example, failure due to `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` can be seen as throwing an exception that contains no data whatsoever, so there is an instance of `[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` that allows `try`` ...``catch`` ...` syntax to be used with `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.

### 6.2.3. State {#fpil-state-monad}

A simulation of mutable state is added to a monad by having monadic actions accept a starting state as an argument and return a final state together with their result.
The bind operator for a state monad provides the final state of one action as an argument to the next action, threading the state through the program.
This pattern can also be expressed as a monad transformer:

```lean
def StateT (σ : Type u)
(m : Type u → Type v) (α : Type u) : Type (max u v) :=
σ → m (α × σ)
```

Once again, the monad instance is very similar to that for `State`.
The only difference is that the input and output states are passed around and returned in the underlying monad, rather than with pure code:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) ([StateT]](#fpil-St___StateT) σ m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x := fun s => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (x, s)
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) result next := fun s => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let (v, s') ← result s
next v s'
```

The corresponding type class has `get` and `set` methods.
One downside of `get` and `set` is that it becomes too easy to `set` the wrong state when updating it.
This is because retrieving the state, updating it, and saving the updated state is a natural way to write some programs.
For example, the following program counts the number of diacritic-free English vowels and consonants in a string of letters:

```lean
structure LetterCounts where
vowels : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
consonants : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
inductive Err where
| notALetter : [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk) → [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
def vowels :=
let lowerVowels := "aeiuoy"
lowerVowels ++ lowerVowels.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___map) (·.[toUpper](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___toUpper))
def consonants :=
let lowerConsonants := "bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz"
lowerConsonants ++ lowerConsonants.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___map) (·.[toUpper](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___toUpper) )
def countLetters (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec loop (chars : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match chars with
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| c :: cs =>
let st ← get
let st' ←
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else -- modified or non-English letter
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) st
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
[set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk) st'
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___countLetters___loop) cs
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___countLetters___loop) str.toList
```

It would be very easy to write `set st` instead of `[set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk) st'`.
In a large program, this kind of mistake can lead to difficult-to-diagnose bugs.

While using a nested action for the call to `get` would solve this problem, it can't solve all such problems.
For example, a function might update a field on a structure based on the values of two other fields.
This would require two separate nested-action calls to `get`.
Because the Lean compiler contains optimizations that are only effective when there is a single reference to a value, duplicating the references to the state might lead to code that is significantly slower.
Both the potential performance problem and the potential bug can be worked around by using `[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify)`, which transforms the state using a function:

```lean
def countLetters (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec loop (chars : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match chars with
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| c :: cs =>
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else -- modified or non-English letter
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
loop cs
loop str.toList
```

The type class contains a function akin to `modify` called `modifyGet`, which allows the function to both compute a return value and transform an old state in a single step.
The function returns a pair in which the first element is the return value, and the second element is the new state; `modify` just adds the constructor of `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` to the pair used in `modifyGet`:

```lean
def modify [[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk) σ m] (f : σ → σ) : m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
modifyGet fun s => ((), f s)
```

The definition of `MonadState` is as follows:

```lean
class MonadState (σ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type u)) (m : Type u → Type v) :
Type (max (u+1) v) where
get : m σ
set : σ → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
modifyGet : (σ → α × σ) → m α
```

`[PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)` is a version of the `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` type that is universe-polymorphic to allow it to be in `Type u` instead of `Type`.
While it would be possible to provide a default implementation of `modifyGet` in terms of `get` and `set`, it would not admit the optimizations that make `modifyGet` useful in the first place, rendering the method useless.

### 6.2.4. `Of` Classes and `The` Functions {#fpil-of-and-the}

Thus far, each monad type class that takes extra information, like the type of exceptions for `MonadExcept` or the type of the state for `MonadState`, has this type of extra information as an output parameter.
For simple programs, this is generally convenient, because a monad that combines one use each of `[StateT]](#fpil-St___StateT)`, `[ReaderT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT)`, and `ExceptT` has only a single state type, environment type, and exception type.
As monads grow in complexity, however, they may involve multiple states or errors types.
In this case, the use of an output parameter makes it impossible to target both states in the same `do`-block.

For these cases, there are additional type classes in which the extra information is not an output parameter.
These versions of the type classes use the word `Of` in the name.
For example, `[MonadStateOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk)` is like `MonadState`, but without an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` modifier.

Instead of an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)`, these classes use a `[semiOutParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#semiOutParam)` for their respective state, environment, or exception types.
Like an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)`, a `[semiOutParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#semiOutParam)` is not required be known before Lean begins the process of searching for an instance.
However, there is an important difference: `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)`s are ignored during the search for an instance, and as a result they are truly outputs.
If an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)` is known prior to the search, then Lean merely checks that the result of the search is the same as what was known.
On the other hand, a `[semiOutParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#semiOutParam)` that is known prior to the start of the search can be used to narrow down candidates, just like an input parameter.

When a state monad's state type is an `[outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam)`, then each monad can have at most one type of state.
This is convenient, because it improves type inference: the state type can be inferred in more circumstances.
This is also inconvenient, because a monad built from multiple uses of `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` cannot provide a useful `[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk)` instance.
Using `[MonadStateOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk)`, however, causes Lean to take the state type into account when it is available to select which instance to use, so one monad may provide multiple types of state.
The downside of this is that the resulting instance may not be the one that was intended when the state type has not been specified explicitly enough, which can lead to confusing error messages.

Similarly, there are versions of the type class methods that accept the type of the extra information as an *explicit*, rather than implicit, argument.
For `[MonadStateOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk)`, there are `[getThe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#getThe)` with type

```lean
(σ : Type u) → {m : Type u → Type v} → [[MonadStateOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk) σ m] → m σ
```

and `[modifyThe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modifyThe)` with type

```lean
(σ : Type u) → {m : Type u → Type v} → [[MonadStateOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadStateOf___mk) σ m] → (σ → σ) → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
```

There is no `setThe` because the type of the new state is enough to decide which surrounding state monad transformer to use.

In the Lean standard library, there are instances of the non-`Of` versions of the classes defined in terms of the instances of the versions with `Of`.
In other words, implementing the `Of` version yields implementations of both.
It's generally a good idea to implement the `Of` version, and then start writing programs using the non-`Of` versions of the class, transitioning to the `Of` version if the output parameter becomes inconvenient.

### 6.2.5. Transformers and `Id` {#fpil-transformers-and-Id}

The identity monad `[Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)` is the monad that has no effects whatsoever, to be used in contexts that expect a monad for some reason but where none is actually necessary.
Another use of `[Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)` is to serve as the bottom of a stack of monad transformers.
For instance, `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) σ [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)` works just like `State σ`.

### 6.2.6. Exercises {#fpil-monad-transformer-exercises}

#### 6.2.6.1. Monad Contract {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--A-Monad-Construction-Kit--Exercises--Monad-Contract}

Using pencil and paper, check that the rules of the monad transformer contract are satisfied for each monad transformer in this section.

#### 6.2.6.2. Logging Transformer {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--A-Monad-Construction-Kit--Exercises--Logging-Transformer}

Define a monad transformer version of `WithLog`.
Also define the corresponding type class `MonadWithLog`, and write a program that combines logging and exceptions.

#### 6.2.6.3. Counting Files {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--A-Monad-Construction-Kit--Exercises--Counting-Files}

Modify `doug`'s monad with `[StateT]](#fpil-St___StateT)` such that it counts the number of directories and files seen.
At the end of execution, it should display a report like:

```
  Viewed 38 files in 5 directories.
```
