## Monad Transformers — 6.3. Ordering Monad Transformers {#fpil-monad-transformers-63-ordering-monad-transformers}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Ordering-Monad-Transformers/

When composing a monad from a stack of monad transformers, it's important to be aware that the order in which the monad transformers are layered matters.
Different orderings of the same set of transformers result in different monads.

This version of `countLetters` is just like the previous version, except it uses type classes to describe the set of available effects instead of providing a concrete monad:

```lean
def countLetters [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) m]
(str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec loop (chars : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match chars with
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| c :: cs =>
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else -- modified or non-English letter
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___Reorder___countLetters___loop) cs
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___Reorder___countLetters___loop) str.toList
```

The state and exception monad transformers can be combined in two different orders, each resulting in a monad that has instances of both type classes:

```lean
abbrev M1 := [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id))
abbrev M2 := [ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) ([StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id))
```

When run on input for which the program does not throw an exception, both monads yield similar results:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countLetters (m := M1) "hello" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
Except.ok ((), { vowels := 2, consonants := 3 })
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countLetters (m := M2) "hello" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
(Except.ok (), { vowels := 2, consonants := 3 })
```

However, there is a subtle difference between these return values.
In the case of `M1`, the outermost constructor is `[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`, and it contains a pair of the unit constructor with the final state.
In the case of `M2`, the outermost constructor is the pair, which contains `[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` applied only to the unit constructor.
The final state is outside of `[Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)`.
In both cases, the program returns the counts of vowels and consonants.

On the other hand, only one monad yields a count of vowels and consonants when the string causes an exception to be thrown.
Using `M1`, only an exception value is returned:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countLetters (m := M1) "hello!" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
Except.error (StEx.Err.notALetter '!')
```

Using `M2`, the exception value is paired with the state as it was at the time that the exception was thrown:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countLetters (m := M2) "hello!" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
(Except.error (StEx.Err.notALetter '!'), { vowels := 2, consonants := 3 })
```

It might be tempting to think that `M2` is superior to `M1` because it provides more information that might be useful when debugging.
The same program might compute *different* answers in `M1` than it does in `M2`, and there's no principled reason to say that one of these answers is necessarily better than the other.
This can be seen by adding a step to the program that handles exceptions:

```lean
def countWithFallback
[[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) m] [[MonadExcept](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) m]
(str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
try
countLetters str
catch _ =>
countLetters "Fallback"
```

This program always succeeds, but it might succeed with different results.
If no exception is thrown, then the results are the same as `countLetters`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countWithFallback (m := M1) "hello" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
Except.ok ((), { vowels := 2, consonants := 3 })
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countWithFallback (m := M2) "hello" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
(Except.ok (), { vowels := 2, consonants := 3 })
```

However, if the exception is thrown and caught, then the final states are very different.
With `M1`, the final state contains only the letter counts from `"Fallback"`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countWithFallback (m := M1) "hello!" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
Except.ok ((), { vowels := 2, consonants := 6 })
```

With `M2`, the final state contains letter counts from both `"hello!"` and from `"Fallback"`, as one would expect in an imperative language:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) countWithFallback (m := M2) "hello!" ⟨0, 0⟩
```

```lean
(Except.ok (), { vowels := 4, consonants := 9 })
```

In `M1`, throwing an exception “rolls back” the state to where the exception was caught.
In `M2`, modifications to the state persist across the throwing and catching of exceptions.
This difference can be seen by unfolding the definitions of `M1` and `M2`.
`M1 α` unfolds to `[LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) → [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) (α × [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts))`, and `M2 α` unfolds to `[LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) → [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err) α × [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts)`.
That is to say, `M1 α` describes functions that take an initial letter count, returning either an error or an `α` paired with updated counts.
When an exception is thrown in `M1`, there is no final state.
`M2 α` describes functions that take an initial letter count and return a new letter count paired with either an error or an `α`.
When an exception is thrown in `M2`, it is accompanied by a state.

### 6.3.1. Commuting Monads {#fpil-commuting-monads}

In the jargon of functional programming, two monad transformers are said to *commute* if they can be re-ordered without the meaning of the program changing.
The fact that the result of the program can differ when `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` and `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` are reordered means that state and exceptions do not commute.
In general, monad transformers should not be expected to commute.

Even though not all monad transformers commute, some do.
For example, two uses of `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` can be re-ordered.
Expanding the definitions in `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) σ ([StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) σ' [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)) α` yields the type `σ → σ' → ((α × σ) × σ')`, and `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) σ' ([StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) σ [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)) α` yields `σ' → σ → ((α × σ') × σ)`.
In other words, the differences between them are that they nest the `σ` and `σ'` types in different places in the return type, and they accept their arguments in a different order.
Any client code will still need to provide the same inputs, and it will still receive the same outputs.

Most programming languages that have both mutable state and exceptions work like `M2`.
In those languages, state that *should* be rolled back when an exception is thrown is difficult to express, and it usually needs to be simulated in a manner that looks much like the passing of explicit state values in `M1`.
Monad transformers grant the freedom to choose an interpretation of effect ordering that works for the problem at hand, with both choices being equally easy to program with.
However, they also require care to be taken in the choice of ordering of transformers.
With great expressive power comes the responsibility to check that what's being expressed is what is intended, and the type signature of `countWithFallback` is probably more polymorphic than it should be.

### 6.3.2. Exercises {#fpil-monad-transformer-order-exercises}

- Check that `[ReaderT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT)` and `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` commute by expanding their definitions and reasoning about the resulting types.
- Do `[ReaderT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT)` and `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` commute? Check your answer by expanding their definitions and reasoning about the resulting types.
- Construct a monad transformer `ManyT` based on the definition of `Many`, with a suitable `[Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk)` instance. Check that it satisfies the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` contract.
- Does `ManyT` commute with `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)`? If so, check your answer by expanding definitions and reasoning about the resulting types. If not, write a program in `ManyT (StateT σ Id)` and a program in `StateT σ (ManyT Id)`. Each program should be one that makes more sense for the given ordering of monad transformers.

---



## Monad Transformers — 6.4. More do Features {#fpil-monad-transformers-64-more-do-features}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/More-do-Features/

Lean's `do`-notation provides a syntax for writing programs with monads that resembles imperative programming languages.
In addition to providing a convenient syntax for programs with monads, `do`-notation provides syntax for using certain monad transformers.

### 6.4.1. Single-Branched `if` {#fpil-single-branched-if}

When working in a monad, a common pattern is to carry out a side effect only if some condition is true.
For instance, `countLetters` contains a check for vowels or consonants, and letters that are neither have no effect on the state.
This is captured by having the `else` branch evaluate to `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()`, which has no effects:

```lean
def countLetters (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec loop (chars : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match chars with
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| c :: cs =>
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else -- modified or non-English letter
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
loop cs
loop str.toList
```

When an `if` is a statement in a `do`-block, rather than being an expression, then `else [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()` can simply be omitted, and Lean inserts it automatically.
The following definition of `countLetters` is completely equivalent:

```lean
def countLetters (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec loop (chars : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match chars with
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| c :: cs =>
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___FancyDo___countLetters___loop) cs
[loop]](#fpil-StEx___FancyDo___countLetters___loop) str.toList
```

A program that uses a state monad to count the entries in a list that satisfy some monadic check can be written as follows:

```lean
def count [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) m] (p : α → m [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| x :: xs => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if ← p x then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) (· + 1)
count p xs
```

Similarly, `if not E1 then STMT...` can instead be written `unless E1 do STMT...`.
The converse of `count` that counts entries that don't satisfy the monadic check can be written by replacing `if` with `unless`:

```lean
def countNot [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] [[MonadState](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadState___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) m] (p : α → m [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| x :: xs => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
unless ← p x do
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) (· + 1)
[countNot]](#fpil-ThenDoUnless___countNot) p xs
```

Understanding single-branched `if` and `unless` does not require thinking about monad transformers.
They simply replace the missing branch with `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()`.
The remaining extensions in this section, however, require Lean to automatically rewrite the `do`-block to add a local transformer on top of the monad that the `do`-block is written in.

### 6.4.2. Early Return {#fpil-early-return}

The standard library contains a function `List.find?` that returns the first entry in a list that satisfies some check.
A simple implementation that doesn't make use of the fact that `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` is a monad loops over the list using a recursive function, with an `if` to stop the loop when the desired entry is found:

```lean
def List.find? (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| [] => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
| x :: xs =>
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) x
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[find?]](#fpil-EarlyReturn___Non___List___find___) p xs
```

Imperative languages typically sport the `return` keyword that aborts the execution of a function, immediately returning some value to the caller.
In Lean, this is available in `do`-notation, and `return` halts the execution of a `do`-block, with `return`'s argument being the value returned from the monad.
In other words, `List.find?` could have been written like this:

```lean
def List.find? (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| [] => failure
| x :: xs => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if p x then return x
find? p xs
```

Early return in imperative languages is a bit like an exception that can only cause the current stack frame to be unwound.
Both early return and exceptions terminate execution of a block of code, effectively replacing the surrounding code with the thrown value.
Behind the scenes, early return in Lean is implemented using a version of `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)`.
Each `do`-block that uses early return is wrapped in an exception handler (in the sense of the function `tryCatch`).
Early returns are translated to throwing the value as an exception, and the handlers catch the thrown value and return it immediately.
In other words, the `do`-block's original return value type is also used as the exception type.

Making this more concrete, the helper function `runCatch` strips a layer of `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` from the top of a monad transformer stack when the exception type and return type are the same:

```lean
def runCatch [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] (action : [ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT) α m α) : m α := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match ← action with
| [Except.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x
| [Except.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) x => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) x
```

The `do`-block in `List.find?` that uses early return is translated to a `do`-block that does not use early return by wrapping it in a use of `runCatch`, and replacing early returns with `[throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk)`:

```lean
def List.find? (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α
| [] => failure
| x :: xs =>
runCatch [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if p x then [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) x else [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
[monadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLiftT___mk) ([find?]](#fpil-EarlyReturn___Desugared___List___find___) p xs)
```

Another situation in which early return is useful is command-line applications that terminate early if the arguments or input are incorrect.
Many programs begin with a section that validates arguments and inputs before proceeding to the main body of the program.
The following version of [the greeting program `hello-name`]](#fpil-running-a-program) checks that no command-line arguments were provided:

```lean
def main (argv : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
let stderr ← [IO.getStderr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStderr)
unless argv == [] do
stderr.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Expected no arguments, but got {argv.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)}"
return 1
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "How would you like to be addressed?"
stdout.[flush](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
let name := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii
if name.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___isEmpty) then
stderr.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"No name provided"
return 1
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Hello, {name}!"
return 0
```

Running it with no arguments and typing the name `David` yields the same result as the previous version:

`lean --run EarlyReturn.lean
``How would you like to be addressed?
``David
``Hello, David!
`

Providing the name as a command-line argument instead of an answer causes an error:

`lean --run EarlyReturn.lean David
``Expected no arguments, but got 1
`

And providing no name causes the other error:

`lean --run EarlyReturn.lean
``How would you like to be addressed?
``
``No name provided
`

The program that uses early return avoids needing to nest the control flow, as is done in this version that does not use early return:

```lean
def main (argv : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
let stderr ← [IO.getStderr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStderr)
if argv != [] then
stderr.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Expected no arguments, but got {argv.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)}"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 1
else
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) "How would you like to be addressed?"
stdout.[flush](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
let name := (← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)).trimAscii
if name.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___isEmpty) then
stderr.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"No name provided"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 1
else
stdout.[putStrLn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___putStrLn) s!"Hello, {name}!"
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 0
```

One important difference between early return in Lean and early return in imperative languages is that Lean's early return applies only to the current `do`-block.
When the entire definition of a function is in the same `do` block, this difference doesn't matter.
But if `do` occurs underneath some other structures, then the difference becomes apparent.
For example, given the following definition of `greet`:

```lean
def greet (name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
"Hello, " ++ [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) return name
```

the expression `greet "David"` evaluates to `"Hello, David"`, not just `"David"`.

### 6.4.3. Loops {#fpil-loops}

Just as every program with mutable state can be rewritten to a program that passes the state as arguments, every loop can be rewritten as a recursive function.
From one perspective, `List.find?` is most clear as a recursive function.
After all, its definition mirrors the structure of the list: if the head passes the check, then it should be returned; otherwise look in the tail.
When no more entries remain, the answer is `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.
From another perspective, `List.find?` is most clear as a loop.
After all, the program consults the entries in order until a satisfactory one is found, at which point it terminates.
If the loop terminates without having returned, the answer is `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`.

#### 6.4.3.1. Looping with ForM {#fpil-looping-with-forM}

Lean includes a type class that describes looping over a container type.
This class is called `ForM`:

```lean
class ForM (m : Type u → Type v) (γ : Type w₁)
(α : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w₂)) where
forM (coll : γ) (f : α → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)) : m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
```

This class is quite general.
The parameter `m` allows some desired effects and is typically a monad, `γ` is the collection to be looped over, and `α` is the type of elements from the collection.
Usually, `m` is allowed to be any monad, but it is possible to have a data structure that e.g. only supports looping in `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)`.
The method `forM` takes a collection and an action to be run for its effects on each element from the collection, and is then responsible for running the actions.

The instance for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` allows `m` to be any monad, it sets `γ` to be `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, and sets the class's `α` to be the same `α` found in the list:

```lean
def List.forM [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → (α → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)) → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
| [], _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| x :: xs, action => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
action x
[forM]](#fpil-Loops___Fake___List___forM) xs action
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : ForM m ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) α where
forM := [List.forM]](#fpil-Loops___Fake___List___forM)
```

The [function `doList` from `doug`]](#fpil-reader-io-implementation) is `forM` for lists.
`forM` can be used to make `countLetters` much shorter:

```lean
def countLetters (str : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [LetterCounts]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts) ([Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [Err]](#fpil-StEx___Err)) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
[forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) str.toList fun c => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if c.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha) then
if [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___vowels).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) := st.[vowels]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___vowels) + 1}
else if [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___consonants).[contains](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___contains) c then
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) fun st => {st with [consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) := st.[consonants]](#fpil-StEx___LetterCounts___consonants) + 1}
else [throw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#MonadExcept___mk) ([.notALetter]](#fpil-StEx___Err___notALetter) c)
```

The instance for `Many` is very similar:

```lean
def Many.forM [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : Many α → (α → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)) → m [PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)
| [Many.none]](#fpil-Many___none), _ => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| Many.more first rest, action => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
action first
[forM]](#fpil-Many___forM) (rest ()) action
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [ForM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) m (Many α) α where
[forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) := [Many.forM]](#fpil-Many___forM)
```

Because `γ` can be any type at all, `ForM` can support non-polymorphic collections.
A very simple collection is one of the natural numbers less than some given number, in reverse order:

```lean
structure AllLessThan where
num : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Its `ForM` operator applies the provided action to each smaller `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
def AllLessThan.forM [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m]
(coll : AllLessThan) (action : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) :
m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let rec countdown : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
| 0 => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| n + 1 => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
action n
[countdown]](#fpil-Loops___AllLessThan___forM___countdown) n
[countdown]](#fpil-Loops___AllLessThan___forM___countdown) coll.[num]](#fpil-Loops___AllLessThan___num)
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [ForM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) m AllLessThan [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) := [AllLessThan.forM]](#fpil-Loops___AllLessThan___forM)
```

Running `[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)` on each number less than five can be accomplished with `ForM`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) { [num]](#fpil-Loops___AllLessThan___num) := 5 : AllLessThan } [IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println)
```

```lean
4
3
2
1
0
```

An example `ForM` instance that works only in a particular monad is one that loops over the lines read from an IO stream, such as standard input:

```lean
structure LinesOf where
stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
partial def LinesOf.forM
(readFrom : [LinesOf]](#fpil-LinesOf)) (action : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) :
[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let line ← readFrom.[stream]](#fpil-LinesOf___stream).[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
if line == "" then return ()
action line
forM readFrom action
instance : [ForM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [LinesOf]](#fpil-LinesOf) String where
[forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) := LinesOf.forM
```

The definition of `LinesOf.forM` is marked `partial` because there is no guarantee that the stream is finite.
In this case, `[IO.FS.Stream.getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)` works only in the `[IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO)` monad, so no other monad can be used for looping.

This example program uses this looping construct to filter out lines that don't contain letters:

```lean
def main (argv : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if argv != [] then
[IO.eprintln](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___eprintln) "Unexpected arguments"
return 1
[forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) (LinesOf.mk (← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin))) fun line => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if line.[any](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___any) (·.[isAlpha](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___isAlpha)) then
[IO.print](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___print) line
return 0
```

The file `test-data` contains:

File: `test-data``Hello!``!!!!!``12345``abc123````Ok`

Invoking this program, which is stored in `ForMIO.lean`, yields the following output:

`lean --run ForMIO.lean < test-data``Hello!
abc123
Ok
`

#### 6.4.3.2. Stopping Iteration {#fpil-break}

Terminating a loop early is difficult to do with `ForM`.
Writing a function that iterates over the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s in an `AllLessThan` only until `3` is reached requires a means of stopping the loop partway through.
One way to achieve this is to use `ForM` with the `[OptionT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#OptionT)` monad transformer.
The first step is to define `OptionT.exec`, which discards information about both the return value and whether or not the transformed computation succeeded:

```lean
def OptionT.exec [[Applicative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Applicative___mk) m] (action : [OptionT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#OptionT) m α) : m [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
action *> [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
```

Then, failure in the `[OptionT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#OptionT)` instance of `[Alternative](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Alternative___mk)` can be used to terminate looping early:

```lean
def countToThree (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) :=
let nums : AllLessThan := ⟨n⟩
OptionT.exec ([forM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) nums fun i => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if i < 3 then failure else [IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) i)
```

A quick test demonstrates that this solution works:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [countToThree]](#fpil-Loops___Transformed___countToThree) 7
```

```lean
6
5
4
3
```

However, this code is not so easy to read.
Terminating a loop early is a common task, and Lean provides more syntactic sugar to make this easier.
This same function can also be written as follows:

```lean
def countToThree (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let nums : AllLessThan := ⟨n⟩
for i in nums do
if i < 3 then break
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) i
```

Testing it reveals that it works just like the prior version:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [countToThree]](#fpil-Loops___countToThree) 7
```

```lean
6
5
4
3
```

The `for`` ...``in`` ...``do`` ...` syntax desugars to the use of a type class called `[ForIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForIn___mk)`, which is a somewhat more complicated version of `ForM` that keeps track of state and early termination.
The standard library provides an adapter that converts a `ForM` instance into a `[ForIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForIn___mk)` instance, called `[ForM.forIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___forIn)`.
This adapter uses `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` and `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` internally, so it requires that the `ForM` instance can be used with monads built from monad transformers, rather than just one specific monad.
To enable `for` loops based on a `ForM` instance, add something like the following, with appropriate replacements for `AllLessThan` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
instance [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m] : [ForIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForIn___mk) m AllLessThan [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[forIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForIn___mk) := [ForM.forIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___forIn)
```

Early return is supported in `for` loops.
The translation of `do` blocks with early return into a use of an exception monad transformer applies equally well underneath `ForM` as the earlier use of `[OptionT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#OptionT)` to halt iteration does.
This version of `List.find?` makes use of both:

```lean
def List.find? (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for x in xs do
if p x then return x
failure
```

In addition to `break`, `for` loops support `continue` to skip the rest of the loop body in an iteration.
An alternative (but confusing) formulation of `List.find?` skips elements that don't satisfy the check:

```lean
def List.find? (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for x in xs do
if [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) (p x) then continue
return x
failure
```

A *range* represents a series of consecutive elements of some type, from a lower bound to an upper bound.
The bounds may be *open*, in which case the bound is not included in the range, or *closed*, in which case the bound is included in the range.
Ranges may also be unbounded, continuing either infinitely or until they reach the least or greatest value in the type.

Ranges are represented by a collection of types with a naming convention that describes their bounds.
Each type's name begins with `R`, and the next two letters determine the lower and upper bounds, respectively:

- `o` represents an open bound, where the bound value is not included.
- `c` represents a closed bound, where the bound value is included.
- `i` represents an infinite bound that does not restrict its range.

For example, the type `[Std.Rco](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Rco___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` represents left-closed right-open sequences of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s that include their lower bound but omit their upper bound, and `[Std.Roi](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Roi___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` represents infinite sequences of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s that begin just above their lower bound.
Infinite bounds do not always result in infinite ranges; for example, even though a `[Std.Rio](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Rio___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` has no lower bound, the sequence is finite because `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` itself has an inherent lower bound of `0`.

Lean has special syntax to construct ranges, in which each bound can be specified.
A range is specified by placing three dots between its bounds, which may themselves be specified as either specific values or asterisks for unbounded ranges.
For example, the range from `3` to `10` is written `3...10` and has type `[Std.Rco](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Rco___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
By default, ranges are left-closed right-open.
This means that `3...10` includes `3` but does not include `10`.
These defaults can be overridden: `<` can be used to specify an open upper or lower bound, and `=` can be used to specify a closed upper bound.
`3<...=10` does not include `3`, but it does include `10`, while `3...=10` includes both and `3<...10` includes neither.
`3<...=10` has type `[Std.Roc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Roc___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and `3<...10` has type `[Std.Roo](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Ranges/#Std___Roo___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
The range `*...5` contains the numbers `0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, and `4`, while `3...*` contains all natural numbers that are greater than or equal to `3`.

Ranges are always in ascending order.
If the lower bound of a range is greater than its upper bound, then it includes no values, rather than proceeding in reverse order.
For example, `10...3` is empty.

Ranges can be used with `for` loops to draw values from the range when instances for the appropriate type classes exist.
This program prints the even numbers from four to eight:

```lean
def fourToEight : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for i in 2...5 do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) (i * 2)
```

Running it yields:

```lean
4
6
8
```

This displays the letters from `'l'` to `'p'`:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for letter in 'l'...='p' do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) letter
```

```lean
l
m
n
o
p
```

Finally, `for` loops support iterating over multiple collections in parallel, by separating the `in` clauses with commas.
Looping halts when the first collection runs out of elements, so the declaration:

```lean
def parallelLoop := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for x in ["currant", "gooseberry", "rowan"], y in 'a'...'e' do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) (x, y)
```

produces three lines of output:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [parallelLoop]](#fpil-Loops___parallelLoop)
```

```lean
(currant, a)
(gooseberry, b)
(rowan, c)
```

Many data structures implement an enhanced version of the `[ForIn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForIn___mk)` type class that adds evidence that the element was drawn from the collection to the loop body.
These can be used by providing a name for the evidence prior to the name of the element.
This function prints all the elements of an array together with their indices, and the compiler is able to determine that the array lookups are all safe due to the evidence `h`:

```lean
def printArray [ToString α] (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for h : i in 0...xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) s!"{i}:\t{xs[i]}"
```

In this example, `h` is evidence that `i ∈ 0...xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`, and the tactic that checks whether `xs[i]` is safe is able to transform this into evidence that `i < xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`.

### 6.4.4. Mutable Variables {#fpil-let-mut}

In addition to early `return`, `else`-less `if`, and `for` loops, Lean supports local mutable variables within a `do` block.
Behind the scenes, these mutable variables desugar to code that's equivalent to `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)`, rather than being implemented by true mutable variables.
Once again, functional programming is used to simulate imperative programming.

A local mutable variable is introduced with `let mut` instead of plain `let`.
The definition `two`, which uses the identity monad `[Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id)` to enable `do`-syntax without introducing any effects, counts to `2`:

```lean
def two : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
x := x + 1
x := x + 1
return x
```

This code is equivalent to a definition that uses `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` to add `1` twice:

```lean
def two : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
let block : [StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) (· + 1)
[modify](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#modify) (· + 1)
return (← get)
let (result, _finalState) := block 0
result
```

Local mutable variables work well with all the other features of `do`-notation that provide convenient syntax for monad transformers.
The definition `three` counts the number of entries in a three-entry list:

```lean
def three : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
for _ in [1, 2, 3] do
x := x + 1
return x
```

Similarly, `six` adds the entries in a list:

```lean
def six : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
for y in [1, 2, 3] do
x := x + y
return x
```

`List.count` counts the number of entries in a list that satisfy some check:

```lean
def List.count (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut found := 0
for x in xs do
if p x then found := found + 1
return found
```

Local mutable variables can be more convenient to use and easier to read than an explicit local use of `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)`.
However, they don't have the full power of unrestricted mutable variables from imperative languages.
In particular, they can only be modified in the `do`-block in which they are introduced.
This means, for instance, that `for`-loops can't be replaced by otherwise-equivalent recursive helper functions.
This version of `List.count`:

```lean
def List.count (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut found := 0
let rec go : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)
| [] => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
| y :: ys => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if p y then found := found + 1
[go]](#fpil-Mut___List___count___go) ys
return found
```

yields the following error on the attempted mutation of `found`:

```lean
Variable `found` cannot be mutated. Only variables declared using `let mut` can be mutated.
      If you did not intend to mutate but define `found`, consider using `let found` instead
```

This is because the recursive function is written in the identity monad, and only the monad of the `do`-block in which the variable is introduced is transformed with `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)`.

### 6.4.5. What counts as a `do` block? {#fpil-do-block-boundaries}

Many features of `do`-notation apply only to a single `do`-block.
Early return terminates the current block, and mutable variables can only be mutated in the block that they are defined in.
To use them effectively, it's important to know what counts as “the same block”.

Generally speaking, the indented block following the `do` keyword counts as a block, and the immediate sequence of statements underneath it are part of that block.
Statements in independent blocks that are nonetheless contained in a block are not considered part of the block.
However, the rules that govern what exactly counts as the same block are slightly subtle, so some examples are in order.
The precise nature of the rules can be tested by setting up a program with a mutable variable and seeing where the mutation is allowed.
This program has a mutation that is clearly in the same block as the mutable variable:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
x := x + 1
```

When a mutation occurs in a `do`-block that is part of a `let`-statement that defines a name using `:=`, then it is not considered to be part of the block:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
let other := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
x := x + 1
other
```

```lean
Variable `x` cannot be mutated. Only variables declared using `let mut` can be mutated.
      If you did not intend to mutate but define `x`, consider using `let x` instead
```

However, a `do`-block that occurs under a `let`-statement that defines a name using `←` is considered part of the surrounding block.
The following program is accepted:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
let other ← do
x := x + 1
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) other
```

Similarly, `do`-blocks that occur as arguments to functions are independent of their surrounding blocks.
The following program is not accepted:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
let addFour (y : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := [Id.run](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id___run) y + 4
addFour [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
x := 5
```

```lean
Variable `x` cannot be mutated. Only variables declared using `let mut` can be mutated.
      If you did not intend to mutate but define `x`, consider using `let x` instead
```

If the `do` keyword is completely redundant, then it does not introduce a new block.
This program is accepted, and is equivalent to the first one in this section:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
do x := x + 1
```

The contents of branches under a `do` (such as those introduced by `match` or `if`) are considered to be part of the surrounding block, whether or not a redundant `do` is added.
The following programs are all accepted:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
if x > 2 then
x := x + 1
```

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
if x > 2 then do
x := x + 1
```

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
match [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) with
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => x := x + 1
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => x := 17
```

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
match [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) with
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => do
x := x + 1
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => do
x := 17
```

Similarly, the `do` that occurs as part of the `for` and `unless` syntax is just part of their syntax, and does not introduce a fresh `do`-block.
These programs are also accepted:

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
for y in 1...5 do
x := x + y
```

```lean
example : [Id](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Id) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let mut x := 0
unless 1 < 5 do
x := x + 1
```

### 6.4.6. Imperative or Functional Programming? {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--More-do-Features--Imperative-or-Functional-Programming___}

The imperative features provided by Lean's `do`-notation allow many programs to very closely resemble their counterparts in languages like Rust, Java, or C#.
This resemblance is very convenient when translating an imperative algorithm into Lean, and some tasks are just most naturally thought of imperatively.
The introduction of monads and monad transformers enables imperative programs to be written in purely functional languages, and `do`-notation as a specialized syntax for monads (potentially locally transformed) allows functional programmers to have the best of both worlds: the strong reasoning principles afforded by immutability and a tight control over available effects through the type system are combined with syntax and libraries that allow programs that use effects to look familiar and be easy to read.
Monads and monad transformers allow functional versus imperative programming to be a matter of perspective.

### 6.4.7. Exercises {#fpil-monad-transformer-do-exercises}

- Rewrite `doug` to use `for` instead of the `doList` function.
- Are there other opportunities to use the features introduced in this section to improve the code? If so, use them!
