## Monad Transformers — 6.5. Additional Conveniences {#fpil-monad-transformers-65-additional-conveniences}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Additional-Conveniences/

### 6.5.1. Pipe Operators {#fpil-pipe-operators}

Functions are normally written before their arguments.
When reading a program from left to right, this promotes a view in which the function's *output* is paramount—the function has a goal to achieve (that is, a value to compute), and it receives arguments to support it in this process.
But some programs are easier to understand in terms of an input that is successively refined to produce the output.
For these situations, Lean provides a *pipeline* operator which is similar to the that provided by F#.
Pipeline operators are useful in the same situations as Clojure's threading macros.

The pipeline `E₁ |> E₂` is short for `E₂ E₁`.
For example, evaluating:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 5 |> toString
```

results in:

```lean
"(some 5)"
```

While this change of emphasis can make some programs more convenient to read, pipelines really come into their own when they contain many components.

With the definition:

```lean
def times3 (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := n * 3
```

the following pipeline:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) 5 |> [times3]](#fpil-PipelineEx___times3) |> toString |> ("It is " ++ ·)
```

yields:

```lean
"It is 15"
```

More generally, a series of pipelines `E₁ |> E₂ |> E₃ |> E₄` is short for nested function applications `E₄ (E₃ (E₂ E₁))`.

Pipelines may also be written in reverse.
In this case, they do not place the subject of data transformation first; however, in cases where many nested parentheses pose a challenge for readers, they can clarify the steps of application.
The prior example could be equivalently written as:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("It is " ++ ·) <| toString <| [times3]](#fpil-PipelineEx___times3) <| 5
```

which is short for:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ("It is " ++ ·) (toString ([times3]](#fpil-PipelineEx___times3) 5))
```

Lean's method dot notation that uses the name of the type before the dot to resolve the namespace of the operator after the dot serves a similar purpose to pipelines.
Even without the pipeline operator, it is possible to write `[1, 2, 3].[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` instead of `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) [1, 2, 3]`.
However, the pipeline operator is also useful for dotted functions when using many of them.
`([1, 2, 3].[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse).[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) 1).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` can also be written as `[1, 2, 3] |> [List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) |> [List.drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) 1 |> [List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)`.
This version avoids having to parenthesize expressions simply because they accept arguments, and it recovers the convenience of a chain of method calls in languages like Kotlin or C#.
However, it still requires the namespace to be provided by hand.
As a final convenience, Lean provides the “pipeline dot” operator, which groups functions like the pipeline but uses the name of the type to resolve namespaces.
With “pipeline dot”, the example can be rewritten to `[1, 2, 3] |>.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) |>.[drop](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___drop) 1 |>.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)`.

### 6.5.2. Infinite Loops {#fpil-infinite-loops}

Within a `do`-block, the `repeat` keyword introduces an infinite loop.
For example, a program that spams the string `"Spam!"` can use it:

```lean
def spam : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
repeat [IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "Spam!"
```

A `repeat` loop supports `break` and `continue`, just like `for` loops.

The `dump` function from the [implementation of `feline`]](#fpil-streams) uses a recursive function to run forever:

```lean
partial def dump (stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) [bufsize]](#fpil-bufsize)
if buf.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___isEmpty) then
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ()
else
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
stdout.[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
dump stream
```

This function can be greatly shortened using `repeat`:

```lean
def dump (stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
repeat do
let buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) [bufsize]](#fpil-bufsize)
if buf.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___isEmpty) then break
stdout.[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
```

Neither `spam` nor `dump` need to be declared as `partial` because they are not themselves infinitely recursive.
Instead, `repeat` makes use of a type whose `ForM` instance is `partial`.
Partiality does not “infect” calling functions.

### 6.5.3. While Loops {#fpil-while-loops}

When programming with local mutability, `while` loops can be a convenient alternative to `repeat` with an `if`-guarded `break`:

```lean
def dump (stream : [IO.FS.Stream](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdout ← [IO.getStdout](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdout)
let mut buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) [bufsize]](#fpil-bufsize)
while [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) buf.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___isEmpty) do
stdout.[write](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) buf
buf ← stream.[read](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk) [bufsize]](#fpil-bufsize)
```

Behind the scenes, `while` is just a simpler notation for `repeat`.

## Monad Transformers — 6.6. Summary {#fpil-monad-transformers-66-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monad-Transformers/Summary/

### 6.6.1. Combining Monads {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Summary--Combining-Monads}

When writing a monad from scratch, there are design patterns that tend to describe the ways that each effect is added to the monad.
Reader effects are added by having the monad's type be a function from the reader's environment, state effects are added by including a function from the initial state to the value paired with the final state, failure or exceptions are added by including a sum type in the return type, and logging or other output is added by including a product type in the return type.
Existing monads can be made part of the return type as well, allowing their effects to be included in the new monad.

These design patterns are made into a library of reusable software components by defining *monad transformers*, which add an effect to some base monad.
Monad transformers take the simpler monad types as arguments, returning the enhanced monad types.
At a minimum, a monad transformer should provide the following instances:

1. A `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk)` instance that assumes the inner type is already a monad
2. A `[MonadLift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Lifting-Monads/#MonadLift___mk)` instance to translate an action from the inner monad to the transformed monad

Monad transformers may be implemented as polymorphic structures or inductive datatypes, but they are most often implemented as functions from the underlying monad type to the enhanced monad type.

### 6.6.2. Type Classes for Effects {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Summary--Type-Classes-for-Effects}

A common design pattern is to implement a particular effect by defining a monad that has the effect, a monad transformer that adds it to another monad, and a type class that provides a generic interface to the effect.
This allows programs to be written that merely specify which effects they need, so the caller can provide any monad that has the right effects.

Sometimes, auxiliary type information (e.g. the state's type in a monad that provides state, or the exception's type in a monad that provides exceptions) is an output parameter, and sometimes it is not.
The output parameter is most useful for simple programs that use each kind of effect only once, but it risks having the type checker commit to a the wrong type too early when multiple instances of the same effect are used in a given program.
Thus, both versions are typically provided, with the ordinary-parameter version of the type class having a name that ends in `-Of`.

### 6.6.3. Monad Transformers Don't Commute {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Summary--Monad-Transformers-Don___t-Commute}

It is important to note that changing the order of transformers in a monad can change the meaning of programs that use the monad.
For instance, re-ordering `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` and `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` can result either in programs that lose state modifications when exceptions are thrown or programs that keep changes.
While most imperative languages provide only the latter, the increased flexibility provided by monad transformers demands thought and attention to choose the correct variety for the task at hand.

### 6.6.4. `do`-Notation for Monad Transformers {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Monad-Transformers--Summary--do--Notation-for-Monad-Transformers}

Lean's `do`-blocks support early return, in which the block is terminated with some value, locally mutable variables, `for`-loops with `break` and `continue`, and single-branched `if`-statements.
While this may seem to be introducing imperative features that would get in the way of using Lean to write proofs, it is in fact nothing more than a more convenient syntax for certain common uses of monad transformers.
Behind the scenes, whatever monad the `do`-block is written in is transformed by appropriate uses of `[ExceptT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ExceptT)` and `[StateT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateT)` to support these additional effects.

---



## Programming with Dependent Types {#fpil-programming-with-dependent-types}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/

In most statically-typed programming languages, there is a hermetic seal between the world of types and the world of programs.
Types and programs have different grammars and they are used at different times.
Types are typically used at compile time, to check that a program obeys certain invariants.
Programs are used at run time, to actually perform computations.
When the two interact, it is usually in the form of a type-case operator like an “instance-of” check or a casting operator that provides the type checker with information that was otherwise unavailable, to be verified at run time.
In other words, the interaction consists of types being inserted into the world of programs, where they gain some limited run-time meaning.

Lean does not impose this strict separation.
In Lean, programs may compute types and types may contain programs.
Placing programs in types allows their full computational power to be used at compile time, and the ability to return types from functions makes types into first-class participants in the programming process.

*Dependent types* are types that contain non-type expressions.
A common source of dependent types is a named argument to a function.
For example, the function `natOrStringThree` returns either a natural number or a string, depending on which `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` it is passed:

```lean
def natOrStringThree (b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) b [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) b [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => (3 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => "three"
```

Further examples of dependent types include:

- [The introductory section on polymorphism]](#fpil-polymorphism) contains `posOrNegThree`, in which the function's return type depends on the value of the argument.
- [The `OfNat` type class]](#fpil-literal-numbers) depends on the specific natural number literal being used.
- [The `CheckedInput` structure]](#fpil-validated-input) used in the example of validators depends on the year in which validation occurred.
- [Subtypes]](#fpil-subtypes) contain propositions that refer to particular values.
- Essentially all interesting propositions, including those that determine the validity of [array indexing notation]](#fpil-props-proofs-indexing), are types that contain values and are thus dependent types.

Dependent types vastly increase the power of a type system.
The flexibility of return types that branch on argument values enables programs to be written that cannot easily be given types in other type systems.
At the same time, dependent types allow a type signature to restrict which values may be returned from a function, enabling strong invariants to be enforced at compile time.

However, programming with dependent types can be quite complex, and it requires a whole set of skills above and beyond functional programming.
Expressive specifications can be complicated to fulfill, and there is a real risk of tying oneself in knots and being unable to complete the program.
On the other hand, this process can lead to new understanding, which can be expressed in a refined type that can be fulfilled.
While this chapter scratches the surface of dependently typed programming, it is a deep topic that deserves an entire book of its own.

1. [7.1. Indexed Families](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/Indexed-Families/#indexed-families)
2. [7.2. The Universe Design Pattern](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/The-Universe-Design-Pattern/#universe-pattern)
3. [7.3. Worked Example: Typed Queries](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/Worked-Example___-Typed-Queries/#typed-queries)
4. [7.4. Indices, Parameters, and Universe Levels](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/Indices___-Parameters___-and-Universe-Levels/#indices-parameters-universe-levels)

## Programming with Dependent Types — 7.1. Indexed Families {#fpil-programming-with-dependent-types-71-indexed-families}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming-with-Dependent-Types/Indexed-Families/

Polymorphic inductive types take type arguments.
For instance, `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` takes an argument that determines the type of the entries in the list, and `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` takes arguments that determine the types of the exceptions or values.
These type arguments, which are the same in every constructor of the datatype, are referred to as *parameters*.

Arguments to inductive types need not be the same in every constructor, however.
Inductive types in which the arguments to the type vary based on the choice of constructor are called *indexed families*, and the arguments that vary are referred to as *indices*.
The “hello world” of indexed families is a type of lists that contains the length of the list in addition to the type of entries, conventionally referred to as “vectors”:

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u where
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → Vect α n → Vect α (n + 1)
```

The type of a vector of three `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`s includes the fact that it contains three `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`s:

```lean
example : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3 :=
.cons "one" (.cons "two" (.cons "three" .nil))
```

Function declarations may take some arguments before the colon, indicating that they are available in the entire definition, and some arguments after, indicating a desire to pattern-match on them and define the function case by case.
Inductive datatypes have a similar principle: the argument `α` is named at the top of the datatype declaration, prior to the colon, which indicates that it is a parameter that must be provided as the first argument in all occurrences of `Vect` in the definition, while the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` argument occurs after the colon, indicating that it is an index that may vary.
Indeed, the three occurrences of `Vect` in the `nil` and `cons` constructor declarations consistently provide `α` as the first argument, while the second argument is different in each case.

The declaration of `nil` states that it is a constructor of type `Vect α 0`.
This means that using `Vect.nil` in a context expecting a `Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3` is a type error, just as `[1, 2, 3]` is a type error in a context that expects a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`:

```lean
example : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3 := Vect.nil
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  Vect.nil
has type
  Vect ?m.3 0
but is expected to have type
  Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3
```

The mismatch between `0` and `3` in this example plays exactly the same role as any other type mismatch, even though `0` and `3` are not themselves types.
The metavariable in the message can be ignored because its presence indicates that `Vect.nil` can have any element type.

Indexed families are called *families* of types because different index values can make different constructors available for use.
In some sense, an indexed family is not a type; rather, it is a collection of related types, and the choice of index values also chooses a type from the collection.
Choosing the index `5` for `Vect` means that only the constructor `cons` is available, and choosing the index `0` means that only `nil` is available.

If the index is not yet known (e.g. because it is a variable), then no constructor can be used until it becomes known.
Using `n` for the length allows neither `Vect.nil` nor `Vect.cons`, because there's no way to know whether the variable `n` should stand for a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that matches `0` or `n + 1`:

```lean
example : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) n := Vect.nil
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  Vect.nil
has type
  Vect ?m.2 0
but is expected to have type
  Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) n
```

```lean
example : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) n := Vect.cons "Hello" (Vect.cons "world" Vect.nil)
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  Vect.cons "Hello" (Vect.cons "world" Vect.nil)
has type
  Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
but is expected to have type
  Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) n
```

Having the length of the list as part of its type means that the type becomes more informative.
For example, `Vect.replicate` is a function that creates a `Vect` with a number of copies of a given value.
The type that says this precisely is:

```lean
def Vect.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : Vect α n := _
```

The argument `n` appears as the length of the result.
The message associated with the underscore placeholder describes the task at hand:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type u_1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:α⊢ Vect α n
```

When working with indexed families, constructors can only be applied when Lean can see that the constructor's index matches the index in the expected type.
However, neither constructor has an index that matches `n`—`nil` matches `[Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and `cons` matches `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Just as in the example type errors, the variable `n` could stand for either, depending on which `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is provided to the function as an argument.
The solution is to use pattern matching to consider both of the possible cases:

```lean
def Vect.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : Vect α n :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => _
| k + 1 => _
```

Because `n` occurs in the expected type, pattern matching on `n` *refines* the expected type in the two cases of the match.
In the first underscore, the expected type has become `Vect α 0`:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type u_1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:α⊢ Vect α 0
```

In the second underscore, it has become `Vect α (k + 1)`:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type u_1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:αk:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ Vect α [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)k [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

When pattern matching refines the type of a program in addition to discovering the structure of a value, it is called *dependent pattern matching*.

The refined type makes it possible to apply the constructors.
The first underscore matches `Vect.nil`, and the second matches `Vect.cons`:

```lean
def Vect.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : Vect α n :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => .nil
| k + 1 => .cons _ _
```

The first underscore under the `.cons` should have type `α`.
There is an `α` available, namely `x`:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type u_1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:αk:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ α
```

The second underscore should be a `Vect α k`, which can be produced by a recursive call to `replicate`:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type u_1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:αk:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ Vect α k
```

Here is the final definition of `replicate`:

```lean
def Vect.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : Vect α n :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => .nil
| k + 1 => .cons x (replicate k x)
```

In addition to providing assistance while writing the function, the informative type of `Vect.replicate` also allows client code to rule out a number of unexpected functions without having to read the source code.
A version of `[replicate]](#fpil-Extras___List___replicate)` for lists could produce a list of the wrong length:

```lean
def List.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => []
| k + 1 => x :: x :: [replicate]](#fpil-Extras___List___replicate) k x
```

However, making this mistake with `Vect.replicate` is a type error:

```lean
def Vect.replicate (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : α) : Vect α n :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => .nil
| k + 1 => .cons x (.cons x (replicate k x))
```

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  cons x (replicate k x)
has type
  Vect α [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)k [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
but is expected to have type
  Vect α k
in the application
  cons x (cons x (replicate k x))
```

The function `[List.zip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___zip)` combines two lists by pairing the first entry in the first list with the first entry in the second list, the second entry in the first list with the second entry in the second list, and so forth.
`[List.zip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___zip)` can be used to pair the three highest peaks in the US state of Oregon with the three highest peaks in Denmark:

```lean
["Mount Hood",
"Mount Jefferson",
"South Sister"].[zip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___zip) ["Møllehøj", "Yding Skovhøj", "Ejer Bavnehøj"]
```

The result is a list of three pairs:

```lean
[("Mount Hood", "Møllehøj"),
("Mount Jefferson", "Yding Skovhøj"),
("South Sister", "Ejer Bavnehøj")]
```

It's somewhat unclear what should happen when the lists have different lengths.
Like many languages, Lean chooses to ignore the extra entries in one of the lists.
For instance, combining the heights of the five highest peaks in Oregon with those of the three highest peaks in Denmark yields three pairs.
In particular,

```lean
[3428.8, 3201, 3158.5, 3075, 3064].[zip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___zip) [170.86, 170.77, 170.35]
```

evaluates to

```lean
[(3428.8, 170.86), (3201, 170.77), (3158.5, 170.35)]
```

While this approach is convenient because it always returns an answer, it runs the risk of throwing away data when the lists unintentionally have different lengths.
F# takes a different approach: its version of `List.zip` throws an exception when the lengths don't match, as can be seen in this `fsi` session:

```
> List.zip [3428.8; 3201.0; 3158.5; 3075.0; 3064.0] [170.86; 170.77; 170.35];;
```

```
System.ArgumentException: The lists had different lengths.
list2 is 2 elements shorter than list1 (Parameter 'list2')
   at Microsoft.FSharp.Core.DetailedExceptions.invalidArgDifferentListLength[?](String arg1, String arg2, Int32 diff) in /builddir/build/BUILD/dotnet-v3.1.424-SDK/src/fsharp.3ef6f0b514198c0bfa6c2c09fefe41a740b024d5/src/fsharp/FSharp.Core/local.fs:line 24
   at Microsoft.FSharp.Primitives.Basics.List.zipToFreshConsTail[a,b](FSharpList`1 cons, FSharpList`1 xs1, FSharpList`1 xs2) in /builddir/build/BUILD/dotnet-v3.1.424-SDK/src/fsharp.3ef6f0b514198c0bfa6c2c09fefe41a740b024d5/src/fsharp/FSharp.Core/local.fs:line 918
   at Microsoft.FSharp.Primitives.Basics.List.zip[T1,T2](FSharpList`1 xs1, FSharpList`1 xs2) in /builddir/build/BUILD/dotnet-v3.1.424-SDK/src/fsharp.3ef6f0b514198c0bfa6c2c09fefe41a740b024d5/src/fsharp/FSharp.Core/local.fs:line 929
   at Microsoft.FSharp.Collections.ListModule.Zip[T1,T2](FSharpList`1 list1, FSharpList`1 list2) in /builddir/build/BUILD/dotnet-v3.1.424-SDK/src/fsharp.3ef6f0b514198c0bfa6c2c09fefe41a740b024d5/src/fsharp/FSharp.Core/list.fs:line 466
   at <StartupCode$FSI_0006>.$FSI_0006.main@()
Stopped due to error
```

This avoids accidentally discarding information, but crashing a program comes with its own difficulties.
The Lean equivalent, which would use the `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` or `[Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error)` monads, would introduce a burden that may not be worth the safety.

Using `Vect`, however, it is possible to write a version of `zip` with a type that requires that both arguments have the same length:

```lean
def Vect.zip : Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect (α × β) n
| .nil, .nil => .nil
| .cons x xs, .cons y ys => .cons (x, y) (zip xs ys)
```

This definition only has patterns for the cases where either both arguments are `Vect.nil` or both arguments are `Vect.cons`, and Lean accepts the definition without a “missing cases” error like the one that results from a similar definition for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`:

```lean
def List.zip : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α × β)
| [], [] => []
| x :: xs, y :: ys => (x, y) :: [zip]](#fpil-Other___List___zip) xs ys
```

```lean
Missing cases:
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil), ([List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) _ _)
([List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) _ _), [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

This is because the constructor used in the first pattern, `nil` or `cons`, *refines* the type checker's knowledge about the length `n`.
When the first pattern is `nil`, the type checker can additionally determine that the length was `0`, so the only possible choice for the second pattern is `nil`.
Similarly, when the first pattern is `cons`, the type checker can determine that the length was `k+1` for some `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` `k`, so the only possible choice for the second pattern is `cons`.
Indeed, adding a case that uses `nil` and `cons` together is a type error, because the lengths don't match:

```lean
def Vect.zip : Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect (α × β) n
| .nil, .nil => .nil
| .nil, .cons y ys => .nil
| .cons x xs, .cons y ys => .cons (x, y) (zip xs ys)
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  Vect.cons y ys
has type
  Vect ?m.10 [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)?m.16 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
but is expected to have type
  Vect β 0
```

The refinement of the length can be observed by making `n` into an explicit argument:

```lean
def Vect.zip : (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect (α × β) n
| 0, .nil, .nil => .nil
| k + 1, .cons x xs, .cons y ys => .cons (x, y) ([zip]](#fpil-Details___Vect___zip) k xs ys)
```

### 7.1.1. Exercises {#fpil-indexed-families-exercises}

Getting a feel for programming with dependent types requires experience, and the exercises in this section are very important.
For each exercise, try to see which mistakes the type checker can catch, and which ones it can't, by experimenting with the code as you go.
This is also a good way to develop a feel for the error messages.

- Double-check that `Vect.zip` gives the right answer when combining the three highest peaks in Oregon with the three highest peaks in Denmark.
  Because `Vect` doesn't have the syntactic sugar that `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` has, it can be helpful to begin by defining `oregonianPeaks : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3` and `danishPeaks : Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 3`.
- Define a function `Vect.map` with type `(α → β) → Vect α n → Vect β n`.
- Define a function `Vect.zipWith` that combines the entries in a `Vect` one at a time with a function.
  It should have the type `(α → β → γ) → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect γ n`.
- Define a function `Vect.unzip` that splits a `Vect` of pairs into a pair of `Vect`s. It should have the type `Vect (α × β) n → Vect α n × Vect β n`.
- Define a function `Vect.push` that adds an entry to the *end* of a `Vect`. Its type should be `Vect α n → α → Vect α (n + 1)` and `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Vect.push]](#fpil-Vect___push) (.cons "snowy" .nil) "peaks"` should yield `Vect.cons "snowy" (Vect.cons "peaks" (Vect.nil))`.
- Define a function `Vect.reverse` that reverses the order of a `Vect`.
- Define a function `Vect.drop` with the following type: `(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → Vect α (k + n) → Vect α k`.
  Verify that it works by checking that `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [danishPeaks]](#fpil-danishPeaks).[drop]](#fpil-Vect___drop) 2` yields `Vect.cons "Ejer Bavnehøj" (Vect.nil)`.
- Define a function `Vect.take` with type `(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → Vect α (k + n) → Vect α n` that returns the first `n` entries in the `Vect`. Check that it works on an example.
