Ideally, the induction hypothesis could be used to replace `Tail.sumHelper (y + n) ys`, but they don't match.
The induction hypothesis can be used for `Tail.sumHelper n ys`, not `Tail.sumHelper (y + n) ys`.
In other words, this proof is stuck.

### 8.2.2. A Second Attempt {#fpil-proving-sum-equal-again}

Rather than attempting to muddle through the proof, it's time to take a step back and think.
Why is it that the tail-recursive version of the function is equal to the non-tail-recursive version?
Fundamentally speaking, at each entry in the list, the accumulator grows by the same amount as would be added to the result of the recursion.
This insight can be used to write an elegant proof.
Crucially, the proof by induction must be set up such that the induction hypothesis can be applied to *any* accumulator value.

Discarding the prior attempt, the insight can be encoded as the following statement:

```lean
theorem [non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → n + NonTail.sum xs = Tail.sumHelper n xs := byxs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper n xs
[skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper n xs
```

In this statement, it's very important that `n` is part of the type that's after the colon.
The resulting goal begins with `∀ (n : Nat)`, which is short for “For all `n`”:

In other words, the goal has become more challenging to prove, but the induction hypothesis is correspondingly more useful.

A mathematical proof for a statement that beings with “for all `x`” should assume some arbitrary `x`, and prove the statement.
“Arbitrary” means that no additional properties of `x` are assumed, so the resulting statement will work for *any* `x`.
In Lean, a “for all” statement is a dependent function: no matter which specific value it is applied to, it will return evidence of the proposition.
Similarly, the process of picking an arbitrary `x` is the same as using `fun x => ...`.
In the tactic language, this process of selecting an arbitrary `x` is performed using the `intro` tactic, which produces the function behind the scenes when the tactic script has completed.
The `intro` tactic should be provided with the name to be used for this arbitrary value.

Using the `intro` tactic in the `[nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` case removes the `∀ (n : Nat),` from the goal, and adds an assumption `n : Nat`:

This goal is very close to matching the induction hypothesis.
There are two ways in which it does not match:

- The left-hand side of the equation is `n + (y + NonTail.sum ys)`, but the induction hypothesis needs the left-hand side to be a number added to `NonTail.sum ys`.
  In other words, this goal should be rewritten to `(n + y) + NonTail.sum ys`, which is valid because addition of natural numbers is associative.
- When the left side has been rewritten to `(y + n) + NonTail.sum ys`, the accumulator argument on the right side should be `n + y` rather than `y + n` in order to match.
  This rewrite is valid because addition is also commutative.

The associativity and commutativity of addition have already been proved in Lean's standard library.
The proof of associativity is named `Nat.add_assoc`, and its type is `(n m k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → (n + m) + k = n + (m + k)`, while the proof of commutativity is called `Nat.add_comm` and has type `(n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → n + m = m + n`.
Normally, the `rw` tactic is provided with an expression whose type is an equality.
However, if the argument is instead a dependent function whose return type is an equality, it attempts to find arguments to the function that would allow the equality to match something in the goal.
There is only one opportunity to apply associativity, though the direction of the rewrite must be reversed because the right side of the equality in `(n + m) + k = n + (m + k)` is the one that matches the proof goal:

The goal now matches the induction hypothesis.
In particular, the induction hypothesis's type is a dependent function type.
Applying `ih` to `n + y` results in exactly the desired type.
The `exact` tactic completes a proof goal if its argument has exactly the desired type:

The actual proof requires only a little additional work to get the goal to match the helper's type.
The first step is still to invoke function extensionality:

```lean
theorem non_tail_sum_eq_tail_sum : NonTail.sum = Tail.sum := by⊢ NonTail.sum [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sum
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#funext-next) xsxs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sum xs
```

The next step is unfold `Tail.sum`, exposing `Tail.sumHelper`:

```lean
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [Tail.sum]xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper 0 xs
```

Having done this, the types almost match.
However, the helper has an additional addend on the left side.
In other words, the proof goal is `NonTail.sum xs = Tail.sumHelper 0 xs`, but applying `[non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum)` to `xs` and `0` yields the type `0 + NonTail.sum xs = Tail.sumHelper 0 xs`.
Another standard library proof, `Nat.zero_add`, has type `(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → 0 + n = n`.
Applying this function to `NonTail.sum xs` results in an expression with type `0 + NonTail.sum xs = NonTail.sum xs`, so rewriting from right to left results in the desired goal:

```lean

[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw) [←Nat.zero_add (NonTail.sum xs)xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper 0 xs]xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper 0 xs
```

This proof demonstrates a general pattern that can be used when proving that an accumulator-passing tail-recursive function is equal to the non-tail-recursive version.
The first step is to discover the relationship between the starting accumulator argument and the final result.
For instance, beginning `Tail.sumHelper` with an accumulator of `n` results in the final sum being added to `n`, and beginning `Tail.reverseHelper` with an accumulator of `ys` results in the final reversed list being prepended to `ys`.
The second step is to write down this relationship as a theorem statement and prove it by induction.
While the accumulator is always initialized with some neutral value in practice, such as `0` or `[]`, this more general statement that allows the starting accumulator to be any value is what's needed to get a strong enough induction hypothesis.
Finally, using this helper theorem with the actual initial accumulator value results in the desired proof.
For example, in `non_tail_sum_eq_tail_sum`, the accumulator is specified to be `0`.
This may require rewriting the goal to make the neutral initial accumulator values occur in the right place.

### 8.2.3. Functional Induction {#fpil-fun-induction}

The proof of `[non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum)` follows the implementation of `Tail.sumHelper` closely.
There is not, however, a perfect match between the implementation and the structure expected by mathematical induction, which makes it necessary to manage the assumption `n` carefully.
This is a small amount of work in the case of `[non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum)`, but proofs about functions whose definitions are further from the structure expected by `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` require more bookkeeping.

In addition to proving theorems about recursive functions by induction on one of the arguments, Lean supports proofs by induction on the recursive call structure of functions.
This *functional induction* results in a base case for each branch of the function's control flow that does not include a recursive call, and inductive steps for each branch that does.
A proof by functional induction should demonstrate that the theorem holds for the non-recursive branches, and that if the theorem holds for the result of each recursive call, then it also holds for the result of the recursive branch.

Using functional induction simplifies `[non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum)`:

```lean
theorem [non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum]](#fpil-non_tail_sum_eq_helper_accum) (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
n + NonTail.sum xs = Tail.sumHelper n xs := byxs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper n xs
[fun_induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#fun_induction) Tail.sumHelper with
| case1 n => [skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)case1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
| case2 n y ys ih => [skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)case2n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ys:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum ys [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ys⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)y [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ys[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ys
```

Each branch of the proof matches the corresponding branch of `Tail.sumHelper`:

```lean
def Tail.sumHelper (soFar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => soFar
| x :: xs => sumHelper (x + soFar) xs
```

In the first, `case1`, the right side of the equality is the accumulator value, called `n` in the proof:

```lean
unsolved goals
case1n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
```

In the second, `case2`, the right side of the equality is the next step in the tail-recursive loop:

```lean
unsolved goals
case2n y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ys:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum ys [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ys⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) NonTail.sum [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)y [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ys[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.sumHelper [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ys
```

The resulting proof can be simpler.
The fundamentals of the argument, including the properties of addition that are used, are the same; however, the bookkeeping has been removed.
It is no longer necessary to manually juggle the accumulator value, and the induction hypothesis can be used directly instead of requiring instantiation:

The `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` tactic is very well suited to this kind of goal.
Unlike `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` and `[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw)`, it is not directional; internally, it accumulates a collection of facts until it either proves the goal completely or fails to do so.
It is preconfigured to use basic facts about arithmetic, such as the associativity and commutativity of addition, and it automatically uses local assumptions such as the induction hypothesis.
Using `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)`, this proof becomes short and to-the-point:

This proof also matches the way the proof might be explained to a skilled programmer: “Just check both branches of `Tail.sumHelper`!”

### 8.2.4. Exercise {#fpil-tail-recursion-proof-exercises}

#### 8.2.4.1. Warming Up {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Proving-Equivalence--Exercise--Warming-Up}

Write your own proofs for `Nat.zero_add`, `Nat.add_assoc`, and `Nat.add_comm` using the `induction` tactic.

#### 8.2.4.2. More Accumulator Proofs {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Proving-Equivalence--Exercise--More-Accumulator-Proofs}

##### 8.2.4.2.1. Reversing Lists {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Proving-Equivalence--Exercise--More-Accumulator-Proofs--Reversing-Lists}

Adapt the proof for `sum` into a proof for `NonTail.reverse` and `Tail.reverse`.
The first step is to think about the relationship between the accumulator value being passed to `Tail.reverseHelper` and the non-tail-recursive reverse.
Just as adding a number to the accumulator in `Tail.sumHelper` is the same as adding it to the overall sum, using `[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` to add a new entry to the accumulator in `Tail.reverseHelper` is equivalent to some change to the overall result.
Try three or four different accumulator values with pencil and paper until the relationship becomes clear.
Use this relationship to prove a suitable helper theorem.
Try proving this helper theorem both using induction on lists and via functional induction.
Then, write down the overall theorem.
Because `NonTail.reverse` and `Tail.reverse` are polymorphic, stating their equality requires the use of `@` to stop Lean from trying to figure out which type to use for `α`.
Once `α` is treated as an ordinary argument, `funext` should be invoked with both `α` and `xs`:

```lean
theorem non_tail_reverse_eq_tail_reverse :
@NonTail.reverse = @Tail.reverse := by⊢ @NonTail.reverse [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) @Tail.reverse
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#funext-next) α xsα:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ NonTail.reverse xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.reverse xs
```

This results in a suitable goal:

```lean
unsolved goals
α:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ NonTail.reverse xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) Tail.reverse xs
```

##### 8.2.4.2.2. Factorial {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Proving-Equivalence--Exercise--More-Accumulator-Proofs--Factorial}

Prove that `NonTail.factorial` from the exercises in the previous section is equal to your tail-recursive solution by finding the relationship between the accumulator and the result and proving a suitable helper theorem.

## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.3. Arrays and Termination {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-83-arrays-and-termination}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/Arrays-and-Termination/

To write efficient code, it is important to select appropriate data structures.
Linked lists have their place: in some applications, the ability to share the tails of lists is very important.
However, most use cases for a variable-length sequential collection of data are better served by arrays, which have both less memory overhead and better locality.

Arrays, however, have two drawbacks relative to lists:

1. Arrays are accessed through indexing, rather than by pattern matching, which imposes [proof obligations]](#fpil-props-proofs-indexing) in order to maintain safety.
2. A loop that processes an entire array from left to right is a tail-recursive function, but it does not have an argument that decreases on each call.

Making effective use of arrays requires knowing how to prove to Lean that an array index is in bounds, and how to prove that an array index that approaches the size of the array also causes the program to terminate.
Both of these are expressed using an inequality proposition, rather than propositional equality.

### 8.3.1. Inequality {#fpil-inequality}

Because different types have different notions of ordering, inequality is governed by two type classes, called `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` and `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)`.
The table in the section on [standard type classes]](#fpil-equality-and-ordering) describes how these classes relate to the syntax:

| Expression | Desugaring | Class Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x < y` | `[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) x y` | `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` |
| `x ≤ y` | `[LE.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x y` | `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` |
| `x > y` | `[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) y x` | `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` |
| `x ≥ y` | `[LE.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) y x` | `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` |

In other words, a type may customize the meaning of the `<` and `≤` operators, while `>` and `≥` derive their meanings from `<` and `≤`.
The classes `[LT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk)` and `[LE](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk)` have methods that return propositions rather than `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`s:

```lean
class LE (α : Type u) where
le : α → α → Prop
class LT (α : Type u) where
lt : α → α → Prop
```

The instance of `[LE]](#fpil-Orders___LE)` for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` delegates to `Nat.le`:

```lean
instance : [LE]](#fpil-Orders___LE) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[le]](#fpil-Orders___LE___le) := Nat.le
```

Defining `Nat.le` requires a feature of Lean that has not yet been presented: it is an inductively-defined relation.

#### 8.3.1.1. Inductively-Defined Propositions, Predicates, and Relations {#fpil-inductive-props}

`Nat.le` is an *inductively-defined relation*.
Just as `inductive` can be used to create new datatypes, it can be used to create new propositions.
When a proposition takes an argument, it is referred to as a *predicate* that may be true for some, but not all, potential arguments.
Propositions that take multiple arguments are called *relations*.

Each constructor of an inductively defined proposition is a way to prove it.
In other words, the declaration of the proposition describes the different forms of evidence that it is true.
A proposition with no arguments that has a single constructor can be quite easy to prove:

```lean
inductive EasyToProve : Prop where
| heresTheProof : EasyToProve
```

The proof consists of using its constructor:

```lean
theorem fairlyEasy : EasyToProve := by⊢ EasyToProve
[constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor)All goals completed! 🐙
```

In fact, the proposition `True`, which should always be easy to prove, is defined just like `EasyToProve`:

```lean
inductive True : Prop where
| intro : True
```

Inductively-defined propositions that don't take arguments are not nearly as interesting as inductively-defined datatypes.
This is because data is interesting in its own right—the natural number `3` is different from the number `35`, and someone who has ordered 3 pizzas will be upset if 35 arrive at their door 30 minutes later.
The constructors of a proposition describe ways in which the proposition can be true, but once a proposition has been proved, there is no need to know *which* underlying constructors were used.
This is why most interesting inductively-defined types in the `Prop` universe take arguments.

The inductively-defined predicate `IsThree` states that its argument is three:

```lean
inductive IsThree : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| isThree : IsThree 3
```

The mechanism used here is just like [indexed families such as `HasCol`]](#fpil-column-pointers), except the resulting type is a proposition that can be proved rather than data that can be used.

Using this predicate, it is possible to prove that three is indeed three:

```lean
theorem three_is_three : IsThree 3 := by⊢ IsThree 3
[constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Similarly, `IsFive` is a predicate that states that its argument is `5`:

```lean
inductive IsFive : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| isFive : IsFive 5
```

If a number is three, then the result of adding two to it should be five.
This can be expressed as a theorem statement:

```lean
theorem three_plus_two_five : IsThree n → IsFive (n + 2) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

The resulting goal has a function type:

```lean
unsolved goals
n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

Thus, the `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)` tactic can be used to convert the argument into an assumption:

```lean
theorem three_plus_two_five : IsThree n → IsFive (n + 2) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) threen:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

```lean
unsolved goals
n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

Given the assumption that `n` is three, it should be possible to use the constructor of `IsFive` to complete the proof:

```lean
theorem three_plus_two_five : IsThree n → IsFive (n + 2) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) threen:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

However, this results in an error:

```lean
Tactic `constructor` failed: no applicable constructor found

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

This error occurs because `n + 2` is not definitionally equal to `5`.
In an ordinary function definition, dependent pattern matching on the assumption `three` could be used to refine `n` to `3`.
The tactic equivalent of dependent pattern matching is `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)`, which has a syntax similar to that of `induction`:

```lean
theorem three_plus_two_five : IsThree n → IsFive (n + 2) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) threen:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) three with
| isThree => [skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)isThree⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

In the remaining case, `n` has been refined to `3`:

```lean
unsolved goals
isThree⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
```

Because `3 + 2` is definitionally equal to `5`, the constructor is now applicable:

```lean
theorem three_plus_two_five : IsThree n → IsFive (n + 2) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ IsThree n → IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) threen:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)three:IsThree n⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) three with
| isThree =>isThree⊢ IsFive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)3 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The standard false proposition `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` has no constructors, making it impossible to provide direct evidence for.
The only way to provide evidence for `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` is if an assumption is itself impossible, similarly to how `nomatch` can be used to mark code that the type system can see is unreachable.
As described in [the initial Interlude on proofs]](#fpil-connectives), the negation `[Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not) A` is short for `A → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`.
`[Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not) A` can also be written `¬A`.

It is not the case that four is three:

```lean
theorem four_is_not_three : ¬ IsThree 4 := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
[skip](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#skip)⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
```

The initial proof goal contains `[Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)`:

```lean
unsolved goals
⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
```

The fact that it's actually a function type can be exposed using `[unfold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#unfold)`:

```lean
theorem four_is_not_three : ¬ IsThree 4 := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
[unfold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#unfold) [Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)⊢ IsThree 4 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

```lean
unsolved goals
⊢ IsThree 4 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

Because the goal is a function type, `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)` can be used to convert the argument into an assumption.
There is no need to keep `[unfold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#unfold)`, as `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)` can unfold the definition of `[Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)` itself:

```lean
theorem four_is_not_three : ¬ IsThree 4 := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) hh:IsThree 4⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

```lean
unsolved goals
h:IsThree 4⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

In this proof, the `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` tactic solves the goal immediately:

```lean
theorem four_is_not_three : ¬ IsThree 4 := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)IsThree 4
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) hh:IsThree 4⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) hAll goals completed! 🐙
```

Just as a pattern match on a `Vect [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) 2` doesn't need to include a case for `Vect.nil`, a proof by cases over `IsThree 4` doesn't need to include a case for `isThree`.

#### 8.3.1.2. Inequality of Natural Numbers {#fpil-inequality-of-natural-numbers}

The definition of `Nat.le` has a parameter and an index:

```lean
inductive Nat.le (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop
| refl : Nat.le n n
| step : Nat.le n m → Nat.le n (m + 1)
```

The parameter `n` is the number that should be smaller, while the index is the number that should be greater than or equal to `n`.
The `refl` constructor is used when both numbers are equal, while the `step` constructor is used when the index is greater than `n`.

From the perspective of evidence, a proof that `n \leq k` consists of finding some number `d` such that `n + d = m`.
In Lean, the proof then consists of a `Nat.le.refl` constructor wrapped by `d` instances of `Nat.le.step`.
Each `step` constructor adds one to its index argument, so `d` `step` constructors adds `d` to the larger number.
For example, evidence that four is less than or equal to seven consists of three `step`s around a `refl`:

```lean
theorem four_le_seven : 4 ≤ 7 :=
open Nat.le in
[step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) ([step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) ([step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) [refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)))
```

The strict less-than relation is defined by adding one to the number on the left:

```lean
def Nat.lt (n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Prop :=
Nat.le (n + 1) m
instance : [LT]](#fpil-Orders___LT) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[lt]](#fpil-Orders___LT___lt) := [Nat.lt]](#fpil-Orders___Nat___lt)
```

Evidence that four is strictly less than seven consists of two `[step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)`'s around a `[refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)`:

```lean
theorem four_lt_seven : 4 < 7 :=
open Nat.le in
[step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) ([step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) [refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl))
```

This is because `4 < 7` is equivalent to `5 ≤ 7`.

### 8.3.2. Proving Termination {#fpil-proving-termination}

The function `Array.map` transforms an array with a function, returning a new array that contains the result of applying the function to each element of the input array.
Writing it as a tail-recursive function follows the usual pattern of delegating to a function that passes the output array in an accumulator.
The accumulator is initialized with an empty array.
The accumulator-passing helper function also takes an argument that tracks the current index into the array, which starts at `0`:

```lean
def Array.map (f : α → β) (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β :=
arrayMapHelper f arr [Array.empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___empty) 0
```

The helper should, at each iteration, check whether the index is still in bounds.
If so, it should loop again with the transformed element added to the end of the accumulator and the index incremented by `1`.
If not, then it should terminate and return the accumulator.
An initial implementation of this code fails because Lean is unable to prove that the array index is valid:

```lean
def arrayMapHelper (f : α → β) (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α)
(soFar : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
arrayMapHelper f arr (soFar.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (f arr[i])) (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) soFar
```

```lean
failed to prove index is valid, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the index is valid
  - Use `a[i]!` notation instead, runtime check is performed, and 'Panic' error message is produced if index is not valid
  - Use `a[i]?` notation instead, result is an `Option` type
  - Use `a[i]'h` notation instead, where `h` is a proof that index is valid
α:Type ?u.7β:Type ?u.9f:α → βarr:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) αsoFar:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) βi:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ i [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
```

However, the conditional expression already checks the precise condition that the array index's validity demands (namely, `i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`).
Adding a name to the `if` resolves the issue, because it adds an assumption that the array indexing tactic can use:

```lean
def arrayMapHelper (f : α → β) (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α)
(soFar : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) inBounds : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
arrayMapHelper f arr (soFar.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (f arr[i])) (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) soFar
```

Lean accepts the modified program, even though the recursive call is not made on an argument to one of the input constructors.
In fact, both the accumulator and the index grow, rather than shrinking.

Behind the scenes, Lean's proof automation constructs a termination proof.
Reconstructing this proof can make it easier to understand the cases that Lean cannot automatically recognize.

Why does `arrayMapHelper` terminate?
Each iteration checks whether the index `i` is still in bounds for the array `arr`.
If so, `i` is incremented and the loop repeats.
If not, the program terminates.
Because `arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)` is a finite number, `i` can be incremented only a finite number of times.
Even though no argument to the function decreases on each call, `arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) - i` decreases toward zero.

The value that decreases at each recursive call is called a *measure*.
Lean can be instructed to use a specific expression as the measure of termination by providing a `termination_by` clause at the end of a definition.
For `arrayMapHelper`, the explicit measure looks like this:

```lean
def arrayMapHelper (f : α → β) (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α)
(soFar : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) inBounds : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
arrayMapHelper f arr (soFar.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (f arr[i])) (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) soFar
termination_by arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) - i
```

A similar termination proof can be used to write `Array.find`, a function that finds the first element in an array that satisfies a Boolean function and returns both the element and its index:

```lean
def Array.find (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) :
[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) :=
findHelper arr p 0
```

Once again, the helper function terminates because `arr.size - i` decreases as `i` increases:

```lean
def findHelper (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let x := arr[i]
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (i, x)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) findHelper arr p (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

Adding a question mark to `termination_by` (that is, using `termination_by?`) causes Lean to explicitly suggest the measure that it chose.
Clicking `[apply]` replaces `termination_by?` with the suggested measure:

```lean
def findHelper (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × α) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let x := arr[i]
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (i, x)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [findHelper]](#fpil-Huh___findHelper) arr p (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) none
termination_by?
```

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] termination_by arr.size - i
```

Not all termination arguments are as quite as simple as this one.
However, the basic structure of identifying some expression based on the function's arguments that will decrease in each call occurs in all termination proofs.
Sometimes, creativity can be required in order to figure out just why a function terminates, and sometimes Lean requires additional proofs in order to accept that the measure in fact decreases.

### 8.3.3. Exercises {#fpil-array-termination-exercises}

- Implement a `[ForM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk) m ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α)` instance on arrays using a tail-recursive accumulator-passing function and a `termination_by` clause.
- Reimplement `Array.map`, `Array.find`, and the `[ForM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#ForM___mk)` instance using `for`` ... ``in`` ...` loops in the identity monad and compare the resulting code.
- Reimplement array reversal using a `for`` ... ``in`` ...` loop in the identity monad. Compare it to the tail-recursive function.

---



## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.4. More Inequalities {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-84-more-inequalities}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/More-Inequalities/

Lean's built-in proof automation is sufficient to check that `arrayMapHelper` and `findHelper` terminate.
All that was needed was to provide an expression whose value decreases with each recursive call.
However, Lean's built-in automation is not magic, and it often needs some help.

### 8.4.1. Merge Sort {#fpil-merge-sort}

One example of a function whose termination proof is non-trivial is merge sort on `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`.
Merge sort consists of two phases: first, a list is split in half.
Each half is sorted using merge sort, and then the results are merged using a function that combines two sorted lists into a larger sorted list.
The base cases are the empty list and the singleton list, both of which are already considered to be sorted.

To merge two sorted lists, there are two basic cases to consider:

1. If one of the input lists is empty, then the result is the other list.
2. If both lists are non-empty, then their heads should be compared. The result of the function is the smaller of the two heads, followed by the result of merging the remaining entries of both lists.

This is not structurally recursive on either list.
The recursion terminates because an entry is removed from one of the two lists in each recursive call, but it could be either list.
Behind the scenes, Lean uses this fact to prove that it terminates:

```lean
def merge [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs, ys [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [], _ => ys
| _, [] => xs
| x'::xs', y'::ys' =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [Ord.compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) x' y' [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) | [.eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) => x' :: [merge]](#fpil-merge) xs' (y' :: ys')
| [.gt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) => y' :: [merge]](#fpil-merge) (x'::xs') ys'
```

A simple way to split a list is to add each entry in the input list to two alternating output lists:

```lean
def splitList (lst : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α × [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) lst [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => ([], [])
| x :: xs =>
let (a, b) := splitList xs
(x :: b, a)
```

This splitting function is structurally recursive.

Merge sort checks whether a base case has been reached.
If so, it returns the input list.
If not, it splits the input, and merges the result of sorting each half:

```lean
def mergeSort [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < 2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => []
| [x] => [x]
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let halves := splitList xs
[merge]](#fpil-merge) (mergeSort halves.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)) (mergeSort halves.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

Lean's pattern match compiler is able to tell that the assumption `h` introduced by the `if` that tests whether `xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < 2` rules out lists longer than one entry, so there is no “missing cases” error.
However, even though this program always terminates, it is not structurally recursive, and Lean is unable to automatically discover a decreasing measure:

```lean
fail to show termination for
  mergeSort
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Not considering parameter α of mergeSort:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
Not considering parameter #2 of mergeSort:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
Cannot use parameter xs:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    mergeSort halves.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)


Could not find a decreasing measure.
The basic measures relate at each recursive call as follows:
(<, ≤, =: relation proved, ? all proofs failed, _: no proof attempted)
            xs #1
1) 70:11-31  ?  ?
2) 70:34-54  _  _

#1: xs.length

Please use `termination_by` to specify a decreasing measure.
```

The reason it terminates is that `splitList` always returns lists that are shorter than its input, at least when applied to lists that contain at least two elements.
Thus, the length of `halves.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` and `halves.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` are less than the length of `xs`.
This can be expressed using a `termination_by` clause:

```lean
def mergeSort [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < 2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => []
| [x] => [x]
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let halves := splitList xs
[merge]](#fpil-merge) (mergeSort halves.[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)) (mergeSort halves.[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
termination_by xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

With this clause, the error message changes.
Instead of complaining that the function isn't structurally recursive, Lean instead points out that it was unable to automatically prove that `(splitList xs).fst.length < xs.length`:

```lean
failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
α:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αh:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 2halves:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α := splitList xs⊢ (splitList xs).[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

### 8.4.2. Splitting a List Makes it Shorter {#fpil-splitting-shortens}

It will also be necessary to prove that `(splitList xs).snd.length < xs.length`.
Because `splitList` alternates between adding entries to the two lists, it is easiest to prove both statements at once, so the structure of the proof can follow the algorithm used to implement `splitList`.
In other words, it is easiest to prove that `∀(lst : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α), (splitList lst).[fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < lst.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) ∧ (splitList lst).[snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < lst.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)`.

Unfortunately, the statement is false.
In particular, `splitList []` is `([], [])`. Both output lists have length `0`, which is not less than `0`, the length of the input list.
Similarly, `splitList ["basalt"]` evaluates to `(["basalt"], [])`, and `["basalt"]` is not shorter than `["basalt"]`.
However, `splitList ["basalt", "granite"]` evaluates to `(["basalt"], ["granite"])`, and both of these output lists are shorter than the input list.

It turns out that the lengths of the output lists are always less than or equal to the length of the input list, but they are only strictly shorter when the input list contains at least two entries.
It turns out to be easiest to prove the former statement, then extend it to the latter statement.
Begin with a theorem statement:


Because `splitList` is structurally recursive on the list, the proof should use induction.
The structural recursion in `splitList` fits a proof by induction perfectly: the base case of the induction matches the base case of the recursion, and the inductive step matches the recursive call.
The `induction` tactic gives two goals:

The goal for the `[nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` case can be proved by invoking the simplifier and instructing it to unfold the definition of `splitList`, because the length of the empty list is less than or equal to the length of the empty list.
Similarly, simplifying with `splitList` in the `[cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` case places `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` around the lengths in the goal:

This is because the call to `[List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)` consumes the head of the list `x :: xs`, converting it to a `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, in both the length of the input list and the length of the first output list.

Writing `A ∧ B` in Lean is short for `[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) A B`.
`And` is a structure type in the `Prop` universe:

```lean
structure And (a b : Prop) : Prop where
intro ::
left : a
right : b
```

In other words, a proof of `A ∧ B` consists of the `[And.intro]](#fpil-AndDef___And___intro)` constructor applied to a proof of `A` in the `left` field and a proof of `B` in the `right` field.

The `cases` tactic allows a proof to consider each constructor of a datatype or each potential proof of a proposition in turn.
It corresponds to a `match` expression without recursion.
Using `cases` on a structure results in the structure being broken apart, with an assumption added for each field of the structure, just as a pattern match expression extracts the field of a structure for use in a program.
Because structures have only one constructor, using `cases` on a structure does not result in additional goals.

Because `ih` is a proof of `List.length (splitList xs).fst ≤ List.length xs ∧ List.length (splitList xs).snd ≤ List.length xs`, using `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) ih` results in an assumption that `List.length (splitList xs).fst ≤ List.length xs` and an assumption that `List.length (splitList xs).snd ≤ List.length xs`:

The `right` goal resembles the `right✝` assumption, except the goal adds a `+ 1` only to the length of the input list.
It's time to prove that the inequality holds.

#### 8.4.2.1. Adding One to the Greater Side {#fpil-le-succ-of-le}

The inequality needed to prove `[splitList_shorter_le]](#fpil-splitList_shorter_le)` is `∀(n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), n ≤ m → n ≤ m + 1`.
The incoming assumption that `n ≤ m` essentially tracks the difference between `n` and `m` in the number of `[Nat.le.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)` constructors.
Thus, the proof should add an extra `[Nat.le.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)` in the base case.

Starting out, the statement reads:


To reveal what's going on behind the scenes, the `apply` and `exact` tactics can be used to indicate exactly which constructor is being applied.
The `apply` tactic solves the current goal by applying a function or constructor whose return type matches, creating new goals for each argument that was not provided, while `exact` fails if any new goals would be needed:

In this short tactic script, both goals introduced by `induction` are addressed using `[repeat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#repeat) ([first](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#first) | [constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor) | [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption))`.
The tactic `first | T1 | T2 | ... | Tn` means to use try `T1` through `Tn` in order, using the first tactic that succeeds.
In other words, `[repeat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#repeat) ([first](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#first) | [constructor](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#constructor) | [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption))` applies constructors as long as it can, and then attempts to solve the goal using an assumption.

The proof can be shortened even further by using `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)`, which includes a solver for linear arithmetic:


Finally, the proof can be written as a recursive function:

```lean
theorem Nat.le_succ_of_le : n ≤ m → n ≤ m + 1
| [.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) => [.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) [.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)
| [.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) h => [.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) ([Nat.le_succ_of_le]](#fpil-Extras___NoTac___Nat___le_succ_of_le) h)
```

Each style of proof can be appropriate to different circumstances.
The detailed proof script is useful in cases where beginners may be reading the code, or where the steps of the proof provide some kind of insight.
The short, highly-automated proof script is typically easier to maintain, because automation is frequently both flexible and robust in the face of small changes to definitions and datatypes.
The recursive function is typically both harder to understand from the perspective of mathematical proofs and harder to maintain, but it can be a useful bridge for programmers who are beginning to work with interactive theorem proving.

The next step is to return to the actual theorem that is needed to prove that merge sort terminates: that so long as a list has at least two entries, both results of splitting it are strictly shorter.

Pattern matching works just as well in tactic scripts as it does in programs.
Because `lst` has at least two entries, they can be exposed with `match`, which also refines the type through dependent pattern matching:

### 8.4.3. Merge Sort Terminates {#fpil-merge-sort-terminates}

Merge sort has two recursive calls, one for each sub-list returned by `splitList`.
Each recursive call will require a proof that the length of the list being passed to it is shorter than the length of the input list.
It's usually convenient to write a termination proof in two steps: first, write down the propositions that will allow Lean to verify termination, and then prove them.
Otherwise, it's possible to put a lot of effort into proving the propositions, only to find out that they aren't quite what's needed to establish that the recursive calls are on smaller inputs.

The `sorry` tactic can prove any goal, even false ones.
It isn't intended for use in production code or final proofs, but it is a convenient way to “sketch out” a proof or program ahead of time.
Any definitions or theorems that use `sorry` are annotated with a warning.

The initial sketch of `mergeSort`'s termination argument that uses `sorry` can be written by copying the goals that Lean couldn't prove into `have`-expressions.
In Lean, `have` is similar to `let`.
When using `have`, the name is optional.
Typically, `let` is used to define names that refer to interesting values, while `have` is used to locally prove propositions that can be found when Lean is searching for evidence that an array lookup is in-bounds or that a function terminates.

```lean
def mergeSort [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < 2 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => []
| [x] => [x]
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let halves := splitList xs
```

```lean
declaration uses `sorry`
```

There is one promising assumption available: `h : ¬List.length xs < 2`, which comes from the `if`.
Clearly, if it is not the case that `xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) < 2`, then `xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) ≥ 2`.
The `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` tactic solves this goal, and the program is now complete:

```lean
| [] => []
| [x] => [x]
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
```
