### 8.4.4. Division as Iterated Subtraction {#fpil-division-as-iterated-subtraction}

Just as multiplication is iterated addition and exponentiation is iterated multiplication, division can be understood as iterated subtraction.
The [very first description of recursive functions in this book]](#fpil-recursive-functions) presents a version of division that terminates when the divisor is not zero, but that Lean does not accept.
Proving that division terminates requires the use of a fact about inequalities.

Lean cannot prove that this definition of division terminates:

```lean
def div (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) n < k [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
1 + div (n - k) k
```

```lean
fail to show termination for
  div
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Not considering parameter k of div:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    div [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk)n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k


failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
k n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) k⊢ n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) k [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n
```

That's a good thing, because it doesn't!
When `k` is `0`, value of `n` does not decrease, so the program is an infinite loop.

Rewriting the function to take evidence that `k` is not `0` allows Lean to automatically prove termination:

```lean
def div (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (ok : k ≠ 0) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : n < k [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
1 + div (n - k) k ok
```

This definition of `div` terminates because the first argument `n` is smaller on each recursive call.
This can be expressed using a `termination_by` clause:

```lean
def div (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (ok : k ≠ 0) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : n < k [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
0
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
1 + div (n - k) k ok
termination_by n
```

### 8.4.5. Exercises {#fpil-inequalities-exercises}

Prove the following theorems without using `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)`:

- For all natural numbers `n`, `0 < n + 1`.
- For all natural numbers `n`, `0 \leq n`.
- For all natural numbers `n` and `k`, `(n + 1) - (k + 1) = n - k`
- For all natural numbers `n` and `k`, if `k < n` then `n \neq 0`
- For all natural numbers `n`, `n - n = 0`
- For all natural numbers `n` and `k`, if `n + 1 < k` then `n < k`

## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.5. Bounded Numbers {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-85-bounded-numbers}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/Bounded-Numbers/

The `[GetElem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem___mk)` instance for `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` requires a proof that the provided `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is smaller than the array.
In practice, these proofs often end up being passed to functions along with the indices.
Rather than passing an index and a proof separately, a type called `Fin` can be used to bundle up the index and the proof into a single value.
This can make code easier to read.

The type `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n` represents numbers that are strictly less than `n`.
In other words, `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 3` describes `0`, `1`, and `2`, while `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 0` has no values at all.
The definition of `Fin` resembles `[Subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk)`, as a `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n` is a structure that contains a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and a proof that it is less than `n`:

```lean
structure Fin (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
isLt : [LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) val n
```

Lean includes instances of `ToString` and `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` that allow `Fin` values to be conveniently used as numbers.
In other words, the output of `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (5 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 8)` is `5`, rather than something like `{val := 5, isLt := _}`.

Instead of failing when the provided number is larger than the bound, the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance for `Fin` returns a value modulo the bound.
This means that `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (45 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 10)` results in `5` rather than a compile-time error.

In a return type, a `Fin` returned as a found index makes its connection to the data structure in which it was found more clear.
The `Array.find` in the [previous section]](#fpil-proving-termination) returns an index that the caller cannot immediately use to perform lookups into the array, because the information about its validity has been lost.
A more specific type results in a value that can be used without making the program significantly more complicated:

```lean
def findHelper (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) × α) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
let x := arr[i]
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse)
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (⟨i, h⟩, x)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [findHelper]](#fpil-Finny___findHelper) arr p (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

```lean
def Array.find (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) × α) :=
[findHelper]](#fpil-Finny___findHelper) arr p 0
```

### 8.5.1. Exercise {#fpil-Fin-exercises}

Write a function `Fin.next? : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n)` that returns the next largest `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` when it would be in bounds, or `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` if not.
Check that

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 8).next?
```

outputs

```lean
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 4
```

and that

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (7 : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 8).next?
```

outputs

```lean
[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.6. Insertion Sort and Array Mutation {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-86-insertion-sort-and-array-mutation}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/Insertion-Sort-and-Array-Mutation/

While insertion sort does not have the optimal worst-case time complexity for a sorting algorithm, it still has a number of useful properties:

- It is simple and straightforward to implement and understand
- It is an in-place algorithm, requiring no additional space to run
- It is a stable sort
- It is fast when the input is already almost sorted

In-place algorithms are particularly useful in Lean due to the way it manages memory.
In some cases, operations that would normally copy an array can be optimized into mutation.
This includes swapping elements in an array.

Most languages and run-time systems with automatic memory management, including JavaScript, the JVM, and .NET, use tracing garbage collection.
When memory needs to be reclaimed, the system starts at a number of *roots* (such as the call stack and global values) and then determines which values can be reached by recursively chasing pointers.
Any values that can't be reached are deallocated, freeing memory.

Reference counting is an alternative to tracing garbage collection that is used by a number of languages, including Python, Swift, and Lean.
In a system with reference counting, each object in memory has a field that tracks how many references there are to it.
When a new reference is established, the counter is incremented.
When a reference ceases to exist, the counter is decremented.
When the counter reaches zero, the object is immediately deallocated.

Reference counting has one major disadvantage compared to a tracing garbage collector: circular references can lead to memory leaks.
If object `A` references object `B` , and object `B` references object `A`, they will never be deallocated, even if nothing else in the program references either `A` or `B`.
Circular references result either from uncontrolled recursion or from mutable references.
Because Lean supports neither, it is impossible to construct circular references.

Reference counting means that the Lean runtime system's primitives for allocating and deallocating data structures can check whether a reference count is about to fall to zero, and re-use an existing object instead of allocating a new one.
This is particularly important when working with large arrays.

An implementation of insertion sort for Lean arrays should satisfy the following criteria:

1. Lean should accept the function without a `partial` annotation
2. If passed an array to which there are no other references, it should modify the array in-place rather than allocating a new one

The first criterion is easy to check: if Lean accepts the definition, then it is satisfied.
The second, however, requires a means of testing it.
Lean provides a built-in function called `[dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)` with the following signature:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)
```

```lean
[dbgTraceIfShared.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared) {α : Type u} (s : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (a : α) : α
```

It takes a string and a value as arguments, and prints a message that uses the string to standard error if the value has more than one reference, returning the value.
This is not, strictly speaking, a pure function.
However, it is intended to be used only during development to check that a function is in fact able to re-use memory rather than allocating and copying.

When learning to use `[dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)`, it's important to know that `#eval` will report that many more values are shared than in compiled code.
This can be confusing.
It's important to build an executable with `lake` rather than experimenting in an editor.

Insertion sort consists of two loops.
The outer loop moves a pointer from left to right across the array to be sorted.
After each iteration, the region of the array to the left of the pointer is sorted, while the region to the right may not yet be sorted.
The inner loop takes the element pointed to by the pointer and moves it to the left until the appropriate location has been found and the loop invariant has been restored.
In other words, each iteration inserts the next element of the array into the appropriate location in the sorted region.

### 8.6.1. The Inner Loop {#fpil-inner-insertion-sort-loop}

The inner loop of insertion sort can be implemented as a tail-recursive function that takes the array and the index of the element being inserted as arguments.
The element being inserted is repeatedly swapped with the element to its left until either the element to the left is smaller or the beginning of the array is reached.
The inner loop is structurally recursive on the `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that is inside the `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` used to index into the array:

```lean
def insertSorted [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) i [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ⟨0, _⟩ => arr
| ⟨i' + 1, _⟩ =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) [Ord.compare](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) arr[i'] arr[i] [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) | [.eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) => arr
| [.gt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ordering___lt) =>
insertSorted (arr.[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i' i) ⟨i', byα:Type ?u.3inst✝:[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) αarr:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) αi:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)i':[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)isLt✝:i' [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)⊢ i' [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) (arr.[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i' ↑i ⋯ ⋯).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
```

If the index `i` is `0`, then the element being inserted into the sorted region has reached the beginning of the region and is the smallest.
If the index is `i' + 1`, then the element at `i'` should be compared to the element at `i`.
Note that while `i` is a `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`, `i'` is just a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` because it results from the `[val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` field of `i`.
Nonetheless, the proof automation used for checking array index notation includes a solver for linear integer arithmetic, so `i'` is automatically usable as an index.

The two elements are looked up and compared.
If the element to the left is less than or equal to the element being inserted, then the loop is finished and the invariant has been restored.
If the element to the left is greater than the element being inserted, then the elements are swapped and the inner loop begins again.
`[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)` takes both of its indices as `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s, using the same tactics as array indexing behind the scenes to ensure that they are in bounds.

Nonetheless, the `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` used for the recursive call needs a proof that `i'` is in bounds for the result of swapping two elements.
The `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` tactic's database contains the fact that swapping two elements of an array doesn't change its size.
Combining this with the fact that `i' + 1` is in bounds for the original array, `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` can conclude that `i'` is in bounds after the swap.

### 8.6.2. The Outer Loop {#fpil-outer-insertion-sort-loop}

The outer loop of insertion sort moves the pointer from left to right, invoking `insertSorted` at each iteration to insert the element at the pointer into the correct position in the array.
The basic form of the loop resembles the implementation of `Array.map`:

```lean
def insertionSortLoop [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
insertionSortLoop (insertSorted arr ⟨i, h⟩) (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
arr
```

While Lean can prove that a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that increases towards a constant bound at each iteration leads to a terminating function, this function has no constant bound because the array is replaced with the result of calling `insertSorted` at each iteration.

Before constructing the termination proof, it can be convenient to test the definition with a `partial` modifier to make sure that it returns the expected answers:

```lean
partial def insertionSortLoop [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
```

#### 8.6.2.1. Termination {#fpil-insertionSortLoop-termination}

Once again, the function terminates because the difference between the index and the size of the array being processed decreases on each recursive call.
This time, however, Lean does not accept the `termination_by`:

```lean
def insertionSortLoop [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : i < arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
insertionSortLoop (insertSorted arr ⟨i, h⟩) (i + 1)
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
arr
termination_by arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) - i
```


The problem is that Lean has no way to know that `insertSorted` returns an array that's the same size as the one it is passed.
In order to prove that `insertionSortLoop` terminates, it is necessary to first prove that `insertSorted` doesn't change the size of the array.
Copying the unproved termination condition from the error message to the function and “proving” it with `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` allows the function to be temporarily accepted:

```lean
declaration uses `sorry`
```

Because `insertSorted` is structurally recursive on the index of the element being inserted, the proof should be by induction on the index.
In the base case, the array is returned unchanged, so its length certainly does not change.
For the inductive step, the induction hypothesis is that a recursive call on the next smaller index will not change the length of the array.
There are two cases two consider: either the element has been fully inserted into the sorted region and the array is returned unchanged, in which case the length is also unchanged, or the element is swapped with the next one before the recursive call.
However, swapping two elements in an array doesn't change the size of it, and the induction hypothesis states that the recursive call with the next index returns an array that's the same size as its argument.
Thus, the size remains unchanged.

Translating this English-language theorem statement to Lean and proceeding using the techniques from this chapter is enough to prove the base case and make progress in the inductive step:

```lean
theorem insert_sorted_size_eq [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) (i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)) :
```

Rather than write proofs for both simple cases, adding `<;> [try](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#try) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)` after `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split)` causes the two straightforward cases to disappear immediately, leaving only a single goal:

Unfortunately, the induction hypothesis is not strong enough to prove this goal.
The induction hypothesis states that calling `insertSorted` on `arr` leaves the size unchanged, but the proof goal is to show that the result of the recursive call with the result of swapping leaves the size unchanged.
Successfully completing the proof requires an induction hypothesis that works for *any* array that is passed to `insertSorted` together with the smaller index as an argument

It is possible to get a strong induction hypothesis by using the `[generalizing](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` option to the `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` tactic.
This option brings additional assumptions from the context into the statement that's used to generate the base case, the induction hypothesis, and the goal to be shown in the inductive step.
Generalizing over `arr` leads to a stronger hypothesis:

However, this whole proof is beginning to get unmanageable.
The next step would be to introduce a variable standing for the length of the result of swapping, show that it is equal to `arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)`, and then show that this variable is also equal to the length of the array that results from the recursive call.
These equality statements can then be chained together to prove the goal.
It's much easier, however, to use functional induction:

In the final case, once the `[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)` is reduced, there will be some work left to do to prove that the next step of the insertion preserves the size of the array.
In particular, the induction hypothesis states that the size of the next step is equal to the size of the result of the swap, but the desired conclusion is that it's equal to the size of the original array:

### 8.6.3. The Driver Function {#fpil-insertion-sort-driver-function}

Insertion sort itself calls `insertionSortLoop`, initializing the index that demarcates the sorted region of the array from the unsorted region to `0`:

```lean
def insertionSort [[Ord](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Ord___mk) α] (arr : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α :=
insertionSortLoop arr 0
```

A few quick tests show the function is at least not blatantly wrong:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) insertionSort #[3, 1, 7, 4]
```

```lean
[#[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 4[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 7[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) insertionSort #[ "quartz", "marble", "granite", "hematite"]
```

```lean
[#[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)"granite"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) "hematite"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) "marble"[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) "quartz"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)
```

### 8.6.4. Is This Really Insertion Sort? {#fpil-insertion-sort-in-place}

Insertion sort is *defined* to be an in-place sorting algorithm.
What makes it useful, despite its quadratic worst-case run time, is that it is a stable sorting algorithm that doesn't allocate extra space and that handles almost-sorted data efficiently.
If each iteration of the inner loop allocated a new array, then the algorithm wouldn't *really* be insertion sort.

Lean's array operations, such as `[Array.set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___set)` and `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)`, check whether the array in question has a reference count that is greater than one.
If so, then the array is visible to multiple parts of the code, which means that it must be copied.
Otherwise, Lean would no longer be a pure functional language.
However, when the reference count is exactly one, there are no other potential observers of the value.
In these cases, the array primitives mutate the array in place.
What other parts of the program don't know can't hurt them.

Lean's proof logic works at the level of pure functional programs, not the underlying implementation.
This means that the best way to discover whether a program unnecessarily copies data is to test it.
Adding calls to `[dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)` at each point where mutation is desired causes the provided message to be printed to `stderr` when the value in question has more than one reference.

Insertion sort has precisely one place that is at risk of copying rather than mutating: the call to `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)`.
Replacing `arr.[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i' i` with `([dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared) "array to swap" arr).[swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap) i' i` causes the program to emit `shared RC array to swap` whenever it is unable to mutate the array.
However, this change to the program changes the proofs as well, because now there's a call to an additional function.
Adding a local assumption that `[dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)` preserves the length of its argument and adding it to some calls to `[grind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#grind)` is enough to fix the program and proofs.

The complete instrumented code for insertion sort is:

A bit of cleverness is required to check whether the instrumentation actually works.
First off, the Lean compiler aggressively optimizes function calls away when all their arguments are known at compile time.
Simply writing a program that applies `insertionSort` to a large array is not sufficient, because the resulting compiled code may contain only the sorted array as a constant.
The easiest way to ensure that the compiler doesn't optimize away the sorting routine is to read the array from `stdin`.
Secondly, the compiler performs dead code elimination.
Adding extra `let`s to the program won't necessarily result in more references in running code if the `let`-bound variables are never used.
To ensure that the extra reference is not eliminated entirely, it's important to ensure that the extra reference is somehow used.

The first step in testing the instrumentation is to write `getLines`, which reads an array of lines from standard input:

```lean
def getLines : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let stdin ← [IO.getStdin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___getStdin)
let mut lines : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := #[]
let mut currLine ← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
while !currLine.[isEmpty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___isEmpty) do
-- Drop trailing newline:
lines := lines.[push](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___push) (currLine.dropEnd 1).[copy](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___Slice___copy)
currLine ← stdin.[getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) lines
```

`[IO.FS.Stream.getLine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Files___-File-Handles___-and-Streams/#IO___FS___Stream___mk)` returns a complete line of text, including the trailing newline.
It returns `""` when the end-of-file marker has been reached.

Next, two separate `main` routines are needed.
Both read the array to be sorted from standard input, ensuring that the calls to `insertionSort` won't be replaced by their return values at compile time.
Both then print to the console, ensuring that the calls to `insertionSort` won't be optimized away entirely.
One of them prints only the sorted array, while the other prints both the sorted array and the original array.
The second function should trigger a warning that `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)` had to allocate a new array:

```lean
def mainUnique : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let lines ← getLines
for line in insertionSort lines do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) line
def mainShared : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let lines ← getLines
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "--- Sorted lines: ---"
for line in insertionSort lines do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) line
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) ""
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "--- Original data: ---"
for line in lines do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) line
```

The actual `main` simply selects one of the two main actions based on the provided command-line arguments:

```lean
def main (args : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec) := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
match args with
| ["--shared"] => [mainShared]](#fpil-mainShared); [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 0
| ["--unique"] => [mainUnique]](#fpil-mainUnique); [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 0
| _ =>
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) "Expected either \"--shared\" or \"--unique\""
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) 1
```

Running it with no arguments produces the expected usage information:

`sort
``Expected either "--shared" or "--unique"
`

The file `test-data` contains the following rocks:

File: `test-data``schist``feldspar``diorite``pumice``obsidian``shale``gneiss``marble``flint`

Using the instrumented insertion sort on these rocks results them being printed in alphabetical order:

`sort --unique < test-data``diorite
feldspar
flint
gneiss
marble
obsidian
pumice
schist
shale
`

However, the version in which a reference is retained to the original array results in a notification on `stderr` (namely, `shared RC array to swap`) from the first call to `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)`:

`sort --shared < test-data``--- Sorted lines: ---
diorite
feldspar
flint
gneiss
marble
obsidian
pumice
schist
shale
--- Original data: ---
schist
feldspar
diorite
pumice
obsidian
shale
gneiss
marble
flint
``shared RC array to swap
`

The fact that only a single `shared RC` notification appears means that the array is copied only once.
This is because the copy that results from the call to `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)` is itself unique, so no further copies need to be made.
In an imperative language, subtle bugs can result from forgetting to explicitly copy an array before passing it by reference.
When running `sort --shared`, the array is copied as needed to preserve the pure functional meaning of Lean programs, but no more.

### 8.6.5. Other Opportunities for Mutation {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Insertion-Sort-and-Array-Mutation--Other-Opportunities-for-Mutation}

The use of mutation instead of copying when references are unique is not limited to array update operators.
Lean also attempts to “recycle” constructors whose reference counts are about to fall to zero, reusing them instead of allocating new data.
This means, for instance, that `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` will mutate a linked list in place, at least in cases when nobody could possibly notice.
One of the most important steps in optimizing hot loops in Lean code is making sure that the data being modified is not referred to from multiple locations.

### 8.6.6. Exercises {#fpil-insertion-sort-exercises}

- Write a function that reverses arrays. Test that if the input array has a reference count of one, then your function does not allocate a new array.
- Implement either merge sort or quicksort for arrays. Prove that your implementation terminates, and test that it doesn't allocate more arrays than expected. This is a challenging exercise!

---



## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.7. Special Types {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-87-special-types}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/Special-Types/

Understanding the representation of data in memory is very important.
Usually, the representation can be understood from the definition of a datatype.
Each constructor corresponds to an object in memory that has a header that includes a tag and a reference count.
The constructor's arguments are each represented by a pointer to some other object.
In other words, `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` really is a linked list and extracting a field from a `structure` really does just chase a pointer.

There are, however, some important exceptions to this rule.
A number of types are treated specially by the compiler.
For example, the type `[UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)` is defined as `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) (2 ^ 32)`, but it is replaced at run-time with an actual native implementation based on machine words.
Similarly, even though the definition of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` suggests an implementation similar to `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`, the actual run-time representation uses immediate machine words for sufficiently-small numbers and an efficient arbitrary-precision arithmetic library for larger numbers.
The Lean compiler translates from definitions that use pattern matching into the appropriate operations for this representation, and calls to operations like addition and subtraction are mapped to fast operations from the underlying arithmetic library.
After all, addition should not take time linear in the size of the addends.

The fact that some types have special representations also means that care is needed when working with them.
Most of these types consist of a `structure` that is treated specially by the compiler.
With these structures, using the constructor or the field accessors directly can trigger expensive conversions between efficient representations and representations designed for use in proofs.

For example, arrays are defined as structures that wrap linked lists.
In compiled code, they are represented as efficient dynamic arrays, and applying the constructor `[Array.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)` to a list converts the list to such an efficient array, which takes linear time.
The field accessor `toList` converts the array back to a linked list, which also takes linear time.
This definition of `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk)` exists entirely to make it easier to prove things about arrays, and these conversions should be avoided in code that is intended to be run.
Similarly, `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` is defined as a structure that contains an array of bytes together with a proof that the bytes are valid UTF-8, but the run-time representation additionally includes a field that caches the number of characters in the string.
Applying the constructor to a byte array can only be done when the byte array is valid, so there's no need to check that the bytes are in fact a UTF-8 sequence, but the character count is computed in linear time.
The accessor `toByteArray` allocates a new byte array object and copies the underlying bytes, taking linear time and space.
Many of the basic operations on strings are replaced by the compiler with efficient versions that mutate the run-time version of the string when possible instead of allocating a new one.

Both types themselves and proofs of propositions are completely erased from compiled code.
In other words, they take up no space, and any computations that might have been performed as part of a proof are similarly erased.
This means that proofs can take advantage of the convenient interface to arrays as inductively-defined lists, including using induction to prove things about them, without imposing slow conversion steps while the program is running.
For these built-in types, a convenient logical representation of the data does not imply that the program must be slow.

If a structure type has only a single non-type non-proof field, then the constructor itself disappears at run time, being replaced with its single argument.
In other words, a subtype is represented identically to its underlying type, rather than with an extra layer of indirection.
Similarly, `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` is just `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` in memory, and single-field structures can be created to keep track of different uses of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`s or `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`s without paying a performance penalty.
If a constructor has no non-type non-proof arguments, then the constructor also disappears and is replaced with a constant value where the pointer would otherwise be used.
This means that `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, and `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` are constant values, rather than pointers to heap-allocated objects.

The following types have special representations:

| Type | Logical representation | Run-time Representation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` | Unary, with one pointer from each `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` | Efficient arbitrary-precision integers |
| `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` | A sum type with constructors for positive or negative values, each containing a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` | Efficient arbitrary-precision integers |
| `[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin) w` | A `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` with an appropriate bound `2^w` | Efficient arbitrary-precision integers |
| `[UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt16](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt16___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)`, `[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)`, `[USize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#USize___ofBitVec)` | A bitvector of the correct width | Fixed-precision machine integers |
| `[Int8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int8___ofUInt8)`, `[Int16](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int16___ofUInt16)`, `[Int32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int32___ofUInt32)`, `[Int64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#Int64___ofUInt64)`, `[ISize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#ISize___ofUSize)` | A wrapped unsigned integer of the same width | Fixed-precision machine integers |
| `[Char](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Characters/#Char___mk)` | A `[UInt32](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt32___ofBitVec)` paired with a proof that it's a valid code point | Ordinary characters |
| `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` | A structure that contains a `[ByteArray](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/#ByteArray___mk)` in a field called `toByteArray`, along with a proof that the array is valid UTF-8 | UTF-8-encoded string and character count |
| `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α` | A structure that contains a `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` in a field called `toList` | Packed arrays of pointers to `α` values |
| `Sort u` | A type | Erased completely |
| Proofs of propositions | Whatever data is suggested by the proposition when considered as a type of evidence | Erased completely |

### 8.7.1. Exercise {#fpil-runtime-special-types-exercise}

The [definition of `Pos`]](#fpil-positive-numbers) does not take advantage of Lean's compilation of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to an efficient type.
At run time, it is essentially a linked list.
Alternatively, a subtype can be defined that allows Lean's fast `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` type to be used internally, as described [in the initial section on subtypes]](#fpil-subtypes).
At run time, the proof will be erased.
Because the resulting structure has only a single data field, it is represented as that field, which means that this new representation of `Pos` is identical to that of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

After proving the theorem `∀ {n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}, n ≠ 0 → k ≠ 0 → n + k ≠ 0`, define instances of `ToString`, and `[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk)` for this new representation of `Pos`. Then, define an instance of `[Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk)`, proving any necessary theorems along the way.

## Programming, Proving, and Performance — 8.8. Summary {#fpil-programming-proving-and-performance-88-summary}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance/Summary/

### 8.8.1. Tail Recursion {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Tail-Recursion}

Tail recursion is recursion in which the results of recursive calls are returned immediately, rather than being used in some other way.
These recursive calls are called *tail calls*.
Tail calls are interesting because they can be compiled to a jump instruction rather than a call instruction, and the current stack frame can be re-used instead of pushing a new frame.
In other words, tail-recursive functions are actually loops.

A common way to make a recursive function faster is to rewrite it in accumulator-passing style.
Instead of using the call stack to remember what is to be done with the result of a recursive call, an additional argument called an *accumulator* is used to collect this information.
For example, an accumulator for a tail-recursive function that reverses a list contains the already-seen list entries, in reverse order.

In Lean, only self-tail-calls are optimized into loops.
In other words, two functions that each end with a tail call to the other will not be optimized.

### 8.8.2. Reference Counting and In-Place Updates {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Reference-Counting-and-In-Place-Updates}

Rather than using a tracing garbage collector, as is done in Java, C#, and most JavaScript implementations, Lean uses reference counting for memory management.
This means that each value in memory contains a field that tracks how many other values refer to it, and the run-time system maintains these counts as references appear or disappear.
Reference counting is also used in Python, PHP, and Swift.

When asked to allocate a fresh object, Lean's run-time system is able to recycle existing objects whose reference counts are falling to zero.
Additionally, array operations such as `[Array.set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___set)` and `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)` will mutate an array if its reference count is one, rather than allocating a modified copy.
If `[Array.swap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___swap)` holds the only reference to an array, then no other part of the program can tell that it was mutated rather than copied.

Writing efficient code in Lean requires the use of tail recursion and being careful to ensure that large arrays are used uniquely.
While tail calls can be identified by inspecting the function's definition, understanding whether a value is referred to uniquely may require reading the whole program.
The debugging helper `[dbgTraceIfShared](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/#dbgTraceIfShared)` can be used at key locations in the program to check that a value is not shared.

### 8.8.3. Proving Programs Correct {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Proving-Programs-Correct}

Rewriting a program in accumulator-passing style, or making other transformations that make it run faster, can also make it more difficult to understand.
It can be useful to keep the original version of the program that is more clearly correct, and then use it as an executable specification for the optimized version.
While techniques such as unit testing work just as well in Lean as in any other language, Lean also enables the use of mathematical proofs that completely ensure that both versions of the function return the same result for *all possible* inputs.

Typically, proving that two functions are equal is done using function extensionality (the `funext` tactic), which is the principle that two functions are equal if they return the same values for every input.
If the functions are recursive, then induction is usually a good way to prove that their outputs are the same.
Usually, the recursive definition of the function will make recursive calls on one particular argument; this argument is a good choice for induction.
In some cases, the induction hypothesis is not strong enough.
Fixing this problem usually requires thought about how to construct a more general version of the theorem statement that provides induction hypotheses that are strong enough.
In particular, to prove that a function is equivalent to an accumulator-passing version, a theorem statement that relates arbitrary initial accumulator values to the final result of the original function is needed.

### 8.8.4. Safe Array Indices {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Safe-Array-Indices}

The type `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n` represents natural numbers that are strictly less than `n`.
`[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` is short for “finite”.
As with subtypes, a `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n` is a structure that contains a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and a proof that this `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is less than `n`.
There are no values of type `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 0`.

If `arr` is an `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α`, then `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) arr.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)` always contains a number that is a suitable index into `arr`.

Lean provides instances of most of the useful numeric type classes for `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)`.
The `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instances for `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` perform modular arithmetic rather than failing at compile time if the number provided is larger than the `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` can accept.

### 8.8.5. Provisional Proofs {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Provisional-Proofs}

Sometimes, it can be useful to pretend that a statement is proved without actually doing the work of proving it.
This can be useful when making sure that a proof of a statement would be suitable for some task, such as a rewrite in another proof, determining that an array access is safe, or showing that a recursive call is made on a smaller value than the original argument.
It's very frustrating to spend time proving something, only to discover that some other proof would have been more useful.

The `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` tactic causes Lean to provisionally accept a statement as if it were a real proof.
It can be seen as analogous to a stub method that throws a `NotImplementedException` in C#.
Any proof that relies on `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` includes a warning in Lean.

Be careful!
The `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` tactic can prove *any* statement, even false statements.
Proving that `3 < 2` can cause an out-of-bounds array access to persist to runtime, unexpectedly crashing a program.
Using `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` is convenient during development, but keeping it in the code is dangerous.

### 8.8.6. Proving Termination {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Programming___-Proving___-and-Performance--Summary--Proving-Termination}

When a recursive function does not use structural recursion, Lean cannot automatically determine that it terminates.
In these situations, the function could just be marked `partial`.
However, it is also possible to provide a proof that the function terminates.

Partial functions have a key downside: they can't be unfolded during type checking or in proofs.
This means that Lean's value as an interactive theorem prover can't be applied to them.
Additionally, showing that a function that is expected to terminate actually always does terminate removes one more potential source of bugs.

The `termination_by` clause that's allowed at the end of a function can be used to specify the reason why a recursive function terminates.
The clause maps the function's arguments to an expression that is expected to be smaller for each recursive call.
Some examples of expressions that might decrease are the difference between a growing index into an array and the array's size, the length of a list that's cut in half at each recursive call, or a pair of lists, exactly one of which shrinks on each recursive call.

Lean contains proof automation that can automatically determine that some expressions shrink with each call, but many interesting programs will require manual proofs.
These proofs can be provided with `have`, a version of `let` that's intended for locally providing proofs rather than values.

A good way to write recursive functions is to begin by declaring them `partial` and debugging them with testing until they return the right answers.
Then, `partial` can be removed and replaced with a `termination_by` clause.
Lean will place error highlights on each recursive call for which a proof is needed that contains the statement that needs to be proved.
Each of these statements can be placed in a `have`, with the proof being `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)`.
If Lean accepts the program and it still passes its tests, the final step is to actually prove the theorems that enable Lean to accept it.
This approach can prevent wasting time on proving that a buggy program terminates.

## Next Steps {#fpil-next-steps}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Next-Steps/

This book introduces the very basics of functional programming in Lean, including a tiny amount of interactive theorem proving.
Using dependently-typed functional languages like Lean is a deep topic, and much can be said.
Depending on your interests, the following resources might be useful for learning Lean 4.

### 9.1. Learning Lean {#fpil-learning-lean}

Lean 4 itself is described in the following resources:

- [Theorem Proving in Lean 4](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/) is a tutorial on writing proofs using Lean.
- [The Lean 4 Manual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/) provides a detailed description of the language and its features.
- [How To Prove It With Lean](https://djvelleman.github.io/HTPIwL/) is a Lean-based accompaniment to the well-regarded textbook [*How To Prove It*](https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/how-to-prove-it/6D2965D625C6836CD4A785A2C843B3DA) that provides an introduction to writing paper-and-pencil mathematical proofs.
- [Metaprogramming in Lean 4](https://github.com/arthurpaulino/lean4-metaprogramming-book) provides an overview of Lean's extension mechanisms, from infix operators and notations to macros, custom tactics, and full-on custom embedded languages.
- [Functional Programming in Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/) may be interesting to readers who enjoy jokes about recursion.

However, the best way to continue learning Lean is to start reading and writing code, consulting the documentation when you get stuck.
Additionally, the [Lean Zulip](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/) is an excellent place to meet other Lean users, ask for help, and help others.

### 9.2. Mathematics in Lean {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Next-Steps--Mathematics-in-Lean}

A wide selection of learning resources for mathematicians are available at [the community site](https://leanprover-community.github.io/learn.html).

### 9.3. Using Dependent Types in Computer Science {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Next-Steps--Using-Dependent-Types-in-Computer-Science}

Rocq is a language that has a lot in common with Lean.
For computer scientists, the [Software Foundations](https://softwarefoundations.cis.upenn.edu/) series of interactive textbooks provides an excellent introduction to applications of Rocq in computer science.
The fundamental ideas of Lean and Rocq are very similar, and skills are readily transferable between the systems.

### 9.4. Programming with Dependent Types {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Next-Steps--Programming-with-Dependent-Types}

For programmers who are interested in learning to use indexed families and dependent types to structure programs, Edwin Brady's [*Type Driven Development with Idris*](https://www.manning.com/books/type-driven-development-with-idris) provides an excellent introduction.
Like Rocq, Idris is a close cousin of Lean, though it lacks tactics.

### 9.5. Understanding Dependent Types {#fpil-Functional-Programming-in-Lean--Next-Steps--Understanding-Dependent-Types}

[*The Little Typer*](https://thelittletyper.com/) is a book for programmers who haven't formally studied logic or the theory of programming languages, but who want to build an understanding of the core ideas of dependent type theory.
While all of the above resources aim to be as practical as possible, *The Little Typer* presents an approach to dependent type theory where the very basics are built up from scratch, using only concepts from programming.
Disclaimer: the author of *Functional Programming in Lean* is also an author of *The Little Typer*.

---
